maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion affords an opportunity, both with respect to an amendment which I propose to move later in the course of my remarks and, by what I say, to direct the attention of the house to a matter of great national importance at this time, namely the unexplained delay in the reconvening of the dominion-provincial conference, particularly in so far as it affects such matters as fiscal and unemployment questions.
No one in this house will fail to agree on the need for federalism in Canada. Our need, of course, is based upon a number of considerations such as geography, physical diversity, the stretch of our territories, regional differences in resources and economic activity and, of course, cultural diversity.
On the other hand we have in Canada a great number of common problems. All of us certainly want to continue to build up a strong nation, and we want to use the existence of these common problems for that purpose. These basic needs which I mentioned are illustrated by such expressions as "Unity without uniformity" or "Unity out of diversity". In order to be reconciled and to be satisfactorily met, they require federalism or in other words the assignment of specific constitutional responsibilities to different governments.
This requirement was recognized by the fathers of confederation, and indeed it was embedded in the constitution itself. It still exists today as a basic need, and for the same basic reasons as in 1867. Federalism is the only political system through which we in Canada can be united and continue to progress as a nation. But federalism involves the

assignment of specific constitutional responsibilities to different governments wholly independent of one another. However, the solution of many of these problems for which the modern state has to assume ultimate responsibility does not respect the constitutional division of powers, and cannot be found by one sphere of government acting alone. In other words, such problems are the joint responsibility of all spheres of government in a country like our own.
A good illustration of this is unemployment, where for a full and effective solution the joint responsibility of all governments within the federal state is required. Tax cuts, unemployment assistance, public works especially to give work in winter to unemployed persons, are all essential remedies capable of coping with mass unemployment. But their application does not lie within the exclusive jurisdiction of one sphere of government. This requires, then, the co-ordinated action of all governments, including the municipalities.
This illustration shows that federalism cannot function effectively to satisfactorily solve the problems facing a country like Canada if the different spheres of government ignore each other. In other words, interdependence must be recognized in concrete terms. Coordination of all governmental activity is essential. Continuing consultations and discussions between the senior levels of government in particular are necessary.
We have current problems in Canada which require concentration and joint action. We have to face at present several very important problems requiring intergovernmental discussion, joint action and consideration. One of those questions has to do with the matter of constitutional amendment. At the present time we have an anomalous situation. Parliament and the provincial legislatures can change our constitutional provisions in matters concerning both levels of government. However, there is no recognized procedure for amending our constitution, and the United Kingdom parliament still has the final responsibility of changing our constitutional provisions in this respect.
Now, is this not an undesirable situation? The previous administration tried to do something about this problem. It tried to solve it. It brought this subject up for discussion in 1950 at a federal-provincial conference which was specially convened for that particular purpose. There were lengthy discussions, and after those lengthy discussions and consultations, which extended far beyond the conference room, no tangible result was produced. The Prime Minister, good constitutional lawyer that he is, will recognize why that 66968-9-52J
Dominion-Provincial Conference was the result. It was because of the failure of certain provincial leaders who are now friendly with the present Conservative government in office. So it is the responsibility of this government to discuss this important question with the provincial premiers and solve this basic constitutional issue just as quickly as possible.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: To which provincial government does the hon. gentleman refer?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I was referring in particular to my friend's colleague, the premier of the province of Quebec. I would hope that because of his well known association and political community of interest with him he would be able to do something that the previous prime minister and the former minister of justice were unable to effect.
Then there is the matter of human rights. VvTe are going to be asked very shortly this session to consider a bill on human rights which apparently would be limited in its application to the federal field of jurisdiction. Quite apart from the substance of this proposed bill, such limitation I think even the Prime Minister, apart from his own immediate responsibility, would regard as being far from satisfactory. Provincial jurisdiction in the field of human rights, through the property and civil rights clause in section 92 of the British North America Act, is very wide indeed, and the government should at least try to find a formula which would permit joint action with respect to a matter so important as this.
This suggestion was made by the Leader of the Opposition in this house on September 5, 1958, when the bill was given its first reading. Here is what the Leader of the Opposition said, and his words are to be found at page 4652 of Hansard:
Indeed, as a result of consultation with the provinces it might be possible to widen the action so as to include both the federal government and provincial governments in a joint declaration on individual rights and freedoms. Then indeed we would have a powerful symbol.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman would excuse me, during the period of office of the last government is it not a fact that the various provinces were consulted with respect to this very important matter, and that several of them did not even deign to reply?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: I am sure if my right hon. friend says that is the case, that is the situation. My memory does not altogether agree with him, but I could be wrong. All I would say in answer is that that is no excuse now, particularly in light of the fact that some of these former objecting premiers may now be more disposed to

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: What was the reaction of the government of that day?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I am going to give the house its reaction right now. The reaction was that we, as the government in office at that time, had the responsibility for doing something. So we did call a conference. A preliminary meeting with the provinces was held on April 26 and 27 of 1955 to consider matters of mutual concern, including the problem of unemployment.
That is the answer I give to the right hon. gentleman. We called a conference to do the very thing which we now urge him to do with regard to unemployment and for other reasons I have already mentioned-reasons why this conference, called in the month of November and adjourned at the end of that month, without reconvening in January as had been promised, should now be held. In answer to the question asked by the right hon. gentleman we did exactly what we are now asking him to do.
At that conference which was called in 1955 we decided that a federal-provincial unemployment assistance sharing plan had become desirable in Canada, and that a special meeting should be organized to consider that plan. A conference on unemployment assistance was accordingly held on June 20 and 21, 1955. The federal government then put forward a specific proposal which was modified during the discussion with provincial representatives and later implemented as amended. Moreover, it was agreed that if at any time in the future the total number of unemployed employables on relief should

exceed 2 per cent of the population, a further conference would be called to review the whole situation.
Now I understand from the Minister of Labour, who will correct me if I am wrong, that there are no current figures available on this point at the present time. But is there any doubt that the total number of people receiving unemployment assistance at the present time exceeds that 2 per cent? Therefore I say that if we were asked what we would do under present conditions, on the basis of what I have just said we did do in 1955 the answer would be that a federal-provincial conference on unemployment would already have been called and conclusions would have been reached.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: We held one last July.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
We would not have held a conference and told the provinces we were going to reconvene it, and then allow a whole year to go by without any action being taken by way of conference or without any indication being given by the Prime Minister as to the government's intention with regard to this particular matter.
Since this government took office the floor of 4.5 per cent of the population has been removed, but the serious unemployment situation has never been discussed with the provinces.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Yes, it has.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
It has never been discussed with a view to reappraising the unemployment assistance plan, or in the light of the other provisions for general assistance in connection with this subject. The Minister of Labour said yes, it has. I want to be fair to him. He is referring to the discussions with the provincial ministers of labour. I am referring to a dominion-provincial conference dealing not only with unemployment but with those other matters involving joint responsibility between the two senior levels of government.
The conference to which the hon. gentleman referred was a conference between ministers of labour who met to consider a program of winter work. As the minister knows, for reasons for which I do not blame him personally the recommendations he was able to make reached the cabinet only many weeks after that conference had been held. Perhaps it was this delay which was responsible for holding up the announcement of the Prime Minister regarding the finance-sharing program of the government until just before he left the country, an announcement which so far as it goes is acceptable, but which really does not meet this problem at all.
Dominion-Provincial Conference
The real fact is-and I hope hon. gentlemen will indicate when they reply whether or not this statement is correct-that at no time since this government came into office, except with respect to the conference of ministers of labour held last summer, has there been any conference on the intergovernmental level, that is to say between the federal government and the provincial governments. Certainly there has been no federal conference between heads of governments on the scale we are talking about now. I heard the Prime Minister in the opening speech he made at the conference in November, and I remember very well what he said about unemployment at that time. He said at that time that the unemployment problem was a temporary situation-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Page?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I have not got it
before me but I will get it. This is from the opening statement of the Prime Minister at the public session of that conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: But what is the hon. gentleman reading from? It would be very interesting to know.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: I am reading from the Prime Minister's speech, but I have not got the page.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has demonstrated recently some very meticulous concern for precise references, and I invite him now to set the house an example by telling us the precise source from which he is now preparing to read.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I think what the hon. gentleman said when he rose to his point of order is quite justified, and before I resume my seat I shall identify the quotation for him.
However, the Prime Minister in the course of this speech did refer to unemployment as a temporary situation. That was in November of 1958. Unemployment was rising and, as we know, during the months of December, January, February and March it rose to an increasing extent until, now when we have a situation in which the figures are more serious. We wonder whether this statement by the Prime Minister about the situation being temporary did justify his belittling the existence of the problem.
The point I am making is that this was the only reference to this matter of unemployment during the public session of this conference. My genial friend, the Minister of Finance whose interjections are always so acute and ingenious-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
And friendly.

Dominion-Provincial Conference

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: -has asked me to give the exact page on which are to be found the words I used a moment ago, and I am now pleased to do so. I refer to the proceedings of the dominion-provincial conference of 1957 issued by the government of Canada, and represented as a verbatim report of the conference held in Ottawa on November 25 and 26, 1957. I draw the hon. gentleman's attention to page 10, the third last paragraph, the second last sentence of that paragraph. In fact I think I had better read the whole paragraph.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The third last paragraph on page 10 reads as follows:
I wish now to say a word or two-
Notice that; a word or two.
-on the question of unemployment. In many countries of the free world there has been a pause this year in the rapid pace of development and, as in 1954 and 1955, an increase in unemployment. You will remember in those years that while the percentage of unemployed in Canada in relationship to the number employed was much higher than it is today, that fact and those circumstances did not herald the beginning of depression. What actually happened was that there was a levelling off process which subsequently led to an even wider development and expansion program.
Then the statement continues:
When I say that, of course, I do not mean that prompt action must not be taken to meet-
And here are the words I used:
-what I believe to be a temporary situation this winter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend read the next sentence?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Yes, I shall be glad to. The paragraph concludes with this sentence:
This government has taken active measures to meet this short term situation and is taking additional ones.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
What my hon. friend has done has been to remind me that this government has taken short term measures for one winter only when, as of January 8, we were confronted with more unplaced applicants than at any time since the dark thirties. A temporary situation indeed. That is why we should have without any delay a dominion-provincial conference. If the ministers of this government want to be consistent with what they used to say when they were in opposition and, with what was done by the former government, they should immediately call a dominion-provincial conference to deal with this question.
Then there is another matter, the question of fiscal relations. We all know-and no one

knows it better than the Minister of Finance- that the subject of fiscal relations between the two senior levels of government in a federal state like ours raises a very complex problem for which no permanent and fully satisfactory solution has yet been devised anywhere. Practical compromises have to be worked out from time to time in the light of changing social and economic conditions as they confront the country, and as well in the light of the evolving allocation of responsibilities between the federal and provincial governments.
The financial settlement reached in 1867 and embodied in our constitution was in itself and by its very nature a compromise. At the time of confederation the federal government received authority for-and I now quote from the constitution:
The raising of money by any mode or system of taxation.
Provincial legislatures were given power to levy direct taxation within the provinces in order to provide for the raising of revenue for provincial purposes. These constitutional provisions which established the right of both levels of government to direct taxation did not appear sufficient to meet the financial requirements of the provinces, and a system of subsidies was devised as an additional source of revenue to meet the growing obligations of the provincial governments. And so, right from the beginning of our confederation and indeed as a prerequisite to its establishment, the principle of payments from one government to the others was recognized, practised and embodied in the constitution.
Between 1867 and the second world war the financial settlement reached at confederation was changed in two ways. First, several major revisions were made to the subsidies and a general readjustment was effected in 1907. Second, the provinces have gained access to new tax fields. This change is seldom noted but is nevertheless most significant. In 1867 the taxing powers of provincial legislatures had been restricted to direct taxation, and the field of indirect taxes had been reserved exclusively to the federal government. Since then, however, the distinction between direct and indirect taxes has become much less significant because the provinces, with the acquiescence of the federal government, have come to use many kinds of commodity taxes in the guise of direct taxes. I think the only sources of revenue which the federal government does not now share with the provinces are customs duties.
This entry of the provinces into the commodity tax field had not been contemplated by the fathers of confederation and it should be recognized as a major step in the direction of financial decentralization when we try to

appraise the evolution of our federalism over the past decades. But it must be noted that while this important new tax field has become accessible to all the provinces, the constitutional position in this particular is not too clear and the method of collecting those taxes which has to be used by the provinces at the retail level is not too effective, so that the several provinces have been reluctant to use that source of revenue.
This is rather important, I believe, and I point it out to the Minister of Finance now. The previous administration had agreed again to submit to the provinces an amendment to the constitution which would have explicitly given to the provinces access to indirect taxation. Approval of the proposed amendment was expressed by nine provinces. The province of Quebec, however, refused approval to that proposal which would have given wider taxation powers to the provinces, and on that account no constitutional amendment was put forward.
It seems to me today that this would be a very useful change to make in our constitution in order to provide additional sources of revenue to the provinces. With that objective in mind the government should review this suggestion just as soon as possible, as was done in 1951. It would probably be more readily acceptable at this time to the province of Quebec which through its premier is certainly more friendly to the present administration that it was to its predecessor. Moreover, the present Prime Minister promised to revise the current tax-sharing arrangements, and more recently several premiers have publicly expressed their dissatisfaction about the present situation and have urged the federal government to call a conference to deal with this problem of mutual concern.
Up to now I have sought to put this question on the basis of historical perspective. I wish now to briefly review some reasons that are incapable of attack as to why this government should now call the provinces together in consequence of a commitment it made to them in November, 1957 and also in fulfilment of promises made by members of this government in the elections of 1957 and 1958.
I want to examine this subject, and I am extremely happy that the Prime Minister is in the house today so that we may deal with the situation face to face and man to man. If there was one promise he gave to the Canadian people it was that if given the opportunity he would, when everyone else had failed, resolve once and for all this matter of fiscal difficulty between the federal and provincial governments. He gave the
Dominion-Provincial Conference world and the country the first intimation of this when he opened his campaign in Massey hall in the month of April, 1957. Before dealing with some of the things the Prime Minister said in that speech I should like to give something of the background of the meeting held in Massey hall, a meeting at which the Prime Minister, then the leader of his party, was only one of the speakers, the other speaker being that genial old man of Ontario, Premier Frost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: A little too young for you.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
My friend says, "A little too young for you." I suppose it all depends on the interpretation one places on my hon. friend's remark, but I would say perhaps a little too complicated for my hon, friend to understand. I have here a Canadian Press story which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of April 26, 1957, and I am sure that anything the Ottawa Journal would report would be a correct representation of the facts. The report has this to say, inter alia:
Mr. Frost started at 9.10 o'clock, drawing a burst of cheers with the statement that Ontario was welcoming John Diefenbaker back home. He was introducing, said Mr. Frost, the next prime minister of Canada.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: He was right, too.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
That prophecy came true and the Prime Minister now sits in the first place and looks at me now in full confirmation of what Mr. Frost said. But Mr. Frost went on.
Mr. Frost turned to a favourite theme-the unfair policies of the dominion Liberal government in distributing tax revenues.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Right again.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I continue:
The premier, who has a way of saying "Ontario" as if it were a caress, could see no hope of fairness for Ontario from the Liberals and proved the steadiness of his nerves when a balloon burst with a loud pop that made everyone but him jump. Mr. Diefenbaker, his national policy speech in his hand, listened attentively as the courtly Mr. Frost completed the listing of Ontario financial grievances ... In the warmth of his regard, Mr. Frost said he had looked with dismay at the rugged schedule of campaign meetings arranged for Mr. Diefenbaker and brought down the house with -"don't let them work you to death, John, we need you."

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: He was speaking for all Canada.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Then the story goes on:
Mr. Diefenbaker, pressed for time-
Obviously Les had spoken too long.

Dominion-Provincial Conference

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Too much.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I go on.
-started his speech at 9.55 p.m.
Now I want to come to some parts of that speech, because that speech laid down the basis of an argument which the Prime Minister made all over this country and which constitutes for him an obligation under the traditions of our public life to reconvene the dominion-provincial conference at the earliest possible moment or subject himself to misinterpretation at the hands of those who look upon what he does sometimes critically but understandably. Here is what the Prime Minister said in that speech as reported by the Canadian Press, and I take this again from the Ottawa Journal:
We believe there can be no national unity in this nation until there is a realization that the federal-provincial matters have handcuffed the provinces of this nation, have denied the municipalities adequate sources of revenue, have placed the provinces and the municipalities in a position where they cannot discharge their constitutional responsibility or permit the necessary development in their own territorial confines of the natural resources that there are.
The Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, speaking at the first meeting of the campaign went on to say:
We believe the provinces and municipalities must have the financial resources to carry out those responsibilities. We believe in the federal system of government. We believe that its preservation is essential to Canadian unity. We believe the federal system is today being challenged by the centralization complex of the St. Laurent government and that a healthy division and balance of revenues as between federal and provincial governments must be assured.
There is his declaration of belief, of faith. Now let us ascertain as I proceed in what I want to say today whether or not the Prime Minister has in any way lived up to this solemn declaration made to the people of Canada. On that occasion the Prime Minister went on to say:
We intend to form a government to immediately convene a dominion-provincial conference to bring about a settlement of these problems, not in the spirit of arrogant domination as displayed by the present government but in the spirit of unity and amity and with mutual tolerance and respect.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen say "hear, hear". These people who say "hear, hear" are supporters of the government. I ask them, particularly those from the province of Quebec, to rise in their places and ask the Prime Minister to carry out this solemn assurance given to the people of Canada.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
It is being carried out.
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).}

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Listen to what was reported in he Soleil of April 20:
(Translation):
Present fiscal agreements between the provinces and the central government were criticized yesterday evening by Mr. John Diefenbaker, leader of the Progressive Conservative party, who promised that his party, if put into power, will correct the situation.
In his speech delivered in Charlottetown, capital of Prince Edward Island, Mr. Diefenbaker gave the assurance that if he were entrusted with the federal power, he would immediately call a conference to redistribute taxation fields.
"Our desire, our wish, our intention, is to give provinces the share which is coming to them."
"While the provinces and the municipalities are moaning," the Conservative leader went on to say, "the government allows itself the luxury of a $400 million surplus".
(Text):
That was what he said in the province of Quebec. In Halifax he said, as reported in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of June 3:
A Conservative government will call a federal-provincial fiscal conference at which there "must be municipal representation".
In London, Ontario, on May 22 the Conservative leader, according to the London Free Press, "called for a new dominion-provincial conference at which the municipalities could sit in because the latter are in financial difficulties." I also have here the Montreal Gazette of February 20, 1957, in which I find the following:
The time has come for the federal government to make outright grants on a 50-50 basis with the provinces who ask for it for the construction of access roads.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: They are.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I continue:
The whole field of taxation will have to be reviewed to assure that the provinces and municipalities may have more equitable share of tax yields.
And so on and so on. The Prime Minister did say to the people in 1957, "Elect me and I will call a dominion-provincial conference in September." There was no dominion-provincial conference called in September. It was only as a result of the prodding of members of the opposition that one was finally called in November of 1957.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: That is so utterly untrue. How ridiculous.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I am going to deal with the Minister of Finance right now. We will see how untrue it is, because I have got a quotation of his. This realization that there had to be a new deal with the provinces and the government's intention to bring it about right away was expressed by the Minister of Finance in this way, according

to the Victoria Daily Times of March 31 of that year, 1957. Here is what the Minister of Finance said:
If there is one subject upon which the people of this country spoke with a clear voice on the 31st of March, it was on the subject of the position of this government with respect to the provinces of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Would my hon. friend give us the date of that again, please?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
June 11, 1958. The minister was speaking to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), and he may not have comprehended the full import of what he said. The words, reported by the Victoria Daily Times, are:
If there is one subject upon which the people of this country spoke with a clear voice on the 31st of March, it was on the subject of the position of this government with respect to the provinces of this country.
I say that is a correct statement, but what is this government doing about it? All that it has done has been to call the provinces to a conference which provided the government with an opportunity of making its own statement, but did not afford opportunity for full discussion with the provinces or the proposals that they had in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member indicate where, according to the newspaper report, those words were uttered?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Yes. I do not want to disturb hon. friend's nervous system, so I did not use the first words. The report says:
Speaking rather angrily in the House of Commons the other day-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Exactly; you see, my hon. friend is leaving the impression that these were words uttered out in Victoria. My hon. friend knows that when he is referring to words alleged to have been uttered in the House of Commons he is required, under the rules of the house, to refer to the verbatim report in Hansard. Reference to a secondary source like a newspaper report concerning something said in the House of Commons is inadmissible. You see, Mr. Speaker, why it is we have to check the hon. gentleman's references all the time.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: At least he gives them.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Because of this second brilliant and ingenious intervention by the Minister of Finance, I shall give him the exact page Hansard within a very few moments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Oh, you have not got it.
Dominion-Provincial Conference

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
If the deduction I have made about the Prime Minister's campaign in 1957 is to be regarded as possibly overstating the case, I want to call as my witness no less a figure than the premier of Ontario. The election, of course, took place before this date. On June 21, the premier of Ontario was interviewed by the Canadian Press. I now quote from the Canadian Press story appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of June 21, 1957. Here is what Premier Frost said:
Premier Frost says he expects the change of governments in Ottawa will make considerable difference on a number of questions affecting the province.
Then, the article goes on:
Mr. Diefenbaker, who officially becomes Prime Minister today, said during the election campaign that if elected he would call a federal-provincial conference this fall. The Ontario premier said the tax split should be top matter for consideration at such a conference.
Mr. Frost has said Ontario needs an additional $100 million to meet demands of provincial and municipal growth. If granted, most of that amount would go to relieve municipal education costs, he said Thursday.
Here is this Ottawa Citizen article with this headline: "Frost sees new look with new government". Let us see whether or not we are getting this new look. Ontario was not the only province that had views about this matter. Mr. Frost came down and saw the Prime Minister on many occasions. The Prime Minister will recall that on one occasion I asked him if he had lunch yesterday with the premier of Ontario. The Prime Minister said, "No, I did not have lunch yesterday with the premier of Ontario", but then the next day the newspapers pointed out that the premier of Ontario had had lunch with him earlier and that they had been discussing this matter, according to Premier Frost. Why had they been discussing dominion-provincial relations? It was because Premier Frost wanted the right hon. gentleman to call a conference, and a conference was called in November but was not reconvened.
Lest there be any mistake about-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Some more of your
personal statistics and personal revisions.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister introduces these light-hearted irrele-vancies, but they do not in any way extricate him from the obvious embarrassment in which he finds himself. Mr. Frost wants this conference reconvened. I have before me an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of June 6, 1958 and which says:
Premier Frost says a dominion-provincial tax conference is "inevitable" before the end of the summer.
818	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Conference
The end of the summer has come and this inevitability has not made itself manifest. The premier told a press conference that he was full of hope that at the conference Ontario would get an additional $78 million from Ottawa. The province asked for $100 million before the last conference and received $22 million as an interim payment.
In predicting a conference by autumn, Mr. Frost said he did not intend to provide any ammunition for Liberal leaders in parliament who have been pressing Prime Minister Diefenbaker for a statement on when the conference will be held.
But Mr. Frost shared with us at that time, as did the provinces, a desire that the conference be reconvened. Here is another story on January 14, 1959, in the Ottawa Journal:
Says government will call provinces to tax meeting. The Tribune says the federal government will probably invite the provinces to a conference in Ottawa to discuss tax-sharing agreements sometime next month.
This was on January 14 of this year.
Premier Roblin of Manitoba said in an interview that he and other provincial premiers have written *Ottawa requesting a conference and said he has suggested it be held before the end of February.
The newspaper said Mr. Roblin seemed optimistic ithat Ottawa will grant the request.
Then, here we have the same story appearing in the Winnipeg Free Press of January 16:
Premier disappointed; still want tax talks-Roblin. Premier Roblin made a number of remarks and then struck them from the record. He then continued :
"My official statement is this. We note this (tax agreement decision), but we will still press for continued discussion between the federal government and the provinces on this matter.
Then the premier of Prince Edward Island, as reported in the Guardian of January, said:
"Nothing short of a full scale federal-provincial conference will meet the requirements of this province," said Premier A. W. Matheson yesterday following receipt of a letter from Prime Minister Diefenbaker.
This was alter the provinces had learned from the speech from the throne, of this unilateral, give it or take it renewed offer of the Minister of Finance, and what the intention of the government was. Then, here we have the Toronto Star of January 20, 1959, quoting Premier Frost:
Premier Frost said he presumes on the basis of remarks by Prime Minister Diefenbaker there will be a meeting sometime this year of the federal-provincial continuing committee on fiscal relations and of the finance ministers.
No word at that point from Premier Frost as to the calling of a full conference, although in the month of September, as I have indicated, he was anxious that there should be such a conference called. I suspect that the Prime Minister and Premier Frost have gotten together. They belong to the same political


party. The Prime Minister would say, "Well now, Les, you are going to have a provincial election; I think the best way not to embarrass you would be for this question not to be officially resolved. I will find some dextrous way, and I am very dextrous in these matters, Les, of not answering the questions put to me by members of the opposition. We will weather this storm and at the end of the session we will not have called a provincial conference."
Then, in the province of British Columbia- I am revealing the opinion of most of the provinces, Mr. Speaker, and trying to indicate the national interest in this problem-here is what Mr. Bonner, the attorney general of British Columbia, said on January 28 as reported in the Province of January 29:
He said dominion-provincial conferences can do much to "improve our situation," and "certainly such a conference concerning the national economy is now overdue."
Then if there was any indication of what really was agreed to and of what the Prime Minister himself gave assurance would take place, it was a story appearing in the Globe and Mail the day after the conference was called on November 25 and 26. In the Globe and Mail of November 27, in an article written by Mr. Clark Davey, we find the following:
Mr. Diefenbaker stressed that another conference would be convened as soon as possible in the new year after the dominion government has had a chance to study the many proposals of the provincial premiers.
I direct attention to the words "another conference will be called in the new year". That was a year ago or more than a year ago.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: And the communique.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: 1 am going to deal with that. As I say, that was more than a year ago. Yet the Prime Minister day after day in this house refuses to tell us when he proposes to carry out a commitment as to a matter in respect of which, if we are to have satisfactory dominion-provincial relations, the federal government is but one party. The decision to reconvene the conference was a matter that was decided by all of the parties, the provinces and the federal government. I can interpret the present attitude of this government as nothing more than contempt of the provinces and of parliament itself.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Hon. members say "oh, oh". I well remember the words of Mr. Bennett, as leader of the opposition on this side of the house, speaking about commitments made by one government to another.

Here is the situation with respect to this particular matter. The Prime Minister says, "I do not propose to answer questions put by members of the opposition". He is within his rights in taking that position. No minister can at a particular moment with respect to a particular question be compelled to answer. But I say that in the spirit of our parliamentary tradition there is nothing which justifies a prime minister, day in and day out, in one session and another, refusing to tell parliament and the country what the government's policy is with regard to a particular matter, and particularly with regard to a matter about which there is the clearest evidence of a solemn commitment; and here it is. I refer to the communique itself after the conference, issued by the Prime Minister on behalf of the members of the conference. This communique I have from the Montreal Star of November 27. It concludes as follows:
It was agreed that a subsequent meeting be held as soon as possible in the new year in accordance with the proposal made by the dominion government in calling this conference.
Will any hon. member say that I was not justified in saying that the action of this government from November 27 up until this particular time constitutes contempt of the provinces and of parliament itself?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Don't be silly.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
But I am not alone in this matter. Even Conservative newspapers bear me out. Here is the Winnipeg Tribune of January 15, 1959:
Several provincial premiers, including Premier Roblin, have been trying to persuade Ottawa to hold new talks on dominion-provincial tax-sharing arrangements.
Most of the provinces are cliff-hanging with regard to the deal they may expect to receive from Ottawa during the months ahead. A new conference should be held.
Then here is the Hamilton Spectator, also a strong supporter of the present administration. In an editorial of July 3, 1958, it states:
It is one of the lesser disappointments of the Fleming budget that it ignored any reference to future relationships between Ottawa and the provinces and municipalities. The government can scarcely avoid an early conference to determine financial arrangements.
I say this to the Prime Minister. I hope that when I shall have finished-and I have not by any means finished yet

he is going to rise in his place and deal with this situation, and tell us precisely what the difficulties are, why this commitment to the provinces is not being carried out, and why he finds its necessary to dodge questions day after day as to the intentions of the government.
But it was not only in the matter of relations with the provinces that the Prime
Dominion-Provincial Conference Minister spoke of the requirements in two election campaigns, both of which I acknowledge were unprecedently successful but of which I am sure there is no evidence that there is likely to be any repetition. I refer to the matter of municipal relations. The Prime Minister felt keenly about the municipalities of our country. Wherever he went he reminded the mayors and the people of our cities and towns and in some cases even the villages what he was going to do if given the opportunity to form a government. I find that on May 3, 1957, in St. Stephen, he said this:
No one could say that municipalities or provinces had the tax resources to carry out their responsibilities.
Then, in a Winnipeg press conference, as reported in the Winnipeg Tribune of May 14,
1957,	he said this:
Municipalities have been placed in a position where property owners are saddled with heavy burden of taxation. He charged that continued centralization of taxation by the federal government was leaving the municipalities as the forgotten people.
Then near his own home town of Prince Albert, in Saskatoon at another press conference on May 27, 1957, as reported in the Star-Phoenix we have this:
The Conservative government, if elected, said the P.C. leader, would remove the crushing burden of municipal taxes.
Then right near Ottawa, namely in Hull, on February 25, 1958, we find this:
He also indicated prompt action on holding an "informal" meeting between the federal government and municipal representatives-he said it would occur after the election-to hear municipal views on their financial problems.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: We did.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
No. That was 1957. The meeting with municipalities occurred in
1958.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: That was fairly soon.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The quotation continues:
Such a meeting, he said, would allow the federal government to draw up proposals to present to the next federal-provincial conference for easing "excessive" municipal real estate taxes.
That is taken from the Canadian Press report in the Montreal Star of February 26, 1958. It is apparent that the attitude of the Prime Minister has changed. His changed attitude is indicated and reflected in the speech which he gave at the informal meeting of representatives of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities on October 6, 1958, the date that I referred to a few moments ago. Here is what was said by the Prime Minister, the man who in Saskatoon,

Dominion-Provincial Conference Hull, St. Stephen, Winnipeg and elsewhere said what he was going to do about the hard-pressed municipalities. Here is what he said to the mayors alter the election when he had them in the conference room not far from this chamber. First of all he said this:
I feel that I should also point out that despite the huge requirements of dominion responsibilities, Canada's progress has been such in the past quarter century that, after federal taxes are taken off, the national Income available to pay provincial and municipal taxes has increased by many times as compared to pre-war years, and the fraction of that remaining income taken as provincial and municipal taxes is less than it was before the war.
So far those are not words that suggest to me that the spokesman is the same man who spoke in Saskatoon, Hull, St. Stephen and Winnipeg during the course of the election campaign. Then he went on to say this:
I know you are particularly conscious of the burden of real estate taxes, upon which you are so dependent, and often they do look high In terms of mill rates, but in the final analysis taxes on real estate are paid by people out of income.
It should be realized that if average income, after income tax is deducted, is considered in its relationship to the total of real property taxes, it will be found that real property taxes are now, on the average across Canada, about 4 per cent of personal incomes, compared with about 5.8 per cent immediately before the war. Therefore, although I have no doubt the situation varies widely in particular cases, municipalities have on the average achieved a relative reduction in the effective burden of real estate taxes.
Here are the words of the Prime Minister in what apparently were his concluding remarks when he met the mayors of Canada in October last, a year after he said that he would meet them to resolve their problems. They came with a six point program, and they returned with nothing from the Prime Minister. His answer was: no.
What was this six point program? The municipalities asked for increased federal participation with municipalities in slum clearance. They asked for the allocation of National Housing Act funds to develop water and trunk sewer lines. They asked for federal aid with regard to street construction when the streets are part of an intercity or interprovincial highway system. They asked for the inclusion of capital costs in hospital construction in the operational costs of the provincial-federal hospitalization scheme. They asked for federal aid to the municipal works projects for winter employment; not the scheme which has been devised by the Minister of Labour (Mr. StarrL They asked for a scheme which would provide assistance, not only in the matter of employment and in the matter of labour costs but in the matter of supplies as well. Finally, they asked the government for the elimination of federal sales tax on municipal purchases.

Not one of those points was accepted, some of which, directly or by implication, were covered by the Prime Minister in the assurances which he gave in the course of the two elections, to the municipalities. They got the same kind of courteous treatment that they got from preceding governments, and they got the same explanation about the constitutional difficulties and the constitutional distribution of powers. They were told that the federal government had heavy social security obligations, heavy defence obligations, and because of these the Prime Minister said "There is nothing that we can do for you." That conference was, if any conference is, an indication of the real purpose for which the various assurances were given to the municipalities in the course of an election. Compare that last statement of the Prime Minister which I quoted with this one which he gave on May 30, 1957, at St. Patrice de Beaurivage, reported in the Montreal Gazette on May 31, 1957. The Prime Minister said:
A Progressive Conservative federal government would give the provinces and municipalities a larger share of the national revenue, John Diefen-baker said today.
The Progressive Conservative leader, in his first Quebec province speech of his current eastern tour, said this would permit the non-central governments to "discharge their constitutional responsibilities and to develop their natural resources".
Then listen to this:
Discussing his pledge to distribute more federal revenue to the provinces and municipalities, Mr. Diefenbaker said that "they are poor but the Ottawa government is rich".
All I can say to the Prime Minister is that that statement undoubtedly had the intended effect. It created the impression that a government which was rich would do something for these municipalities which were poor. He whetted their appetites, and if consequences flow from his present action he will have no one else to blame but himself and these words uttered on May 30 at St. Patrice de Beaurivage.
Mr. Speaker, what is the situation now? What is the record of the Prime Minister's method? Here we have a promise in an election speech in 1957 to settle this question with the provinces once and for all. No conference was called in September. One was called in the fall of 1957 as a result, I say again, of prodding by members of the opposition and the demands of certain provincial premiers. The record of Hansard for the fall of 1957 is there to prove what I say. The conference was called in November of 1957. It adjourned after two days. As I have indicated, it was to resume in January; the communique said so. The Prime Minister's letter to Premier Campbell

at the end of December 1957 said so likewise, but no conference has been reconvened.
What did the federal government do? What did this government do, a government Which criticized the so-called arrogance of the preceding government, which criticized a government which gave formulae which the Prime Minister said were on a take it or leave it basis? What did this government, which refused to negotiate with the provinces on equal terms, do? One day the Minister of Finance, in all of his glory, stood up in this house and told us that he had telegraphed the provinces and that he had provided them, as spokesman for the government, with further grants which would total some $62 million, and if account were taken of the Atlantic provinces, this figure would total $87 million.
First of all, that was a unilateral act. That was a decision arrived at not as a result of a conference, but as a result of a decision made by this government which for some reason or other is now reluctant to meet the provinces again regarding this matter of fiscal relations. He told the provinces, "You will be getting another $62 million." He told the Atlantic provinces, "You will be getting a fixed $25 million." There was to be granted some $7.5 million to three of the maritime provinces, and I think $2.5 million to Prince Edward Island. The provinces, on the basis of this particular unilateral act, framed their budgets, many of them only to find themselves now in the face of falling revenues in an embarrassing position. But I will deal with that later.
As I say, the provinces were advised by telegram, and whatever the Prime Ministei may say there is no justification for that kind of action. Incidentally, as we all recall, the figures used in the telegrams were not accurate. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Finance will, I am sure, tell me if I am not right in saying that the information given him as to the share of each province of that $62 million was on the basis of figures not provided him by any civil servant in the government of Canada, but by Mr. George Gathercole of the department of finance in the government of the province of Ontario. I see the hon. minister laughs, but this is an important matter. He can deny right now whether or not my statement is true. If it is true, it is an unfortunate reflection on the confidence that the Minister of Finance should have demonstrated at that time in his own officials. Then in the session of 1958, no conference having been convened, we kept on prodding the government, but all we were able to get from the Prime Minister was an assurance that there would be a conference with the municipalities.
Dominion-Provincial Conference
The next chapter in this sorry record of government failure was the further unilateral action of the government, this time using the vehicle of the speech uttered by the representative of the crown, to inform the governments of the provinces that the government would continue for a new year this arrangement which had been announced by telegram, which was both unilateral and irregular. This government, which has now been in office 18 months; this government which was going to solve this problem for all time, now deals on a year to year basis- on a unilateral basis-imposing its will and giving evidence of its distrust of common discussion and negotiation, and says to the provinces: here is what we are going to give you; if you do not want it; as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) said the other day to Mr. Fines: propose something else. Now we have reached the present situation and we find that the government still refuses to tell us when they are going to call a meeting of the provinces, as was promised and by their own spokesmen and supporters.
One of the things which the Minister of Finance has failed to remind this house in speaking of this arrangement for an additional $62 million was this: that it now turns out to be about half of that sum, and the hon. gentleman will correct me if I am wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: If I were to take up the time of the house by correcting all the errors in the hon. gentleman's speech I am sure he would not get started again for a long time.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: That evasive reply is characteristic of my former classmate who was more punctilious as a student than he has learned to be as a minister of the crown. But the answer confirms what I said-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: No, it does not.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
that this statement made by the Prime Minister in Winnipeg that the government intended to give the provinces another $62 million was not correct, and that the telegram sent by the Minister of Finance on the eve of the election was misleading because the $62 million has turned out not to be $62 million at all. It is true that the formula was raised. This government said that instead of continuing the formula of 10-9-50 of the St. Laurent government it would produce another formula based on a proportion of 13-9-50, that is, 13 per cent of income taxes, 9 per cent of corporation taxes and 50 per cent of succession duties. But, in fact, it is not any such thing. What the Minister of Finance failed to do when he sent his telegrams to the provinces was to tell them there was not going to be any

Dominion-Provincial Conference change at all in the stabilization clause. He was also very remiss in not telling them that the final sum depended on whether or not there would be an increase or a decline in revenues from these three tax fields.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Do you not think they understood that very well?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman asked me whether I do not think they understood that very well. I think that no one could give a proper interpretation to the meaning of the telegram which the Minister of Finance sent and which, shortly afterwards, he had to correct in this house.
Let us see what the situation is with regard to at least six of the provinces on the basis of the fiscal year 1958-59 in comparison with revenues received in 1957-58. Six of these provinces did not receive from this government what the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister said they would receive. That is the situation. For the fiscal year 1958-59, Newfoundland expected $25,214,000, and received $24,213,000; Nova Scotia expected $36,691,000 and received $34,595,000; New Brunswick expected $30,990,000 and received $29,518,000. In Manitoba there was an expectancy of $35,755,000 and the province actually received only $33,202,000. In the case of Saskatchewan it was anticipated the province would receive $36,552,000 and received only $33,885,000. In the case of the other province, $48,231,000 was expected and the actual yield will be about $45,836,000. Thus, all that the provinces really received, apart from some possible $30 million, was what they had already received from the previous administration, namely a guarantee that they would receive 95 per cent of what they had received in the preceding year. This was a guarantee put into the tax agreement by Mr. Harris in respect of the agreements which became effective on April 1, 1957.
And so, when the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister spoke about this great new change on a unilateral basis they neglected to indicate that there would not be a corresponding change in the stabilization clause, as I have already pointed out. But we must not stop there, because this is a serious matter for the provinces; it is the kind of matter one is forced to discuss in this house in detail because this government refuses to meet the provinces and permit them to have a discussion on these very questions which mean so much to the operations of government in the ten provinces. When one realizes that in a province such as Manitoba almost 40 per cent of the total budget is spent out of grants made by the federal government, and that the same is


generally true of all the other provinces with the exception of Ontario and Quebec, one can see how much this question means to the provinces. Thus we are forced to do in this chamber what the provinces would normally be doing themselves at a dominion-provincial conference.
I say to the Prime Minister that not only did he overstate the case in so far as the yield to the provinces for 1958-59 is concerned, but that the situation in 1959-60 will be that several provinces will receive less than they received in 1958-59. These provinces are Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The hon. gentleman seems to question this. He looks somewhat mystified at my statement. Does he challenge the statement I have just made that these provinces in the fiscal year 1959-60 will receive less than they will have received in the fiscal year 1958-59? I have seen this estimated on the basis of the hon. gentleman's estimates tabled the other day. The figures will support it, and I hope that when the Minister of Finance speaks he will indicate whether or not I have stated the situation correctly.
I have been giving the reason why I feel this conference should be called. I have put side by side the plan of the previous administration and the plan of this government with regard to fiscal arrangements with the provinces. We have not yet received from this government any firm statement as to what the Prime Minister meant when during the course of an election he said he was in favour of the principle of equalization.
We all remember in this house how in the winter session of 1957-58 we sought to ask the Minister of Finance to tell us whether or not he would agree to the extension of the principle of equalization beyond the year. This is something which means a great deal to the provinces because under the equalization clauses payments are made to all the provinces except Ontario, bringing their receipts up to what they would have been if the three taxes yielded as much as the average paid by residents of British Columbia and Ontario.
This means everything, not only to the maritime provinces but to every province in our country except the province of Ontario. Yet we do not know from this government which was going to resolve once and for all this matter of fiscal relations what its attitude is regarding equalization. The Prime Minister was the only member of the government who sought to deal with this question at all, and it was after his speech in Massey hall when he found the reaction in the west was such as to warrant the suggestion that he, the Prime

Minister, had been "taken in" by Mr. Frost who could get his $100 million only at the expense of provinces like Saskatchewan and Manitoba. But the Prime Minister is a good politician, and I mean that in the best sense of the word; he is dexterous, tactful and imaginative. He addressed himself to the people of Manitoba and said, "No, that will not happen. I am going to look after the poor provinces like my own, the province of Saskatchewan and the province of Manitoba because I, too, am in favour of the principle of equalization."
I ask the Prime Minister at this time what he meant by that. On what basis will he have the equalization clause operate? Will it be on the basis of the national average? On what basis will it be? We must know; otherwise it means no more than the friendly observation of Mr. Coolidge who said he was against sin. That is all the Prime Minister's statement means: "I am in favour of equalization but do not ask me to tell you what I mean by equalization because I either do not know or I might be embarrassed by what I should have to say."

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, am I not correct in pointing out that Mr. Coolidge did not say he was against sin. As I understand it he said the parson was.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I accept that theological intervention of my hon. friend and I shall accept his interpretation of what Mr. Coolidge did say. I am less interested in presidents of the United States than I am in the present Prime Minister of Canada.
I mentioned several reasons for the calling of this conference including the present muddle of fiscal affairs, the necessity of doing something about human rights and the matter of being able to amend the constitution in so far as it applies to the federal government. There is another reason why a dominion-provincial conference should be called and that relates to the problem of unemployment.
I appreciate that the Minister of Labour in the last few days has been very touchy on this subject. I understand that because I know he has been working extremely hard and I have a suspicion that he does not get in regard to this matter the kind of co-operation that his energy and his devotion to duty really deserve. Because of that I do not want him to think I am making any personal observations when I tell him that the situation now is even more serious than some of us have already been able to indicate. For instance, in looking at the most recent data, a press release issued jointly by the Department of Labour and the domion bureau of statistics dated January 20, 1959, I find in
Dominion-Provincial Conference the second paragraph a statement about which we should be reminded at this time and which I think is worth quoting in full. As I say, the Minister of Labour will understand the spirit which moves me in reminding him of this paragraph which I am sure he has by this time learned by heart. It reads as follows:
Unemployment continued to rise more slowly than last year. The number of persons without jobs and seeking work was estimated at 440,000 in December, 79,000 more than in the previous month and 48,000 more than a year earlier. Those on temporary layoff numbered 26,000 up from 18,000 in November but slightly less than last year. The seeking-work figure was 7.2 per cent of the labour force in December, compared with 6.5 per cent in December 1957.
The paragraph illustrates a worsening condition on three counts: more persons seeking work than a year ago, more persons seeking work than in the preceding month, and finally a greater proportion of the labour force without jobs and seeking work than was the case a year earlier.
As a matter of fact I have before me here -and this is available to all hon. members of the house and I am sure the Minister of Labour knows it-a document entitled "Comparative Data from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics Monthly Labour Force Survey, Revised Estimates, from January 1954 on". One of the conclusions to be drawn from this, if one looks at the last column, is that in March of 1956, 6.6 per cent of the paid workers were without jobs and in March 1958, 12.1 per cent were in that category. One could go on citing other comparisons indicating the seriousness of the situation. As the Minister of Labour, I know, has already pointed out to his colleagues, this is a serious state of affairs.
A detailed picture of the regional impact of unemployment is contained in the publication of the dominion bureau of statistics entitled "The Labour Force, December 1958" and on the basis of what is contained in that document we find that the number of persons without jobs and seeking work not only for Canada as a whole but for various regions of Canada reflects a very disturbing situation. It shows that the problem of unemployment is bearing down heavily on particular regions where the volume of unemployment is greater than the national average.
I wish to read into the record the percentage of persons without jobs and seeking work, representing the labour force in Canada, and giving the percentage for Canada and its regions. After he has a chance of

Dominion-Provincial Conference examining these figures I challenge the Minister of Labour to tell me whether or not my statement is correct. The figures are as follows:
Per cent
Canada	 7.2
Atlantic region	 14
Maritimes	 10
Newfoundland	 27
Quebec	 9
Ontario	 5
Manitoba	 4
Saskatchewan	 4
Alberta	 4
British Columbia	 8
The press release of January 20 to which I have already referred makes the following comment with respect to the Atlantic region:
The increase in unemployment was widespread in December and resulted in the reclassification of 13 of the 21 areas from the moderate to the substantial surplus category.
Since that comment was made on January 20 we now know there has been a mass layoff of 4,000 persons in the Nova Scotia coal mines. On Tuesday, February 3, 1959, I asked the Minister of Labour for the number of unplaced applicants in relation to paid workers for Canada as a whole. The question and the answer given me will be found at page 667 of Hansard of that date. The question reads as follows:
What is the percentage of unplaced applicants in relation to paid workers as at December 31, 1958, in the following Canadian communities:
I draw the attention of the house to the answer filed by the Minister of Labour in response to my question:
The percentage of persons registered for jobs at all national employment service offices across Canada to the total number of paid workers, as reported by the dominion bureau of statistics monthly labour force survey during the week ending December 13, 1958, the latest date such figures are available, was 11.4 per cent.
That is not my statement. That was the reply of the Minister of Labour.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. gentleman would read the rest of the answer?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The answer
covered two or three pages.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: I refer just to the next consecutive paragraph that followed the one just read by the hon. member.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: I do not have it before me but I want to be fair and if there is anything my hon. friend wishes to produce I invite him to do so at this time.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I should like to read the next paragraph in the answer because there is no relevancy between the two figures to which you referred. The concluding paragraph of

that answer as reported at page 669 of Hansard of February 3, reads as follows:
The figures of paid workers include those with jobs and those without jobs and seeking work but do not include employers, own account workers and unpaid family workers all of whom are included in the total labour force figure.
There is no relevancy between the two figures referred to by the hon. member.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The paragraph my hon. friend has read certainly does not help him. It really makes the situation worse because it does not include self-employed workers. I want to be fair to him but I think he will recognize that what I am saying is true. The true significance of my hon. friend's reply today and in the written submission he tabled-and it ought to be drawn very forcibly to the attention of the administration-is that it simply means that 11.4 per cent of the paid workers, that is, salary and wage earners, are registered for jobs at national employment service offices in our country. Paid workers is a less broad group than the total labour force. As I said a moment ago, it does not include employers, the self-employed and unpaid family workers, all of whom are included in the total labour force figure. In that sense, and I make this additional comment, the paid worker group measured against the number of unplaced applicants can be regarded as a more precise measure of unemployment.
What is my authority for this statement? I give as my authority a statement that appeared in the bulletin, Labour Research, of the Canadian Congress of Labour for January to April, 1958. Here is the statement:
For our purposes, it is perfectly ridiculous to measure unemployment against a conglomerate mass of workers, employers, the self-employed and unpaid family workers. The unemployed are looking for work as wage earners or salary earners, nothing else. So they should be taken as a percentage of the total number of people who have or are looking for wage and salary jobs. Who ever heard of an unemployed employer? Who ever heard of an unemployed self-employed? Who ever heard of an unemployed unpaid family worker? Of course there are unemployed people who have been employers, or self-employed, or unpaid family workers. But they are not now; and not one of them will present himself at an N.E.S. office or anywhere else asking for a job as an employer, or asking to be set up in his own business or given a farm, or asking for a job as an unpaid worker in a business or on a farm.
I would think that the statement in the Canadian Congress of Labour bulletin, Labour Research, would be regarded as logical and would not be contested by the Minister of Labour. On the basis of taking unplaced applicants as a percentage of paid workers, as I pointed out the latest data at our disposal

show that 11.4 per cent of paid workers are registered as unplaced applicants at the national employment offices.
In the face of this situation I say to the Prime Minister: Is there any overstatement or any extravagance in the suggestion that the Prime Minister must, without delay, tell the house what his intentions are regarding the calling of a dominion-provincial conference if for no other reason than to deal with the problem of unemployment on the basis of the Prime Minister's speech in 1955 and the recommendation of the leader of the opposition of that day that the provinces should be called together to deal with unemployment, a matter of joint intergovernmental responsibility in a country like our own? If the Prime Minister refuses then he cannot be regarded as having carried out his promise of seeing to it that "if I become Prime Minister no one will suffer as long as my government is in office."
If the Prime Minister, who undoubtedly meant what he said when he used those words, wants to give proof of that sincerity let him tell the house frankly now why, in spite of the agreement that there would be a reconvening of the conference, the government persists in not calling it and in not giving any reason for it not being reconvened. I repeat that in my judgment his failure to do so will constitute contempt of parliament and contempt of the provinces.

We have given reasons why a conference with the provinces should be called, and
Dominion-Provincial Conference before taking my seat I want to try to analyse the reason why the government has not met the provinces. Can it be that the government, in the light of heavy deficits now confronting it of at least $700 million on the basis of the statement of the Minister of Finance, would be embarrassed by additional demands on the government? We know what Mr. Frost's formula is now. Our formula was 10-9-50; the present government's formula is 13-9-50; Mr. Frost's formula is 15-15-50; then we know that Mr. Duplessis' formula is 50-50-50.

speechtext:
Is it because the Minister of Finance knows that if the conference were reconvened he would have demands from the provinces, including the province of Ontario, that would add to the obligations of the federal government by several hundreds of millions of dollars? Is that the reason why the conference has not been called? Is it also because the premier of Manitoba and the premier of Saskatchewan have joined together with the premier of Ontario in support of the latter's formula of 15 per cent of income taxes, corporation taxes and succession duties? The premier of Manitoba also proposes that the equalization clause should be tied in, not to the wealthiest provinces, British Columbia and Ontario, but to Ontario alone.
Is it because the Minister of Finance feels that now, having a deficit of close to $1 billion, we say-he says $700 million-he does not want to add to that burden? Is it because of financial reasons? If those are the reasons, then why should the government not rise and tell the house frankly that that is the situation. I think we would respect the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance if they took that course, but to sit here day after day and give no reason gives us, of course, the right to conclude that there are other reasons besides the ones I mentioned, and I am now going to give some of those other reasons. There is to be a provincial election in Ontario very soon. There is to be a provincial election in the province of Manitoba very soon.
