speechtext:
Mr. Frost told the legislature on Friday, "I am still after my $100 million and more"-he is even adding to it-"but I must tell the legislature that I have great faith in John and I know that his study of the program now is going to result in a real reassessment of the whole tax structure of our country, but I want my

Dominion-Provincial Conference $100 million and I am going to get it whether or not that reassessment justifies it."
Mr. Roblin is in a very difficult position because he is going to have an election too. He needs this additional revenue. He is in favour of the 15-15-50 formula, but if there is a dominion-provincial conference now and it is turned down what is he going to say to the people of Manitoba? He is going to come back on that agreeable train that proceeds from Ottawa and arrives in Winnipeg at 10 o'clock in the morning. He will meet the newspapermen and have to say, "Sorry, boys; I have a lot of faith in John, but he let me down this time." I know that no one is naive enough to think Mr. Roblin is going to take that course. The only way he can avoid taking that course is to have the genial Prime Minister do exactly what he is doing, and that is nothing.
Since he is not doing anything, the provinces are not able to discharge their functions, and the right hon. gentleman is not giving effect to the assurances that he gave to the people of Canada that he would, once and for all, resolve this problem involving fiscal matters with the provinces.
Then, I suspect that there is another reason. Mr. Duplessis has problems at home and so has the Conservative party problems in the province of Quebec. This greatly concerns, and understandably so, the rt. hon. gentleman who is not only Prime Minister but leader of the Conservative party. What would happen if there were a conference now and the premier of Quebec said, "We want 50-5050, John". What would happen if he went back to the people of Quebec and did not have his 50-50-50? Would there not be an increasing estrangement between the present government and the government of Quebec?
Is there still another reason? Has the province of Ontario changed its formula altogether? Mr. Macaulay, who is now a member of that government, says that so far as he is concerned he would completely change the basis of the tax agreements. He thinks that the present basis of allocation is fictitious, wrong and inequitable. He would distribute grants to the provinces on the basis of the gross national product, forgetting of course that the dominion bureau of statistics does not provide the gross national product figure on a provincial or regional basis. However, it may be that these speeches delivered by Mr. Macaulay in the legislature and in by-elections would be very embarrassing at the present time to the provincial Conservative party and to the other Conservative governments throughout the country.
I say this to the Prime Minister: In 1957, he went from one end of Canada to another

and, by the effectiveness of his speech, his capacity for debate, he gave a picture of sincerity which the people of Canada believed. Now, I am saying this to him as one man to another across the floor-my hon. friend now laughs, but he did not laugh during the election. He said this arrogant St. Laurent government has overlooked the interests of the provinces; it has not been concerned with the proper allocation of powers and revenues. It has embarked on a policy of centralization, but give me a chance and I will give you a new heaven and a new earth. That is what the Prime Minister said. If he wants us or if he wants the people of Canada to continue to have faith in his assurances, he cannot renege on this question any longer. We on this side of the house will, day after day, ask him questions about his intentions and the intentions of the government, until they discharge their obligations to the people ol Canada and to this parliament.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"This house is of the opinion the government should call a federal-provincial conference at once to deal with serious problems of common concern such as unemployment and fiscal relations."

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
We in the
C.C.F. agree that the immediate calling of a federal-provincial conference at this time is absolutely necessary. We believe that Canada today has an economic crisis and that the treasuries that have the most difficulty meeting this crisis are the treasuries of the provincial governments. Our country at this time faces widespread unemployment. This is a great burden on our provinces and on the municipalities. The provinces, by our constitution, are required to take care of the costs of education, roads and public health. They find themselves in an impossible position, with falling provincial revenues and with reduced payments from the federal treasury.
Is this government to allow the Canadian economy to drift into a deeper and deeper recession? Is the government to be satisfied with the very tiny effort now made to deal with unemployment? Is the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) himself satisfied with the government's winter works projects that have placed directly less than 20,000 people at work? Is the government prepared to allow the provincial governments to face greater and greater difficulties in obtaining the money necessary to carry on their services and obtaining money in the capital markets? Is the government prepared to allow the municipalities in this country to face higher and

higher costs with greater and greater difficulty in obtaining revenues?
There are many things that members on the government side of the house fought for while they were in the opposition. They were the champions of the rights of many Canadians. They were the champions of a bill of rights as has already been stated this afternoon. They were certainly the champions of provincial rights. Leaders of the opposition in years gone by such as the Hon. George Drew and the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), when he was in opposition, session after session, day in day out, castigated the former government for having gobbled up the lion's share of taxation revenues in this country. They castigated the former government for not having called, on a regular basis, a federal-provincial conference. How their voices were raised in this chamber whenever the government announced financial policy without discussion of the question with the provinces.
But anything that the former Liberal government has done in the past by way of insulting the provinces, by way of overlooking the provinces, is very small in relation to the arrogant attitude of this government toward the provinces during their 17 months in office. When this government came into power there was to be a new federal-provincial conference called immediately in September. The conference was not held until November. When the conference adjourned there was to be a new conference early in the year. This was not just a statement from the government or from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) or the Prime Minister. This was a statement contained in the official communique, the agreed upon communique, published at the conclusion of the conference. It was agreed that a subsequent meeting be held as soon as possible in the new year, in accordance with a proposal made by the dominion government in calling this conference.
There we have the pledged word of the federal government that a new conference would be held at the beginning of 1958. Was such a conference held? Of course it was not held. Were the provinces consulted as to whether this conference could be postponed from early 1958? There was no consultation. They were not asked whether they would like to postpone the conference. Instead, the Minister of Finance sent a telegram to the provinces. This is the kind of arrogant attitude from which this government should keep away. The telegram did not reach all the provinces in time. It did not reach the province of Saskatchewan. The premier was obliged to read about his telegram in the
Dominion-Provincial Conference newspapers and finally, I assume by some other means the communication was delivered to the premier of Saskatchewan.
There was to be a conference in 1958. It never took place. Does this government have any intention now of calling another federal-provincial conference? There is no indication of it. It was bad enough that the government served notice on the provinces by the telegram of January 24, 1958 that they were taking certain unilateral action with regard to federal-provincial payments. But after having been safely returned to office, after having been given the largest majority ever afforded a government in the history of this country, what is their action with respect to the provinces? With this all-powerful majority they say, "We are not obliged to discuss anything with the provinces; we are not compelled to keep our pledged word and have a federal-provincial conference. If the opposition moves an amendment we will call in the members and will vote them down even though the amendment is asking the government to keep their pledged word". Apparently their pledged word means little or nothing to the government. In the speech from the throne the government tell the provinces what is to be done. Here is what we find:
My government will recommend an amendment to the Federal-Provincial Tax Sharing Arrangements Act to extend for another year the increase made last year in the provincial share of personal income tax revenue.
Then the speech goes on to say that it is intended that a continuing committee of provincial treasurers will study the whole question of federal-provincial relations. Mr. Speaker, this is not good enough. Does the Minister of Finance not recall the many speeches he himself made when he was in opposition asking for a federal-provincial conference to deal with the extremely important questions which such a conference should now consider? Of course he recalls them. But when, as a member of the cabinet, he had the opportunity to make a recommendation that would go into the speech from the throne, he does nothing. There is to be no conference. The government says to the provinces, "Here is what you will get", on a "take it or leave it" basis.
I think this attitude is not only an insult to the provinces but is completely incomprehensible in the light of the statements made by members of the present government when they were in opposition. I have in my hand a statement that was made by the present Prime Minister on July 24, 1956, as

Dominion-Provincial Conference reported at page 6370 of Hansard of that day. He had this to say about a federal-provincial conference:
I believe this. I think it is lair to say that the attitude taken by the government at the last conference was an arbitrary one. The government simply said, "These are the terms".
This government did not do that. They had the conference. They let the premiers talk. Then after the premiers had gone home, they sent them a telegram. Instead of telling them face to face "These are the terms", they sent the terms in a telegram. The Prime Minister went on to say this:
No opportunity was given for amendment or for amelioration of any term. The recipe for a division of taxation was as final as the laws of the Medes and Persians; and how similar that attitude was to the attitude of the government in this house, which is that power makes perfect anything they do.
What could be more true of the government in power at the present time? Then the present Prime Minister, on July 24, 1956, went on to say this:
There was no opportunity for negotiation; there was simply the attitude of a feudal lord bringing into being a modern feudalism and laying down the law to the vassals.
That is not the attitude, that is not the consideration to which the provinces are entitled under a constitution which allocates powers as between the federal and provincial governments. That is not an attitude which will remove the road blocks which today deny Canada the development which should indeed be hers. I feel that even yet if there were an attitude on the part of the federal government to negotiate, terms could be achieved which would be acceptable and which would go a long way toward solving this difficult and complex problem.
We could understand the position of the government today if they were following a consistent policy they had taken over the years. But the government in office today is following precisely the opposite policy of that laid down by the Prime Minister in 1956. He said then that if such a conference were called,
-terms could be achieved which would be acceptable and which would go a long way toward solving this difficult and complex problem.
What is the attitude of the provinces and the municipalities? Have they endeavoured to co-operate with the government? I think they have done so. They have been most anxious to co-operate with the government. They have co-operated on the winter work program. More and more provinces are cooperating in the hospitalization program. By their action they have shown that all this government needs to do, in order to obtain co-operation from the provinces, is to show some leadership in the field of development and in the field of extending social services. If the federal government called a conference

I have no doubt that the provincial governments in attending the conference would take a co-operative attitude. As a matter of fact in this house the other day, in discussing the way in which the governments of the provinces have co-operated with the federal government, the Minister of Labour said that if the government had from members of the opposition "the same co-operation and constructive and reasonable suggestions" as they obtained from the provinces and the municipalities and organizations and individuals across the country, more and more would be gained. We have there from the Minister of Labour a statement that the provinces and municipalities have shown cooperation, and have put forward constructive and reasonable suggestions. If that is the attitude of the provinces, why does the government refuse to call a conference? Why does the government refuse to bring them in so that discussion can take place and action can be taken on the great Canadian problems of unemployment, high interest rates, agricultural crises, inflation and many others that are facing this country? The government's action has not been one to help the provinces or the municipalities.
We heard so much for so long of a conference that was to be held with the municipalities. It was not an officially constituted conference at all. It was a kind of listening conference. The municipalities came down and did the talking, and we expected that the Prime Minister would do the listening.
Just the other day Mr. Claude Jodoin, president of the Canadian Labour Congress presented for the C.L.C. their brief to the Prime Minister and his cabinet. After presentation of this comprehensive brief the Prime Minister took it upon himself to lecture the Canadian Labour Congress and to tell them that they cannot have it both ways. He said, "You cannot have increased expenditures and reduced taxes." If they had been reading the Prime Minister's speeches in the past, they would have seen that that was quite possible. The Prime Minister campaigned in two elections. He said, "The Liberals and others say you cannot have it both ways. Give me a chance and I will show you that you can reduce taxes and increase expenditures."
That was to be a listening conference from the standpoint of the Prime Minister and the government. The municipalities came here, presented their case to the government, and not only did the Prime Minister hold out no promise of assistance but he told them to go back home and to increase their taxes. What an original idea. What kind of advice was that to give in relation to very heavy

costs of municipal services. There is scarcely an authority in this country which would not say that real property taxes are very high and should not be increased.
The Prime Minister goes back, according to this newspaper report, to a comparison of real property tax-a municipal property tax as compared with net income-and says that before the war the percentage was 5.8, but since then it is down to 4 per cent. Why should the Prime Minister suggest to the municipalities that they should have the relatively high taxes that they had in a period of depression? Surely that is not the kind of advice that municipalities should be given by the Prime Minister of this country.
Of course, municipal taxes may have to be increased as a result of action by this government. This is the government that was going to have a federal-provincial conference early in 1958. Then they gave the lamest excuse possible why they could not have a conference, that the session was going on. Since when has a session of parliament meant that the Minister of Finance had to stay in the house all the time? Since when has a session meant that the Prime Minister had to stay in the house all the time? I do not know when cabinet meetings are held. Rumour around the corridor has it that many cabinet meetings are held with the house in session, and I think that rumour must be based on the attendance of cabinet ministers in general. I do not expect them, of course, to be here all the time, but certainly a federal-provincial conference can be held at any time whether parliament is in session or not.
One of the reasons why the municipalities of this country require action to help them now is the increased difficulty which they are experiencing in raising money necessary for capital improvements. One of the reasons we need a federal-provincial conference at this time is to enable the provinces to provide the capital necessary to carry on expansion in the provinces. Since this government has taken office, since the bond conversion program the cost of provincial credit has increased. The cost of municipal credit has also increased. This government is making it more and more difficult for provinces to finance. That is their responsibility. This government is making it more and more difficult for the municipalities to carry on. This is the policy of a government that was going to reduce the high interest rates which had been charged under a former administration. This government was going to get rid of the tight money policy, yet the rediscount bank rate at the Bank of Canada for Thursday last was 3.62 per cent, one of the highest rates that this country has ever experienced.
Dominion-Provincial Conference As I say, this government, by its high interest policies, is making it more and more difficult for the provinces to finance the programs for which they are responsible.
One of the additional reasons why we need a federal-provincial conference is to deal with the whole question of unemployment. As one picks up the newspapers from time to time these days one finds statements that give great cause for concern. The amendment specifically says that one of the reasons we should have a federal-provincial conference is to deal with unemployment. In the Montreal Gazette of February 7, there is a news item which says:
Some 42,000 Newfoundlanders-one out of every ten-are now on relief and another 75,000 are largely dependent on federal unemployment insurance benefits.
The article goes on to say that Newfoundland faces a public debt of $80 million, that Newfoundland has greater and greater difficulty meeting its financial obligations, and that Premier Smallwood had been in Ottawa in an attempt to get a sizable federal grant and to get money in keeping with the recommendation for an increase made by the royal commission. If one reads about the condition of the province of Newfoundland he sees that that province faces a real financial crisis.
Unemployment in this country is serious. It is serious in every province. In spite of the government's glib statements, unemployment is still with us. I have in my hand a newspaper report dated February 3, 1959, headed " 'We want work' flags in B.C. lobby march". It goes on to state that the British Columbia federation of labour, its leaders and unemployed workers have participated in a march on the capital of Victoria, pointing out the very serious unemployment situation in that province. They made the statement to Premier Bennett that more than 70,000 persons are without jobs in the province, and many have their backs to the wall. William Black, the president of the British Columbia federation of labour, recalled the terrible days of the thirties. "Mr. Black said that he would never have guessed we would return to the poverty of those days. Today the situation is much more desperate". A Conservative government in office in the thirties was unable to deal with unemployment in an effective manner.
A Conservative government is in office today, and we have widespread unemployment. They have no policy to deal with unemployment and remove the huge numbers from the unemployment rolls. We have a government which even has no policy to provide for an early federal-provincial conference in keeping with its own promises to the Canadian public.
830	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Conference
There are other things that such a conference should deal with. The provinces have great calls on provincial finances. There is room for much discussion at such a conference of the whole field of education. There should be a great amount of consultation and study in order to obtain a program of assistance from the federal government which will make education in this country available to all Canadians who are capable of acquiring a higher education. Then there is the question of a modern highway program. We are 40 years behind the United States in providing a system of modern federal highways.
This is the type of over-all program which should be considered at such a conference, and it should be considered in such a way as to provide employment, and to provide these very important services in an expanding economy. At a federal-provincial conference consideration should be given to the whole problem of marketing agricultural products and giving to the producers of those products a fair return for their labour. This government should not stand idly by while many farmers in this country are eradicated by vertical integration and removed from the normal type of farming which we have known for so many years. This is the kind of problem which should be discussed at a federal-provincial conference.
The premiers of the provinces have been asking for a conference. Premier T. C. Douglas of Saskatchewan wrote to the Prime Minister on September 19 asking for such a conference. And it is no wonder they are asking for a conference. Not only are they faced with greater difficulties in obtaining revenue by taxation and not only are they faced with higher interest rates on the money market, but they are faced with the latest insult contained in the estimates which were tabled in this house the other day which showed that the special payment which the great majority of the provinces would receive from the federal government for 1959-60 will be less than they received in 1958-59. Oh yes, these were just tentative figures placed there to indicate what the Minister of Finance expected to happen. But before the election the figures showed that the provinces would receive a great deal more money than in fact has accrued to them; and according to the latest figures tabled in this house the government does not hold out any hope at this time that they will receive as much money as was forecast in January.
A federal-provincial conference was solemnly promised. It was promised for April, 1958. The government advanced a phoney excuse as to why a conference could not be held at that time. The government said it


could not be held while parliament was in session because, presumably, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and other members of the cabinet were too busy. Of course, the conference might have been held last fall had the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance been in Ottawa at the time. But where were they? The Prime Minister was on a world tour and the Minister of Finance, not to be outdone, said: I am going on a world tour, too. They both went and I am sure they studied very carefully the financial positions of the countries they visited. Perhaps they studied the finances of the provinces of some of the countries they visited. They should have stayed at home, Mr. Speaker, and held a federal-provincial conference to deal with the problems of unemployment and inflation and to deal with the difficulties in which the agriculture industry finds itself today. But no. They have no time for the provinces; they have no time for a federal-provincial conference.
Between sessions this has become a suitcase government and a suitcase cabinet. As soon as the session is over ministers charter transport for a trip to as many countries as possible for a long as possible. They pack their suitcases and while the country faces an unemployment crisis and a crisis of inflation and while the agriculture industry is in difficulties no dominion-provincial conference can be called because the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are not available.
The present attitude of the federal government, if it remains unchanged, threatens the financial solvency of the provinces of this country. If this attitude does not change it will condemn the Canadian people in the course of the next three years or longer-the term of office of this government-to continuing widespread unemployment. If the present attitude of the government does not change, vertical integration will wipe out thousands upon thousands of farmers who are today still endeavouring to take a living in an ordinary way in the agriculture industry. We have often heard the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance when in opposition call upon the government of the day to hold a federal-provincial conference, to take the provinces into the confidence of the government and to undertake financial policies which would enable the provinces to meet their constitutional responsibilities. I call on the government and I challenge the government to do those things that it said, in opposition, it would do if the people of Canada placed confidence in it.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house is indebted to the hon. gentleman who represents Essex East (Mr. Martin)-should I say to the social and economic planner for Essex East-for introducing the present amendment into this discussion today. May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, of the terms of the amendment. The hon. gentleman moved, seconded by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion the government should call a federal-provincial conference at once to deal with serious problems of common concern such as unemployment and fiscal relations."
Mr. Speaker, will you permit me one preliminary observation about the breadth of this debate. The hon. gentleman, you will observe, speaks generally in his amendment about calling a conference to deal with serious problems of common concern. He has introduced at the end of his amendment the two subjects, unemployment and fiscal relations, merely by way of illustration. This is somewhat significant, Mr. Speaker, because you will recall that in the course of his two-hour long speech the hon. member for Essex East sought to justify his demand for the calling of a dominion-provincial conference at this time on many grounds other than unemployment and fiscal relations. Since he has sought to base his contention on these broad grounds I propose, Mr. Speaker, to meet him on his broad grounds and, indeed, on all of them.
I draw your attention, also, Mr. Speaker, to the similarity which this present motion bears to one which was introduced a year ago. I think this similarity portends a similarity of tactics in the course of the present session to those which we witnessed a year ago. It was on the first government motion in the 1958 session to resolve the house into committee of supply that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) seconded on that occasion by the hon. member for Essex East, introduced the following motion, which will be found in Hansard of June 2, 1958, at page 733:
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that the government has failed to call a federal-provincial conference to discuss unemployment and other urgent problems of common concern to federal and provincial authorities: and that the government has failed to give assurance that it would maintain or improve the principle of equalization of direct tax revenues of the provinces embodied in the existing law."
Mr. Speaker, you will observe in the first half of the 1958 amendment the purport and indeed many of the terms are those that are reproduced in today's amendment. Last year that amendment was introduced only a matter
Dominion-Provincial Conference of a fortnight before the budget was brought down and a two-day debate ensued in which, if you please,-it may have some bearing on the matter for the present-the Minister of Finance, among others as I recall it, took part. But when we came to the budget speech on June 17 I thought that the house had already heard sufficient on the subject of dominion-provincial relations. I referred to that fact and made reference to the debate that had occurred on the subject two weeks earlier. I said in effect that I thought there was no occasion, for that reason, to go into the subject all over again. And from that time on hon. members opposite have been saying, as they said during the course of the budget debate, "Isn't it shocking that the Minister of Finance did not discuss dominion-provincial relations in the course of his budget speech." It is extremely unfortunate that hon. members opposite are not capable of a little novelty, some small measure of variety. Do you see what they are doing today? They are simply trying to beat the gun again.

Why do I say that? You are well aware, Mr. Speaker, that in the throne speech the government indicated a course of action that would be submitted to this house with respect to the division between the dominion and the provinces of the revenues from the common fields of taxation. That was one of the things in respect of dominion-provincial fiscal relations proposed in the throne speech. I will have something to say in a moment about the other.
Today there was a motion on the order paper in this respect. I moved today and the house adopted the motion that at its next sitting the house should resolve itself into committee on the following government resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act to extend for a further period of one year the rate of 13 per cent for standard individual income tax for the purpose of calculating the tax equalization payments to the provinces and the amounts payable to the provinces under the tax rental agreements.
It is perfectly obvious that my hon. friends opposite when they proceeded with this amendment today were well aware that the government had on the order paper and had advanced a stage today a resolution dealing with this very subject. But you see, they are not content. These are members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition who are determined to beat the gun. It does not matter to them that this means repetition of debate. Oh, no, Mr. Speaker, they wish to make it appear
832	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Conference to the people of Canada that it was their idea that something should be done at this session about dominion-provincial fiscal relations. And so, with this resolution on the order paper staring every one of them straight in the eye they nevertheless decided to take up the time of the house for these two days to debate a resolution to the effect that the house should now address itself to the subject of dominion-provincial relations and that there should be, if you please, a conference. This is an interesting tactic but indeed a familiar one since hon. gentlemen opposite find themselves in the situation where they do not know what to do in this house from one week to another.
I said, Mr. Speaker, there was perhaps something else of interest in the other part of last year's amendment. You will remember that as I read it the amendment moved last year by hon. members opposite said this:
-and that the government has failed to give assurance that it would maintain or improve the principle of equalization of direct tax revenues of the provinces embodied in the existing law.
Why have they not added that today? You will notice, because it is so conspicuous, that they have dropped the second half of last year's amendment. It is like a great many other mantles with which my hon. friend, the social and economic planner from Essex East, sought to adorn himself. They are in some cases very good mantles but on him they look like a notorious misfit. They never were intended to be worn by him and I shall have something to say as I proceed about the way in which my friend the hon. member for Essex East sought today to wear clothes that do not belong to him.
I draw attention to proposals that this government made to the house in the throne speech and upon which we sought the approval of the house and which I believe received the approval of the house in the votes which occurred at the conclusion of the throne speech debate and at various stages when amendments were disposed of that had been introduced by hon. members opposite. May I remind hon. members of the announcement in that respect contained in the throne speech in the following language:
My government will recommend an amendment to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act to extend for another year the increase made last year in the provincial share of personal income tax revenue.
That paragraph outlined the government's intention to proceed in the manner I have indicated today as embodied in the resolution on the order paper which was advanced one stage this afternoon. But the government did not stop there. I shall now read the next following paragraph in the speech from the throne, the report the government gives to the house with respect to its program for the session. In this particular, with reference to dominion-provincial relations, the next paragraph in the throne speech reads:
My government proposes that the entire subject of financial relations between the dominion and the provinces shall receive continued active cooperative study. All provincial governments are being asked to agree to the use, for this purpose, of the machinery of the existing federal-provincial continuing committee on fiscal and economic matters working under the direction of a committee consisting of the Minister of Finance and all provincial treasurers.
In the face of that clear statement, Mr. Speaker, in the face of a comprehensive study of the entire subject of dominion-provincial financial relations, how can any

member of the house laying claim to intellectual honesty come before the house and say that this government is proposing to do nothing to advance the study or discussion between the dominion and the provinces of the question of their joint fiscal relations? We have proposed concrete action in this respect. We have proposed that the entire subject, not part of the subject but the entire subject, of financial relations between the dominion and the provinces should be submitted to active, co-operative study by the representatives of the federal and provincial levels of government in this country. I will have something further to say in the course of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, about the method that is proposed and about the breadth and scope of this study, but I propose before proceeding on that theme to have a word further to say about some of the other striking aspects of the amendment and the treatment of this subject in general by hon. gentlemen opposite.
I think it is noteworthy, Mr. Speaker, that there is one other item of business on the order paper of the house dealing with this same subject. It is resolution No. 43 which appears on page 14 of today's order paper under the heading "Notices of Motion." It is a resolution of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson).

My hon. friends opposite, not having anything factual to lay before the house, not having any grievance to bring before the house that has any basis to it, will go on mouthing as they have been doing today the same empty, baseless charges without facts to support them.
Just by way of introduction to the next subject I should like to take up after the dinner adjournment, may I say that when it comes to advocating the calling of dominion-provincial conferences or appearing before the Canadian parliament or the Canadian people as champions of the rights of the provinces, the last people in the house who have any right to cast themselves in that role are the hon. gentlemen who today constitute Her Majesty's loyal opposition. On that note, Mr. Speaker, I will call it six o'clock.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
At six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I had just indicated that I proposed to proceed in these remarks to discuss the question of whether hon. gentlemen opposite, Her Majesty's loyal opposition, have any right to pose as the champions of provincial rights or to picture themselves before this house and before the Canadian people as amongst those who have supported the calling of dominion-provincial conferences in the past. Listening to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) this afternoon, one would almost have thought he was putting before the house the proposition that the Liberal party, in recent times, favoured the calling of dominion-provincial conferences. One almost got the impression that that was what he was arguing for.
Perhaps those who are not acquainted with the record of the hon. gentleman and his party might almost have sensed that that is what he was driving at. If the calling of dominion-provincial conferences forms such an important part, holds such a signal place in the program and in the thinking of the Liberal party, one would surely have thought that one would find the calling of a dominion-provincial conference would have occupied


a place of high importance in the official pronouncements of the Liberal party. We have been hearing this afternoon a good deal of ancient history and some fairly modern history from the hon. member for Essex East. I might say that his history is just about as accurate as his statistics have been.
But, Mr. Speaker, is it a fact that the Liberal party, whose representatives in this house chose to make the calling of a dominion-provincial conference and the discussion of dominion-provincial fiscal relations the subject of their first amendment to a supply motion in the 1958 session and the subject of their first amendment to a supply motion in the 1959 session, favour the calling of dominion-provincial conferences? The Liberal party had a national convention in January, 1958, just a year ago. I have a document before me which is entitled, "New statements of Liberal policy". It is "for a greater Canada", and contains the 1958 resolutions adopted by the fourth national Liberal convention held in Ottawa January 14, 15, 16, 1958. I have read this document with some degree of care. You can read it from cover to cover and you will not find in it anywhere a demand or a plea for a dominion-provincial conference. This document, of course, is much truer to the history of the Liberal party than were the pronouncements we heard in this house today. One does not look for consistency on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite; that would be asking too much of them.
As I mentioned earlier in my remarks, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Essex East chose to support his demand for the condemnation of the government in relation to the matter of dominion-provincial relations, not simply on the basis of fiscal relations or the question of unemployment but he went into almost every facet of dominion-provincial relations, and I propose to follow him in that respect. The hon. member talked about methods of amending the constitution, and I should like to say something on that subject and on dominion-provincial relations so far as they affect the larger question of the Canadian constitution. In this respect, I am simply following what was said by the hon. member for Essex East this afternoon.
It has been my privilege to be a member of this house now for 14 years. Those of us who came to this house in the general election of 1945 had not been in the house very long before we heard, and some took part in, one of the most important debates on the constitution of this country that had been held for many a year. It will not be forgotten what were the positions taken respectively by the Liberal party, then the

government, and the Conservative party, then in opposition, in relation to the calling of a dominion-provincial conference before hands were laid upon the constitution of Canada. So that hon. members may have their recollections refreshed and may not be misled by the statements made this afternoon by the hon. member for Essex East, may I recall to hon. members some of the things that appeared in the course of that notable debate.
It was in the course of that debate that the then minister of justice, who later became the prime minister of Canada, Mr. St. Laurent, spoke in support of a proposal that an amendment to the constitution should be sought from the Westminster parliament in relation to the provision of the British North America Act concerning the basis of representation in the House of Commons by provinces. He proposed that that should be done without any consultation with the provinces. It was the position that he took, and firmly held in that debate, that there was no obligation whatever on the federal government to consult the provinces by way of any dominion-provincial conference before seeking that amendment of our basic act of confederation in the Westminster parliament. The Conservative party in opposition took the position that there ought to be a dominion-provincial conference before that amendment to the constitution was sought.
In the course of the debate a question was put to the then minister of justice, Mr. St. Laurent, by the hon. member for Calgary West, the late Arthur Smith. The question he put to the then minister of justice, Mr. St. Laurent, was this, and I am reading from the unrevised Hansard of June 18, 1946, at page 2696:
The hon. gentleman-
That is the hon. member for Calgary West.
-asked, what about section 133, which provides: "Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec: and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec."
The question asked by the hon. member for Calgary West was, could that section be amended by the Canadian parliament without any consultation with the provinces simply by seeking an amendment from the Westminster parliament. That was the question asked by the hon. member for Calgary West and this is how Mr. St. Laurent answered it. He paraphrased the question this way:
66968-9-53J
Dominion-Provincial Conference
Can that be dealt with without the consent of the provincial legislatures? Legally I say it can.
Mr. Speaker, that was the position of the Liberal party on June 18, 1946, those who pretend today to be the champions of the rights of the provinces, those who have the unmitigated temerity to stand up in this house and pretend they are the people who down through the years have been in the lead in consulting the provinces.
The Conservative party's position in this respect was pressed to the point of an amendment in 1946. It is interesting now, looking back, to see what became of that amendment. The Liberal government resolution to seek this amendment to the British North America Act without any consultation with the provinces on a very important constitutional point was followed by an amendment which you will find in Hansard, page 2235, June 6, 1946. It was an amendment introduced on behalf of the then Conservative loyal opposition by the man who holds today the distinguished office of Prime Minister of Canada. This was the amendment which he put forward:
That the motion be amended by deleting the words: "A humble address be presented to His Majesty the King in the following words:'' and substituting therefor:-And whereas it is desirable that the government should consult with the several provinces in respect of the said matter.
Now therefore be it resolved that the government be required to consult at once the several provinces and upon satisfactory conclusion of such consultations be authorized to present an humble address to His Majesty in the following terms.
Mr. Speaker, there we find the difference between the two parties in 1946. It was the Conservative party, as you may judge by the amendment introduced by the man who is today the Prime Minister of Canada, which called for consultation with the provinces before hands were laid upon the constitution of this country.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
And we had
those consultations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
We have the
Liberal party of that day, through its official spokesmen, rejecting the idea that they should consult with the provinces before seeking an amendment to the constitution. In doing so, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal party not only set the tone and tenor of its attitude towards the provinces in these post-war years but they proved themselves false to the standards of the Liberal party in previous days. They proved themselves faithless to the position that had been taken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and by Mr. Lapointe. Mr. Speaker, if you will forgive a reference, I should like to remind you of some passages from the utterances of these great Liberals of other days that were forgotten then and have largely

Dominion-Provincial Conference been forgotten since then by those who profess to be the heirs of these Liberal great men of days gone by. This is what Laurier said in this house on January 28, 1907.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Would the minister give
the page reference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Page 2269, volume II. He said this:
(Translation):
Confederation is a compact, made originally by four provinces, but adhered to by all the nine provinces who have entered it, and I submit to the judgment of this house and to the best consideration of its members, that this compact should not be lightly altered. It should be altered only for adequate cause, and after the provinces themselves have had an opportunity to pass judgment on the same.
(Text):
Then, Mr. Speaker, there came the words of the eloquent Ernest Lapointe, first of all in 1924, as found at page 520 of Hansard: (Translation):
Now this treaty cannot be changed, it has been the contention of many constitutional authorities, and I think it is only fair that no change should be accepted without the consent of all those who were parties to it. It is a sacred treaty just as is any other treaty; it is no "scrap of paper."
(Text) .*
Then in the following year again this chamber heard from the eloquent tongue of the late Ernest Lapointe. In 1925, as reported st page 301 of Hansard of that year, he said:
(Translation):
I think I cite history correctly when I say that every time there has been a dispute in Canada as regards provincial rights, those who were on the side of provincial rights were victorious in the end I do not think there can be any attempt to change the mutual charter of both the Dominion and the provinces by the arbitrary action of this parliament. I do not think it is possible to do it. To those who want changes, and I am willing to admit that there might be the necessity for changes, I would say that the only way to get them is the constitutional way, to ask the consent of the various parties to confederation.
(Text):
That was the position of the Liberal party in those past days, the days of Laurier and of Lapointe. But, Mr. Speaker, that position of the Liberal party was departed from in the most blatant fashion in 1946. But the sorry tale of Liberal departure from its soundest positions does not end there. One does not need to debate here today the compact theory of confederation or to take a position on that subject in order to be able to point out the glaring inconsistencies in the position of the Liberal party taken from time to time and to expose in this house today the fact that it would be impossible to conceive of anything much more hypocritical than that any member of this house should pretend that the Liberal party is the party

that has stood for consultation with the provinces or for dominion-provincial conferences.
Let us move on, Mr. Speaker, to the year 1949. The Liberal party in modern times is running true now to the position in 1946. In 1949, flushed with the success of 1946 when they defeated the Conservative opposition in this debate to which I have referred, they decided to go a step further and without, the slightest consultation with the provinces introduced an amendment to section 91 of the British North America Act for the purpose of taking unto the parliament of Canada power to amend the constitution in what was regarded as a federal matter without any consultation with the provinces. The position of the Conservative party then in opposition was consistent with the position they had taken in 1946. Mr. Drew, the then leader of the opposition, introduced the following amendment, seconded by the then hon. member for Lake Centre who is today the Prime Minister of Canada, on October 17, 1949. As found at page 841 of Hansard, these are the terms of the amendment introduced by the then leader of the opposition:
That the said proposed resolution be amended by striking out all the words after the first word "that" and substituting therefor the following:
"That His Excellency the Governor General in Council be requested to convoke as soon as may be possible a constitutional convention of representatives of the dominion and provincial governments to devise a method of amending within Canada the constitution of Canada, and of safeguarding minority rights; so that such method may become the subject later of an humble address, when adopted, to His Majesty the King praying an amendment of the British North America Act, 1867 accordingly".
It was as simple as that. The Conservative party said that there should be consultation with the provinces, that there should be a dominion-provincial conference. The attitude of the Liberal party then, in opposition, was that there should be no conference; that they would have nothing to do with any conference; that they would go right ahead and seek an amendment to the constitution in this important particular without provincial consultation.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a point of order. These interesting perversions of history are no doubt as usual amusing. My point of order is that there is before the house a motion which was introduced by my friend the hon. member from Essex East and which relates to the present and the future. I would be interested to see how the Minister of Finance relates these irrelevancies to that motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

Mr. Speaker, I
think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate (Mr. Pickersgill) was not in the house this afternoon to hear the speech which was made by his colleague.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I was giving him credit for intelligence and ability to follow the twisting and tortuous remarks of his colleague from Essex East, but he has just demonstrated to me that although he was in the house he did not follow what his colleague was saying. I need not remind you that it was the hon. member for Essex East who opened up the subject wide this afternoon and who went back to discuss methods of amending the constitution of Canada, and the positions of the respective parties in regard to that question. That is why I am dealing with this question, to set the record right. It is for his instruction and also for that of his colleague from Bonavista-Twillingate, who sits here listening to his colleague from Essex East, but evidently does not follow him. I was referring to the amendment which had been introduced on October 17, 1949-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my point of order was a serious one and I ask for a ruling.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Order. Perhaps I should read the amendment again. It was moved by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion the government should call a federal-provincial conference at once
Dominion-Provincial Conference to deal with serious problems of common concern such as unemployment and fiscal relations."
As long as hon. members who are speaking stay within the matter of a federal-provincial conference I am sure they are in order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while my hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate is thinking up his next point of order may I go on to say that the amendment introduced by Mr. Drew, to which I have just made reference, was ruled out of order. But that was not the end of the matter. I refer the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to the speech made by the present Prime Minister of Canada in the course of that debate. He will find that speech reported in Hansard of October 18, 1949, and I commend it to his most serious perusal and contemplation. I want to quote from the final paragraph of the speech of the hon. member who is today the Prime Minister of Canada, which is to be found in Hansard of October 20, on page 957. He concluded his speech with these words:
So once more Mr. Speaker, I ask, why the haste? Why not postpone this measure until the next session of parliament? Call a conference. If it proves abortive, if we have the power to do what the Prime Minister contends must be done, I will join with him, no matter what others may do, and support him. I shall make my contribution, humble though it may be, to the rebuilding of a foundation that will bring about a constitution in keeping with our responsibility as a nation.
Mr. Speaker, he pleaded with the government to call a conference, but his remarks fell upon unhearing ears. It fell to my lot, just at the conclusion of the debate, as found in Hansard of October 27, 1949, page 1210, to introduce on behalf of the then Conservative opposition an amendment in the following words:
That the said proposed resolution be amended by striking out all the words after the first word "that'' and substituting therefor:
"This house is of the opinion:
1.	That an humble address should be presented to His Majesty the King praying that His Majesty may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom providing for an amendment to the British North America Act, 1867, relating to the amendment of the constitution of Canada by the parliament of Canada.
2.	That as a condition precedent to the presentation of such address the scope and form of the amendment prayed for should be made the subject matter of a conference of the dominion and provincial governments and the subsequent approval of the parliament of Canada."
On October 27, 1949, the voting on that amendment followed at once, and interestingly enough among those whom I find voting against the amendment, voting against the calling of a conference of the dominion and

Dominion-Provincial Conference provinces to discuss this very important amendment of the constitution, is the name "Martin".

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so much for the subject of conferences to amend the British North America Act which has been very agreeably introduced this afternoon by my hon. friend for Essex East.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us go on to another aspect of federal-provincial relations which was touched on by him this afternoon. The hon. member talked about unemployment. He said that there had been no dominion-provincial conference which had discussed the subject of unemployment. I am sure that all hon. members of the house acquainted with the fact inferred at once, correctly, that there had been a dominion-provincial conference recently where the subject of unemployment had been discussed. This subject was referred to at the dominion-provincial conference of November, 1957, in relation to a proposal from the present federal government that the so-called "threshold" provision of the Unemployment Assistance Act should be removed. Those who were in the house in the years prior to 1957 will not have forgotten that the stoutest defender of that threshold provision, which had the effect of denying federal assistance in matters of unemployment in any province unless the proportion of unemployment exceeded 4.5 per cent of the population was the hon. member for Essex East. When we came into office we proposed to eliminate that limitation, and we put that proposal before the dominion-provincial conference in November of 1957. It is referred to in the speech made to the conference by my leader, the Prime Minister, and it was approved by the conference.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Would the minister indicate where in the proceedings of the conference that proposal was approved by the conference, because I have examined it several times but have never been able to find anything to that effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is regrettable that the hon. member cannot find it, but-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Would the minister show me where it is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Would the hon. member give me the opportunity? The hon. member has overlooked the fact that after the public statements as published in the official report were made the conference went into private session. No doubt the provinces liked the idea of this proposal being put forward, because this was something for the benefit of the provinces. The hon. member simply cannot understand why any federal government should do something to assist the provinces. That measure was duly enacted into law, without very much help, I may say, from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate or from the hon. member for Essex East or any of their colleagues in the house. The threshold provision was eliminated and now the federal government assists the provinces without there being any such limitation.
May I say at this point that provincial conferences are not simply those attended by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and by the premiers of the provinces. There are also those conferences which are held at the ministerial level, and in July, 1958 there was a dominion-provincial conference on unemployment and on labour matters held here in Ottawa and was attended on behalf of the federal government by my colleague the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) who thus had an opportunity to meet his opposite numbers in the governments of the provincial legislatures. At that conference they discussed matters pertaining to unemployment, and I put this fact alongside the empty, baseless assertions made in this house this afternoon by the hon. member for Essex East who said there had been no dominion-provincial conference held in recent times to discuss unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, we have become so accustomed in this house to witnessing these lachrymose exhibitions by hon. members opposite-none better, of course, than the act put on by the hon. member for Essex East- on the subject of unemployment. The week before last he could not wait to begin the discussion of measures pertaining to unemployment. He wanted us to stop talking- or, rather, he wanted other people to stop talking; he had already made his speech- so that he could get on and talk about unemployment. The opportunity was given last week. We have been waiting now for two days to get on to an item relating to the winter works program in the supplementary

estimates, but hon. members opposite are talking about everything under the sun in order to prevent our reaching the discussion of this winter works program.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Last week we saw two days given over to interminable discussions, and one can only conclude that there is not bursting the bosoms of hon. gentlemen opposite an irresistible urge to discuss the question of unemployment and the government's measures to meet it.
I might tell the hon. member for Essex East, if he can bear another observation, that the exchanges between the dominion government and the governments of the provinces in relation to unemployment and the winter works program have not been confined to conferences. My colleague the Minister of Labour has been conducting exchanges of correspondence with the governments of the provinces with regard to the winter works program for the last three or four months, and this has been issuing in action, the kind of vigorous, constructive action which is associated with the present government.
The hon. gentleman from Essex East dragged in by the forelock the subject of municipal relations. He is forgetting, of course, that for the first time in history there was held in Ottawa at the end of September last year a conference, informal it is true, between the dominion government and representatives of the municipal governments of this country to discuss questions pertaining to the problems of municipalities in this country and the relationship of those problems to other spheres of dominion-provincial relations.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Held every year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: There is one other point I should like to bring to the faltering memory of the hon. member for Essex East-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Leave the poor member alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: If I did not love my old friend from Essex East I would really bear down on him, I would really expose him.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Is this the new humanity?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman had forgotten when he made his jumbled speech in which he appeared to be advocating-if it was capable of any interpretation at all-that there should be a dominion-provincial conference to talk about amendments to the constitution, municipal relations,
Dominion-Provincial Conference dominion-provincial fiscal relations, unemployment and I do not know how many other things-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Human rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Oh yes, human rights, fundamental freedoms and the bill of rights. These are some of the things he mentioned this afternoon. He wanted them all discussed at the one conference. I can only recall to his mind the program with regard to these matters of the government of which he was a member.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: A distinguished member.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Well, of which he was perhaps the most distinguished member. What we used to hear from his less distinguished colleagues of those days, such as the prime minister and the minister of justice of those days, was the contention that when you call a dominion-provincial conference you should call it for one purpose; in other words, that you should not get the subjects mixed up. I can remember discussions with those colleagues of his on just this question, and they expressed their firm belief that if you hoped for any success from a dominion-provincial conference you must confine it strictly to one subject. However, the hon. member for Essex East has forgotten all about that in his approach to this question.
May I turn now to a different subject? I wish to go back to the year 1956 and correct the mythology in which the hon. gentleman indulged this afternoon as to the events of the past two and a half years. It was in 1956 that the then Liberal government, having met the provinces in a conference, brought to the house for enactment a measure which appears on our statute books as the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Agreements Act, 1956. It was at that conference that was reflected for the last time in hard, unyielding form, the stiff-necked attitude of the former government in meeting the provinces in a conference. I suppose that if there should ever be a federal government in office such as the one that was in office in 1956, and if it were to take the same stiff-necked attitude that that unyielding government took toward the representatives of the provinces, the case for calling dominion-provincial conferences would be greatly weakened. Some might even say: what is the use of calling conferences if the federal government is going to take that kind of attitude? That may be a point, Mr. Speaker. But in that conference the federal government took such an attitude, and the result was that the provinces all went away dissatisfied. I do not deny that nine of them signed agreements with the federal government, eight of them going the full way

Dominion-Provincial Conference by renting all three of the joint fields of taxation to the federal government. One, the province of Ontario, rented only the field of personal income tax. But, Mr. Speaker, were those provinces satisfied? Were they content in entering into agreements with the federal government to accept the terms that were imposed upon them? No, they were not.
May I remind the house of some of the things several of the provincial premiers said. I select those who are Liberals. These are excerpts from their comments quoted in the debate in this house in July, 1956, when we Conservatives who were then in the opposition opposed this legislation because we said it was unfair to the provinces and that they would be deprived of what they were entitled to expect at the hands of the federal government. This is what Mr. Campbell, then premier of Manitoba, had to say at that time as reported at page 6290 of Hansard of July 23, 1956:
However Manitoba was still disappointed that so little attention had been paid to the question of the actual financial requirements faced by the provincial governments in the next few years.
And again:
It is our recommendation that before any new pattern in federal-provincial relations is adopted a thorough reassessment of the relative responsibilities and revenue sources of the various governments in Canada should be undertaken.
We then have Premier Matheson of Prince Edward Island saying this, as reported at page 6038:
No recognition of a province's fiscal need problem or its tax-raising ability was taken into consideration in the re-allocation or distribution of the tax monies, but the same old factors were again used in the formula-the gross national product of Canada and the population of the provinces.
Here is what the provincial premier of Alberta had to say:
The federal government has retained for itself the broader and higher-yielding tax fields and, plagued with its financial problems at national level, has failed to recognize the financial needs of its provinces and their municipalities.
We hope that the shift toward centralization of governing authority which has resulted from a complex system of grants will be reversed so that more than ever the decisions can be made by representatives close to the people.
This, Mr. Speaker, was the tone of these statements that were referred to from time to time in the debate in July 1956 in this house. Those were our criticisms and the federal government enjoying lush times and enjoying a favourable financial position at that time declined to do anything more for the provinces.
In assessing later events let it be clearly understood that the federal government, of which the hon. member for Essex East, the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member

for Bonavista-Twillingate were then members, said emphatically that the provinces could have the 10 per cent of the yield from the personal income tax, 9 per cent of the yield from the corporation tax and 50 per cent of the yield from the succession duties but not another cent. That was the position when the 1956 legislation was written.
When we came into office in 1957 we moved to call a dominion-provincial conference to discuss this and other questions. We moved in that direction not because of any pressure from the opposition. It is crudely laughable to hear the hon. member for Essex East expounding that phantasy in this house today. His imagination soared to heights hitherto unreached even by the hon. member for Essex East. That conference was called in November of 1957 and the provinces realized that there was in that conference an entirely different atmosphere from anything they have known for many years.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: There certainly was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: A number commented after the conference that they had never seen a conference like it because the provinces had been invited there to act as equals, to state their cases and were afforded the opportunity of discussing in the freest way whatever proposals they wished to put forward. At the conclusion of that conference there was a communique issued which correctly states the conclusions of the conference. I draw attention to one of the comments which was completely overlooked this afternoon by the hon. member for Essex East which was to this effect-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Page?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I am reading from page 104 of the proceedings of the dominion-provincial conference of November 1957:
It was generally agreed that the over-all economic position of the Atlantic provinces is now such as to justify some special grants in aid to the governments of those provinces from the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, we moved diligently in the face of that decision taken by the dominion-provincial conference. Steps were taken to convene in Halifax representatives of the four Atlantic provincial governments. Federal officials went down there simply to assist in any way they could and a decision was reached there on the part of those four provinces through their representatives that if the federal government would move to bring about the payment of a special Atlantic adjustment grant they were prepared to divide it among themselves in an agreed ratio: 3, 3, 3 and 1-the 1 to go to Prince Edward Island. Having regard to relative populations that was a generous act on the

part of the governments of Nova Scotia and New	Brunswick-particularly	of Nova
Scotia-when they were prepared to accord to Newfoundland an equal share of the Atlantic adjustment grant with them and to the province of Prince Edward Island they were prepared to accord one-third as much as any of the others even though on a population basis Prince Edward Island would not have been entitled to as large a share.
When parliament met as soon as we could after the decision was reached, we moved in January in this house for the implementation of this agreement and asked parliament to enact into law the provision of an Atlantic adjustment grant of $100 million to be paid to the Atlantic provinces at the rate of $25 million a year for the next four years. Today Prince Edward Island is receiving $2,500,000 and New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland are each receiving $7,500,000 per annum that they would not have received but for the change of government in 1957.
However, Mr. Speaker, we did not stop there. As the communique issued at the conference indicates we had hoped to see this conference resumed early in 1958. But, Mr. Speaker, those who today would have you in your innocence believe that they wanted the re-convening of the dominion-provincial conference did their level best in this house-and it was not very level, either; they did their very worst in this house-to put in our path every possible obstacle to the calling of such a conference or doing things outside this house that the government might have wished to do at the time.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that we were a minority government. We were being pressed and harried at every turn in those January days by hon. members opposite who were doing their best to encompass our downfall day by day. We did not know from one day to another whether we would be continued in office. Under those circumstances, followed by the dissolution of parliament on February 1, it was a physical impossibility to call a conference. Parliament was sitting that January, morning, afternoon and night and on Saturdays. Hon. gentlemen opposite now say, "Why did you not call a dominion-provincial conference"? The responsibility I lay at the door of hon. members opposite.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: That was 12 months ago. You have not done anything since.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Yes, it was 12 months ago. The hon. member will recall that in the face of that situation we moved in this house before the end of January to take care of the situation during the next 12 months. What we did in that situation 66968-9-54
Dominion-Provincial Conference was to ask parliament to approve an increase in the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax from the Liberal 10 per cent to the Conservative 13 per cent.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Here I draw your attention to the necessity for correction in the statements made in this house this afternoon by the hon. member for Essex East, like the statements made by his colleagues at the last session. The action taken by this government was not a repetition of the tactics of the former Liberal administration in saying to the provinces, "There are the terms. Take them or leave them. If you want this much you must yield up your right to collect revenue from these common fields of taxation." No, Mr. Speaker, that was not what we did.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: When the Speaker asks me to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speechtext: Order.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
