speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: I am reviewing some facts that the hon. gentleman does not like. I think I would prefer to complete this review of the facts and then I would be glad to have his question.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: All right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I said that we did not ask anything of the provinces, yet in this talk, this empty, misleading talk that hon. gentlemen opposite indulge in now, you would think we had asked something of the provinces when they talk about a take it or leave it attitude. We simply offered to give the provinces another three per cent. We did not ask anything of them in return, not a thing. That is the difference between the tactics of hon. members opposite when they formed the government, the highhanded, rigid, stubborn, unyielding attitude that they took and our attitude in not asking anything of the provinces but simply asking parliament to increase from 10 pfer

Dominion-Provincial Conference cent to 13 per cent the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Question.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: -as much more tax as they like.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
apparently the hon. member did not know this afternoon what his colleague, the hon. member for Essex East was saying and tonight he does not know what a question is. It is not the first time. I would ask the hon. gentleman to try to bring his mind under control and cast it back to 1956. I would ask him not to be jumping up and down and letting his mind jump but just to think calmly now, to concentrate and direct his mind to 1956. He will recall that what the government of which he was a member said to the provinces was, "If you want these revenues then you must yield up the right to us to collect these taxes."

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
"If you do not
give them up, all right, we are not prepared to go further", and when the provinces in the course of the discussions-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: -tried to persuade the federal government to look at the problems of the provinces and of their municipalities and be a little more generous they said "no" and the hon. member opposite was one of those who said "no" to the provinces. The provinces today can thank the present government for the additions they have received since we came into office and can recall that they would not have had one cent of these additional revenues if the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and his colleagues had remained in office.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: I do not wish to appear persistent but I should like the minister to answer my question. My question was this.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: What is there in this statute-

speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Order. Do I understand that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate wishes to ask a question?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Does the Minister of Finance wish to have one asked?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: I did answer the hon. gentleman's question and I answered the assertion that followed his question which, of course, was not an assertion of fact but of Liberal fancy.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: In view of the minister's opinion of my intelligence, may I ask another question? Will the minister answer another question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Oh, no, that was not what I was dealing with at all.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: That is what you said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

You said yours was
different.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: We are not going to get an answer. That is obvious.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

-to take steps to increase their share of the revenues and to do so at once because of the fact they had to know in planning their budgets what we

were going to do. That was what led to the sending of the urgent reply in the form of a telegram and to the urgent action that was taken in the house in the last week of January, 1958 to increase the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax. When my hon. friends enjoy the fact that the telegram under those circumstances in the amounts that it contained by way of estimate, and estimate only, did not take account of the stabilization payments, let me say to them that nobody in this country was misled by the error in the estimates in the telegram. Nobody was-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

Now, Mr. Speaker, we thus made provision for the needs of the provinces for the ensuing 12 months and today, as I indicated in opening my remarks this afternoon, we are taking action in two respects. We are asking parliament to extend for another 12 months this important provision made for the assistance of the provinces and we are proposing at the same time that the study of dominion-provincial fiscal or financial relations be carried forward.
I think it is well that hon. members should know something of the assistance which has accrued to the provinces as a result of the measures which we took a year ago and what, according to our present best calculations, are estimated to be the provisions that the provinces may expect to receive in this coming fiscal year in respect of the unconditional payments provided for under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act as amended.

I made it quite clear that these were our estimates because my hon. friend knows they could not be more than estimates as applied to what remained of the current fiscal year and the ensuing fiscal year. I give these figures by way of illustration and in doing so I am leaving out any reference to the Atlantic adjustment grants. In the year 1957-58, on the basis of the Liberal 10-9-50 formula the payments made to the provinces amounted to $639,-
909,000.	Then, we move forward to the fiscal year, the present one, 1958-59. Again not including the Atlantic adjustment grants, the figure that would have resulted from the 10-9-50 Liberal formula would have been $613,483,000 in the present fiscal year. Under the present government's 13-9-50 formula the yield to the provinces is estimated at $661,-
298,000.	Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there was a difference of $47,815,000 between the two formulae.
Now let me add at once that in the actual payments to be made this year, had there been no change in the formula, $20,926,000 would have been due on account of stabilization payments. Nevertheless there was an actual increase of $47,815,000, even after allowing for the above stabilization payments. If my hon. friend opposite will listen I think his wish may be gratified but I cannot promise that he will like it.
I have drawn to the attention of the house the reference to this subject in the speech from the throne. Hon. members opposite have expressed their resentment of the fact that this subject found its way into the speech from the throne as the first information to the nation of our proposals with reference to the dominion-provincial program for this ensuing year. Let us look at that contention for a moment, Mr. Speaker.
There were two things that were in the speech from the throne. One was the statement that parliament would be asked to continue the government's 13-9-50 formula of unconditional grants for another year. They evidently say that matter should not have been brought to parliament first, but that it should have been drawn first to the attention of the provinces. Then with regard to our proposal that there should be now inaugurated an active co-operative study on the part of

Dominion-Provincial Conference the proper body, on which the dominion and provincial governments are represented, of the whole field of dominion-provincial fiscal relations, they say that we ought to have brought that matter to the attention of the provinces before we brought it to parliament.
No one knows better than yourself, Mr. Speaker, that if we had not brought this matter to the attention of parliament first, hon. members opposite would have been loud in their denunciation of the government for, they would have said, ignoring and by-passing parliament. We took the proper constitutional course and there was no discourtesy to the provinces in the course that we took.
As soon as the speech from the throne was read by His Excellency the Governor General a letter was dispatched by the Prime Minister to each of the provincial premiers drawing their attention to the text of the proposal appearing in the speech from the throne and inviting their co-operation in the proposed study. I may say-and this will not please hon. gentlemen opposite but it is the fact-[DOT] that it is a tribute to the broader view that the provinces took; broader than that of hon. members opposite-that eight of the provinces have already, through their premiers, responded to the Prime Minister's letter and have indicated that they are prepared to participate in the study. We wait yet to hear from the governments of Newfoundland and Alberta.
As the house is well aware, the proposal was that we should follow up the present situation with a study conducted by the federal-provincial continuing committee on fiscal and economic matters operating under a committee of ministers consisting of the provincial treasurers or ministers of finance of the provinces and the federal minister of finance. Earlier in my remarks, I drew attention to the breadth of the field of study which this body is asked to undertake, namely the whole field of financial relations between the dominion and the provinces. We are not proposing to place any limitations on the reasonable scope of that proposed study. Hon. members opposite, who ought to know better, now deride this extremely important proposal. It is not amiss, Mr. Speaker, to remind them that they participated in setting up this important body. The federal-provincial continuing committee on fiscal and economic matters grew out of a proposal made by the province of Ontario at the agenda conference of April, 1955, which preceded the federal-provincial conference of October, 1955.
Several other provinces indicated their belief that a continuing joint federal-provincial committee of officials would promote the exchange of factual information, secure a better understanding of mutual problems, and

promote greater co-operation among the various governments in the fields of national development, income and employment maintenance. In his opening address to the October 1955 conference, Mr. St. Laurent placed the question of establishing such a committee before the conference, and the conference, in its concluding communique, stated:
There was general agreement that the conference should authorize the establishment of a committee of federal and provincial officials to meet from time to time to exchange information and examine technical problems in the field of federal, provincial, fiscal and economic relations. Representatives on this committee would be designated by the Prime Minister or premier of each government and the chairman would be designated by the Prime Minister of Canada. The committee will not take collective action but each of the members will report to his own government on the subjects discussed.
The federal-provincial continuing committee on fiscal and economic matters, set up as a result of the above conference, is composed of federal and provincial officials designated by the heads of their respective governments. The officials are generally drawn from the deputy minister ranks of the departments of finance, economics or provincial treasuries. These officials may have associated with them additional officials in an advisory capacity. The federal deputy minister of finance serves as chairman of the committee, and the director of the federal-provincial relations division as secretary. The committee generally meets twice a year, the spring meeting being in Ottawa and the fall meeting being in a provincial capital. The meetings are held in camera, and fiscal and economic matters of interest to the various governments are examined. No decisions are reached, but the committee members report to their own government the tenor of the discussions.
It is to this committee of officials that the government wishes to direct a re-examination of the present tax-sharing arrangements. Associated with this technical committee will be the committee of ministers of finance and provincial treasurers who will be empowered to direct the process of re-examination and to make any necessary decisions.
Mr. Speaker, not only does this federal government believe that this is the proper way, under the circumstances, to proceed with what we believe will be a timely co-operative study of this whole question of dominion-provincial financial relations, but we believe that it will be the most fruitful way of proceeding. There are many problems in this field. You do not solve those problems simply by calling a two-day conference of prime ministers. The success of such a conference depends on the preparatory work, and this federal-provincial continuing committee was

conceived when first set up as the kind of technical committee which would review the difficult questions, and in that way pave the way to decisions to be taken at the ministerial level or the prime ministerial level of conference to be called later.
This is not the end of the story. This is not ruling out dominion-provincial conferences at which the Prime Minister of Canada and the premiers of the provinces will be meeting. Not at all. This is rather a sensible and constructive, indeed the most sensible and constructive way which could be proposed for the study of this whole field in the broadest and most comprehensive way in order that we may arrive, we hope, in the end at more effective and acceptable fiscal arrangements between the federal and provincial governments. Believe me, sir, we do not propose to take anything away from the provinces in these discussions. The provinces know that. They know they are dealing with a federal government which has done more to recognize the provincial problems and help the provinces to meet their problems than has any federal government in Canada's history.
As my final word, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. The hon. member for Essex East took it upon himself this afternoon to acuse the Prime Minister of this country of not carrying out undertakings that he had given. Mr. Speaker, I say to you that none knows better than the hon. member for Essex East that that was a hollow, false charge, and that when the hon. member, or any other hon. member opposite makes charges of that kind in this house against the Prime Minister of Canada he will find 207 loyal members and followers of the Prime Minister of this country rallying to his support.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about federal-provincial relations with special reference to the tax-sharing agreements. In Canada we have a federation, and we cannot have a strong federation and good unity in our country unless we strive to provide equality of opportunity in all parts of our country no matter where the people may live. We cannot achieve this end in a short time because of the unevenness of our country's development. The areas of the greatest population are in the central provinces, Ontario and Quebec, and in those areas, along with British Columbia we have centres of manufacturing and finance with a consequent concentration of wealth. Most of the rest of the country is contributory to these more fortunate areas.

Dominion-Provincial Conference
I do not think there is any difference of opinion among members of this house that the less fortunate areas should receive subsidies. In fact, I heard the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) say this afternoon that the fathers of confederation recognized this. I was looking up the records the other night and I noticed that on 16 occasions between confederation and 1937 the subsidies to some or all of the provinces were increased. After the great depression and during its aftermath the Rowell-Sirois commission was set up. The commission made its report in 1940. I read some parts of that report and I was struck by one very significant item, namely that the weaker provinces which were overwhelmed by the depression suffered hard times even when the other provinces were enjoying good times. This report suggested that a minimal national standard of services should be set up and that grants should be given to the less fortunate provinces when it was impossible for them to raise enough money to pay for these minimal services.
A dominion-provincial conference was called at that time and there was failure to agree. Then the war came on and we had the war taxes agreement. Then, in 1947, we had the first peacetime agreement. All the provinces came in with the exception of Ontario and Quebec. When these agreements were revised in 1951 the province of Ontario came in, renting its corporation and income tax fields. The last Liberal revision to this agreement was in 1956 and it came into effect in 1957. At that time, as hon. members know, the principle of equalization was introduced. Stabilization was also effected by the federal government guaranteeing 95 per cent of the amount of the payment for the previous year. The equalization was reached by a formula somewhat complicated in its end result.
This formula is used at the present time although there was an amendment introduced in the last session of parliament. The wealth of each province was measured in accordance with the per capita sum of the income tax, the corporation tax and the succession duties tax, which were called the standard taxes. The average or per capita yield of the wealthiest provinces, Ontario and British Columbia, are taken as the national standard and all the other provinces are paid sums equal to the difference between the per capita yield of the standard taxes in the province and the standards set by Ontario and British Columbia.
To give an example, I have here a paper which shows the standard taxes of the different provinces, and the national standard set by British Columbia and Ontario amounts to $38.16 in the fourth estimate of the payments for these provinces for this year. The

preliminary estimates as contained in this paper show that the standard tax for Newfoundland is $10.65 and for Prince Edward Island $7.59. Under the equalization formula, each province must receive the difference between this amount and $38 for every person living in this province. Under these arrangements therefore Newfoundland will receive something in excess of $12 million and Prince Edward Island an amount in excess of $3 million in payments. The formula applies to every province across the country except that almost every year there are some minor readjustments.
The agreement reached at the 1956 conference gave to the provinces 10 per cent of the federal income tax collection, 9 per cent of the corporation tax and 50 per cent of the succession duties tax, and this was called the 10-9-50 formula. Up to those levels, individuals and corporations living in the province, and paying taxes in the province in those provinces that did not participate under that agreement, were allowed full deduction for federal taxes but beyond this amount no deductions would be allowed. It makes no great net difference to the federal treasury whether these taxes are collected federally or by the provincial governments themselves. Premier Frost of Ontario advocated a 15-1550 formula under which the federal government would give up the collection of 15 per cent of the income tax plus 15 per cent of the corporation tax plus 50 per cent of the succession duties tax to the provincial government, and this came to be known as the 15-15-50 formula.
When this government came to power a federal provincial conference was held in November, 1957 and Premier Frost proposed again this 15-15-50 formula. He got the 10 per cent personal income tax increased to 13 per cent, but he is still demanding $100 million extra.
The formula proposed by Mr. Frost, without equalization, would of course weigh against the less wealthy provinces. It would cost the federal treasury about $130 million of which Ontario would receive about $118 million. No doubt the other provinces would take a dim view of this arrangement. This is the real crux of the situation as I see it.
The 15-15-50 formula based on the present equalization and standardization, taking the two wealthy provinces as the standard, would cost the federal government about $1 billion. The previous Liberal government could not afford this amount and most certainly we cannot afford it now because our deficit exceeds the total amount paid under the tax sharing agreement to the provinces. Mr. Frost claims that Ontario pays about half of the

standard taxes and that he collects a little more than one-third in return. If he were to get his $100 million under the present equalization formula it is not difficult to figure out that the people of the province of Ontario would have to pay approximately $140 million extra in taxes. Ontario is developing at a fast rate and our provincial government has many obligations to meet not only on its own account but in respect to municipalities as well. I have every sympathy for Mr. Frost's demand and I hope he gets more money.
I know that the premier of Ontario agreed to a special grant to the Atlantic provinces in the sum of $100 million to be paid in amounts of $25 million over a period of four years and that occurred at the time the extra 3 per cent personal income tax was allowed but the premier still insisted on getting his $100 million. One thing to remember is that the stabilization applies only to the formula introduced by the Liberal government and does not apply to the increase of 3 per cent in personal income tax.
I have in my hand an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of February 5 and which states in part:
Premier Frost says he plans to get a full $100 million a year in extra tax revenues from Ottawa- and then some.
He told the Ontario legislature Wednesday he has retreated "not one quarter of an inch" from the position he took when the Liberals were in power at Ottawa.
I should like to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) if he thinks these words of Premier Frost are empty and misleading. In the last election campaign Premier Frost appeared on the same platform with the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on different occasions. I recall seeing one photograph of the Premier pointing his finger at the Prime Minister and it stated under the photograph that Mr. Frost was saying, "There is the man who will give me the $100 million."
I have here some extracts taken from Hansard of the Ontario provincial legislature in which Premier Frost clearly indicates that the $22 million he got by telegram from this government was purely an interim payment and that he was still pressing for the 15-15-50 formula namely $100 million. One very significant interjection in the debate by hon. Mr. Dunbar, M.L.A. for Ottawa was, "He will get it."
When the federal-provincial conference met in November of 1957 and the provinces put forth their demands I think it must have set the Minister of Finance to do some figuring. He must have been shocked when he heard what the provinces wanted and the conference adjourned after only two days.
Dominion-Provincial Conference If you read the record of that conference and the various statements of the premiers attending I do not see how you could come to any conclusion other than that the conference would meet again in January or February last.
During the election campaign a rosy picture kept coming up in my mind as I am sure it did in the minds of others, that if the Progressive Conservatives were successful the provinces and municipalities would be called here and would divide the spoils and that this government would get along on the little that would be left. But what happened? The municipalities did not get in on the meeting at all. Afterwards some of the mayors were called here and were told some of the facts of life, and it was explained to them that the Liberals had left the cupboard bare.
I thought there might be some excuse for the government not calling the federal-provincial conference last January or February because at that time the Prime Minister was planning his zig-zag plane trip to Quebec city and of course nothing so insignificant as finances should interfere with that jaunt. But now another whole year has passed and the provinces have again received word that the federal payments are to be the same as last year. It is perfectly obvious that this government does not want to face the provinces at this time and it appears as though the provinces will continue to be told what they will receive by letter, telegram or by some other means of communication.
It is possible that we can carry this business of collecting money for the provinces too far. We must of necessity have to collect a good deal of money for the provinces in order to maintain a strong federation but the spending of money by anybody who is not responsible for collecting it is not conducive to good responsible government. On a smaller scale we have all seen frequent irritations between municipal councils and boards of education or school boards. The school boards s'et down their own financial requirements and the council must collect the money. While it would not be practical for the school boards to collect the funds they need it has often occurred to me that if the various boards of education had to collect their own money and be thus responsible to the people there would be less irritation in the municipalities and probably in some cases a greater scrutiny of expenditure.
When the Liberal government was in power I often attended dinners where a minister of the provincial government told the audience that the federal government took so much of the tax dollar that there was not

Dominion-Provincial Conference enough left for the provinces and the municipalities. I have often attended dinners addressed by Hon. Charles Daley, minister of labour of Ontario, but he never said that in my presence because he, I know, understood that much federal money was returned to the provinces directly or through social security and other payments.
I can recall attending a dinner at Niagara Falls that was also attended by the speaker of the Ontario legislature. While he was speaking he turned to me and said that the federal Liberal government was collecting 75 per cent of the tax dollar and that the province and the municipalities did not have enough left to meet their obligations. He did not refer at all to any of the money that was coming back to the province. I do not know if the 75 per cent figure is correct but I would suggest to that hon. gentleman that if the figure was right he will certainly soon have to jack up the 75 per cent because as soon as this government gets around to balancing its budget it will take a great deal more money than the Liberal government ever did. I say this after seeing the current estimates which were tabled the other day.
It is interesting to examine the record of the federal-provincial conference of 1957. The previous year the present Prime Minister laid down the position of the Progressive Conservative party, as found on page 6370 of Hansard for July 24, 1956, where, referring to the St. Laurent government, he said:
The government simply said, "These are the terms" . . . The recipe for a division of taxation was as final as the laws of the Medes and Persians . . . There was no opportunity for negotiation: there was simply the attitude of a feudal lord bringing into being a modern feudalism and laying down the law to the vassals.
There was much more along the same line. He was speaking of the former Liberal government which had met the provinces at three full conferences. I think I am right when I say there were three. There were at least two and I think there were three full conferences. The federal government had made its final offer. All the provinces were at the conference table. They were told what the government could give, and this was done after full discussion.
In contrast, the present government met with the provinces for two days in November of 1957, submitted no proposal to the provinces but notified the provinces of its decision by telegram some time in January at the very moment when this matter was coming before the house for decision. There was no conference then. There was no opportunity for concurrence, no opportunity to express disapproval or to express any comment. It was simply a take it or leave it attitude.

The point is that the government has no decided policy in dealing with the provinces and the Toronto Globe of January 16 has a long article dealing with the row that looms because of the delay in settling the tax deal. It gives some reasons for this. One is that the old standardization formula of 10-9-50 does not apply to the extra three per cent additional allowance with regard to income tax. A second reason is that apart from the $25 million going to the Atlantic provinces the extra three per cent allowed the provinces will fall considerably short of the $62 million estimated at first by the government.
Following the federal-provincial conference of November, 1957 there were some heated exchanges by letter between the Minister of Finance and some of the premiers of the provinces, some of which reached the press. There was some difficulty of interpretation with Premier Douglas of Saskatchewan, for example, and also there was a threat to the premier of Prince Edward Island that the Minister of Finance would restrict his dealings with that province unless the premier withdrew some remarks he had made concerning one or two civil servants. There was a love feast, however, in Toronto, between the Prime Minister and Premier Frost and according to the Globe and Mail-I have a copy here-Premier Frost compared the Prime Minister to the late Franklin Delano Roosevelt. The Prime Minister took some exception to this comparison. He referred to the earlier Roosevelt, Theodore Roosevelt, and said that he was trying to give Canadians the same vision of development and the same pride in their country as the earlier Roosevelt. After much patting of one another on the back they parted but Mr. Frost is still taking his 22 cents on the dollar from the government, although some people tell me that it is now only 19 cents.
As I have said before, I hope that Mr. Frost can get more help but the fiscal policy of the government involving a huge deficit and a foolish conversion loan has made it more difficult and more expensive for every province and every municipality in the country to borrow money. Provinces must now pay at least 5J per cent to get money and most of our municipalities must pay 6 per cent. In fact, I know some that cannot get money at that rate and I have heard of some that cannot borrow money at any interest rate at all. Whether or not that is true I cannot tell you but I know that some are paying over 6 per cent in Ontario.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should like to address a question to the Prime Minister. Can the Prime Minister inform the house whether it is his intention to recommend the appointment of a committee either of the House of Commons or of both houses of parliament to hear and receive representations and suggestions with respect to the effectiveness of the bill on human rights and fundamental freedoms which he proposes to introduce this session?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I thank the hon. gentleman for having given me notice of this question. He will recall that on September 5 last a draft bill of rights was introduced into the house and given first reading and some discussion, and then allowed to stand with a view to giving individuals and representatives of various organizations across the country

interested in fundamental freedoms, an opportunity of placing their views before the government. In so far as setting up another committee is concerned, while I am not speaking with finality at the moment I cannot see any good reason why a further committee should be set up. As the hon. gentleman knows, some time ago, in two successive years, as I recall it, a committee of both houses of parliament sat and dealt with matters affecting fundamental freedoms.
I can go no further at this time than to say, while not necessarily closing the door to the possibility, that I cannot now see any good reason why a further committee should be set up, especially in view of the fact that this matter was brought before the house last September and, in the intervening months, an opportunity has been provided for the representations which he apparently has in mind.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Can the Prime Minister inform the house whether any approach has been made by the government to the provincial governments in respect of the adequacy or otherwise of this particular bill?

At that time it seemed to be generally accepted by the government of that day that a bill of rights in the form of an amendment to the constitution which would cover not only those rights that are specifically allotted to parliament but as well those which fall within provincial jurisdiction was not acceptable to many of the provinces.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE
speechtext: I wonder if I might ask a further supplementary question. maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to participate in this extremely important debate. I am happy especially because it was initiated by my friend the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) for whom I entertain the highest regard and with whom I spent some time pleasantly last summer at an international gathering. I have always admired him, but never did I admire him more than I did yesterday, when he put on a performance so different from that which he put on a few days earlier over television. Yesterday he seemed to be everywhere at once and on the previous occasion he did not seem to be anywhere at all when a question was asked.
This earlier performance was matched only by his ecumenical display of knowledge yesterday. He dipped into philosophy, into history, into logic, and one of his favourite fields of sport, statistics. But I think he was at his best when he was bristling with moral indignation. In his beginning as he lectured in federalism, I thought he was extremely interesting. Until he became more of a partisan and less of a constitutionalist I was applauding his every word in my dignified silent style. One who might have been led along in such similar general thoughts in the field of political science might have thought of the important part that political parties play, and he might think of, and theorize on the desperation with which some political parties seek to recapture office and regain the position which once they held.

Dominion-Provincial Conference
Some of us who are devoted to the two-party system are at times a little unhappy at the way in which the present opposition reveal on occasion a lack of astuteness when it comes to an opportunity to grasp an issue. There is either a tendency to fire so many broadside shots that they all miss target, or to grasp the very subject upon which the government is strongest in the view of the Canadian people. On the question of dominion-provincial relations I feel they were in the second category.
In the part of Canada from which I come we are vitally concerned with the very questions to which the hon. gentleman has directed our attention, namely the question of dominion-provincial relations and their place in a federal state. The purist, of course, would say that Canada is indeed not precisely a federal state but perhaps a quasi-federal state, but our development has certainly been along that line. All down through the years we have talked about having a rigid constitution. Of course the British North America Act is not our whole constitution but merely a part of it. We have found flexibility and, if I may use the expression, constant change. In no area of the country has there been greater interest and greater concern and indeed greater need for a readjustment of the fiscal relations of the units of the nation than in my area. A great scholar who was also a great politician and statesman, namely the late Norman McLeod Rogers, at one time said:
A federation defeats its primary purpose if through its constitutional arrangements or through policies instituted by the national government it accomplishes the gradual debilitation of one or more of the provincial communities of which it is composed.
Here surely is an opportunity for a representative of a maritime constituency to make a comment which may indeed be germane to the discussion before us and may have a direct bearing upon some of the actions of national governments in the past and the action of the national government in the present. I am sure that down through the years this house has heard speeches on maritime claims, for in our area we have suffered from economic inequality. We came into confederation in a period of great prosperity but our golden age, it seems, has long since passed behind us. Many things which our people were led to believe would come from the new and greater entity have not come at all or have been very slow in coming.
We in the maritimes have watched this great country expand to the west and now to the north. This new northward expansion has caught our imagination as it has caught the imagination of the rest of the citizens of Canada. But as our great country has
[Mr. Macquarrie.l moved and developed we feel too often that we, in the region where it all began, have been left behind.
Of all the vexed questions of dominion-provincial relations in which the maritimes are concerned, one in my opinion has never yet even approached a final settlement or a thorough-going examination. I refer to the question of the great lands to the north. We look forward to our expansion there, and we know that under the guiding genius of this government it will come. But let it not be forgotten that if the north is developed, it must be developed by a united Canada and that in that union the maritimes form a great part.
Only once or twice in our national story have we seemed to find a statesman who recognized the importance of this fact. One whom I refer to and who will go down in history as one of our greatest leaders, namely Sir Robert Borden, caught the significance of this. In 1912 an hon. member from New Brunswick said in this House of Commons:
The three maritime provinces have but 52,000 square miles, and it is proposed at once, without consulting the other provinces, without seeing what New Brunswick or Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island may think, to add something like 200,000 square miles to the territory of the province of Manitoba.
The then prime minister later replied:
I would like to point out to my hon. friend that one of his own colleagues on that side of the house has raised an important question this afternoon, and has expressed views with which perhaps my hon. friend may not be inclined to concur, namely, that when this question of the transfer of the natural resources to the prairie provinces does come to be considered some regard will have to be given to the claims of some of the provinces in Canada and especially the three maritime provinces whose boundaries have not been increased, whose boundaries cannot very well be increased on account of their natural situation.
In the days ahead it is our fervent hope that considerations along that line will be taken into account.
Mr. Speaker, in examining the question of dominion-provincial relations I believe it would be fitting to look at the province of Prince Edward Island, my native province, as a sort of touchstone on this very question. Why would Prince Edward Island be the appropriate place to make a study of this problem? One reason, of course, is that confederation was born in my province. The city of Charlottetown is the birthplace of confederation, and we can therefore at least be expected to express paternal feeling on the whole process. It is also the smallest province of all, and it is the province in

which contributions from the dominion treasury proportionately play the largest part in the provincial budget.
Indeed, Prince Edward Island makes an ideal touchstone for the wisdom of any government in the national arena concerned with national development. The Rowell-Sirois report states that the province does not form a satisfactory unit from the point of view of public finance, and particularly for raising revenue. The subsistence nature of the economy, the low average net value of agricultural production, and the lack of urbanization are reflected in a total real property rate which is only one-fifth the Canadian per capita average. The province's lack of any public domain is responsible, of course, for the absence of revenue from that source. Under these circumstances Prince Edward Island, through the years, has found it necessary, as someone has said, to tax everything, tangible and intangible.
Another reason which I think might be cited is that of all the provinces of Canada, none has been so faithful to the Liberal party over the years. For 23 years we have had in the province a Liberal government. Indeed in 1935, from the very community in which I was born, there arose a Liberal leader to capture every seat in the provincial legislature, and for four years there was not a single opposition voice raised. In the federal field Prince Edward Island was looked upon as a haven for cabinet ministers. From time to time migrating ministers were given safe seats in Prince Edward Island. We had the minister of finance, Mr. Dunning, in Queens; and in that especially safe seat, Prince, the former prime minister, Mr. King, found refuge for a short time. We also had Mr. Ralston. Prince county, was a Liberal seat from 1904 to 1957, when my colleague cracked the sound barrier, so to speak, and in 1958 he did it again, increasing his majority one hundredfold. It is perhaps symptomatic-

As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate raised a point of order, and the hon. member who has the floor has spoken to it, I think it might be well to remind the hon. member who has the floor that the motion is in these terms:
This house is of the opinion the government should call a federal-provincial conference-
That is the basic matter under discussion. The necessity for, or the desirability of, calling a federal-provincial conference opens the door for a discussion of federal-provincial relations in connection with that necessity.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was my intention to look at the financial status of one province at the present time in relation to development in the past in order to argue that the amendment, so far as that province is concerned, is not a matter of immediate moment. I shall endeavour to relate more clearly and more directly the question at issue.
Throughout the years the need for greater financial assistance for my province has been pressed, not only at dominion-provincial conferences but on many occasions through contacts between the dominion and provincial governments. At the recent dominion-provincial conference the premier of Prince Edward Island recalled the previous condition which had developed from the unfortunate economic difficulties in which the province, through no fault of its own, found itself. Originally in 1873 we were given a subsidy of $45,000, which was nearly all eaten up by the interest on an extensive loan of $800,000 which was made necessary by certain financial operations of the province. In 1887 our subsidy was raised $20,000, in 1900 it was raised $30,000 and in 1912 it was raised by $100,000. At that time a Conservative government was in office in both Prince Edward Island and at Ottawa. It was at that time that the question of public domain in northern lands was discussed and very sympathetically entertained by Mr. Borden and Mr. White. In 1934 our subsidy was raised by another $275,000.
The situation in Prince Edward Island at the present time, and in the maritimes in the recent past, was very well recorded by many, many people who looked at the unequal

Dominion-Provincial Conference economic development of this country. I suppose an outstanding document on this is the famous Gordon commission report. We were so far behind in development that it was implied that perhaps in order to maintain a better standard of living some of our people had better leave and go to other parts of the country. Surely that was a strain upon dominion-provincial relations in the whole federal system of this country. Unfortunately some people did leave and that, of course, made the revenue situation in the poorer provinces even worse than it was before. In the many years during which the Liberal party was in office, the aggravating question of financial relations came up again and again. From my province there came constant appeals for greater aid and many, many of these were turned back. On one occasion instead of getting greater aid the Prince Edward Island government received a bill for $1,142,000 as a result of the 1952 agreement, when a miscalculation on the population projection had been made by dominion authorities.
In 1957 there came new hope for the maritime provinces, especially for the province of Prince Edward Island, where we had had several set-backs and reverses one after the other. With amazing alacrity there came a movement by the present government which expressed itself in the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant.
What does that mean? It means to the province of Prince Edward Island every year an additional amount of $2J million, which might be interpreted as $100 per capita over the four-year period. This is a sum which represents nearly one-third of the provincial budget, and it represents the greatest single grant our province has received from Ottawa since confederation. This is the result of the meeting called by this government shortly after the election.
It is interesting to find hon. gentlemen opposite so concerned about the alacrity of fulfilling promises. One might think of some of the promises which were made on their platform in 1919; if they really want to go back, they might go back to 1883. An important part of the economic inequality as between the provinces is the lack of adequate social services which some of the provinces possess. In the small province of Prince Edward Island which I think, as I have indicated, might serve as the touchstone of present policy, we are now seeing some improvement as a result of the dominion-provincial negotiations carried out by this government. Teachers are being paid higher salaries, though they are still not high enough; roads are being built which the province could not afford to build before, and all across

the board there is an improvement as a result of the justice which has been accorded to the small province of Prince Edward Island by this government.
In passing one might note also that the dominion government is picking up a greater portion of the total expenditures in the province than ever before; the largest item in history ($11,000,000) stands in the estimates we hope to pass. Referring to one of the statements made yesterday, is this an insult to the provinces? Is it contempt? Has Prince Edward Island been insulted by the way in which this government has handled dominion-provincial relations? I need hardly say that such is not the case. Referring to the situation the Charlottetown Guardian had this to say on January 28, 1958:
Our chief grievance with the St. Laurent government was the manner in which our fiscal claims were ignored, forcing us to impose additional taxes and bringing strong condemnation from Liberal as well as Conservative members of the legislature. Hon. Mr. Harris had nothing to offer us commensurate with what the Diefenbaker government is now legislating to do. Yet the Liberals claim that the country was much better off financially under their administration than it is at present.
I suppose it would be appropriate to go to the head of the government, Premier Matheson who on his way to a certain event which took place in the middle of January, 1958, said that his party would seek a better deal for the maritimes than the Liberal party had ever given before. Then he gave a little explanation; on the result of the 1957 election "that is why the Liberals were defeated last June. They did not give the maritimes half a deal." The statements which have been made by those who say that the provinces of Canada have been insulted by the present government have aroused righteous indignation. The events to which I have referred have taken place in the province which perhaps more than any other deserved a second look and a little more consideration.
This is a new era. There are those who mock and smile about the expression "the new vision." But it is not a joke in the maritime provinces, because we came very near to a state of discouragement and intellectual depression which might have been very dangerous for us. It was because there appeared on the scene a man with a national vision- and you cannot have a national vision unless you are concerned with the problems of all the provinces-that the situation seemed at last to offer hope. That man, the present Prime Minister, came with a national vision and rapidly took measures to deal with our situation.
Yet there are some who say that the government has moved slowly. I can point to government activities in the province of

Prince Edward Island which are being carried out today which would have been impossible before the present dominion government took office. Let no man tell us, in our island province, that this government has been lax in the field we have been discussing. None of us is here to say that a full measure has been meted out; none of us will say to this government that they have heard the last of maritime claims. But a sense of realism and a sense of decency impel us to say that in this field the government has moved and moved with consideration for the provinces.
It is perhaps an inevitable part of the political process that a party in opposition should seek to find some device by which to make itself popular, but I think with regard to this question the opposition has not struck gold. Perhaps it is something like the balloon at the meeting in Ontario which was mentioned yesterday.
On this question of dominion-provincial relations now before us the answer can be found most readily in the maritime provinces, where it is underscored and underlined. One does not have to listen only to Conservative members of parliament; one will find it on the lips of the leaders of those areas, people of all parties who are more devoted to the areas in which they live than to political partisanship. I could if I wished quote from the most ardent Liberal newspapers in the maritime provinces and place upon the record words of commendation and congratulation to this government for action so long delayed and for justice so long denied by its predecessors, for a national policy which began with a recognition that the area from which I come has for too long been denied what was its just due.
Now at last a way has been devised which will give the people of my area an opportunity to go forward with the rest of Canada to the great days which lie ahead.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I do not propose to reply directly, Mr. Speaker, to the very erudite historian from Queens who has just spoken. I have no doubt that in a very short time one of my colleagues from the maritime provinces will address himself to his most interesting and exceedingly well delivered address. I am chiefly concerned about some of the points we heard last night in connection with the magniloquence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). Unfortunately, as so often happens with his spread-eagle type of oratory, we did not hear too much about the resolution that is before us, but we were treated to a rather silk-hatted Barnum-type of trumpeting about other matters of governmental administration. Then, of course, he gave the
Dominion-Provincial Conference signal, as is typical, at the end of his long address by raising his voice as his arguments were weakening and got, as he expected, the applause of the large group of followers behind him. His theme seemed to be at this point that might is right.
I believe we should be reasonably sympathetic toward the Minister of Finance because on many occasions in the last 19 months-somebody said last night 16 months, but I remind the house that in a week it will be 20 months-since this administration took office the minister has certainly had his nose rubbed into a lot of hard facts. The point I want to make is that the country today, despite his form of oratory, is looking behind the rhetoric and is very concerned about the jettisoning of so many promises by this administration. Despite the arguments that we heard last night I remind the Minister of Finance that fog is not dispelled either by a fan or even by a windmill. I just want to remind him of a phrase I have heard him use at least ten times since he became a member of this house, that a tree is known by its fruit. I say the public is certainly equating the promises with performance.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) is recognized as a great admirer of Lincoln. I am sure he has not overlooked one of Lincoln's wise sayings, to the effect that we must not promise what we ought not, lest we be called upon to perform what we cannot. I think that is the position in which the Prime Minister has so frequently found himself recently.
Now, I do not propose at this moment to deal with some of the new estimates about tax sharing revenues that were given by the Minister of Finance in his address last night. It is well known to the house that there is a resolution on the order paper that will permit us to discuss more carefully the financial results of a continuation of the formula of tax sharing to which reference has been made. The minister and I did last night have a word or two with respect to the question of whether or not this had from the beginning, when introduced a year ago, been called by the minister an estimate. I simply want to point out that on January 27, 1958-I was wrong by a day because it was the next sitting of the house, and I said January 25 last night-at page 3849 of Hansard, you will find this reported, and these are the words of the Minister of Finance. He was referring to the new formula that he announced so hurriedly, probably having in his mind that dissolution was very close at hand. He said:
It will assure for the fiscal year_

Dominion-Provincial Conference
I emphasize the word "assure".
-commencing April 1 next an additional sum of $62,203,000-
It is true that in the very small print in the table that was placed upon Hansard the word "estimate" is used. Despite the denial last night of the minister that he ever used that word "assured" I draw the attention of the members to that page of Hansard, 3849, for January 27, 1958. The question before us is not some of the points that we heard from the minister last night, but why not have a dominion-provincial conference before we consider the resolution the minister has on the order paper.
The motion moved by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), and which I seconded yesterday, appears on page 826 of Hansard for February 9, 1959. Since this is a subsequent sitting of the house I think it might be repeated. The motion reads:
This house is of the opinion the government should call a federal-provincial conference at once to deal with serious problems of common concern such as unemployment and fiscal relations.
It is to this that we should direct our attention. I well realize that there are just about 100 members in this house who were not in the house at the time the proposal of January 1958 was advanced. I think it is very desirable that we have on the record the assurances in solemn, definite form that were given that this was an interim matter, and that a dominion-provincial conference would be called at a subsequent date. I refer to the communique of November, 1957 itself which at that time made it exceedingly clear that it was intended to have in the new year another dominion-provincial conference.
This is the indictment against the government at the present time in connection with this motion. Again, they are not carrying out one of their promises which was very, very firmly planted with the Canadian people. The Minister of Finance himself repeatedly emphasized in January, 1958, that this was simply an interim matter. On the other hand, we have before us on the order paper a proposal to renew this formula for another year. The minister said it was an interim measure only for the forthcoming fiscal year. I emphasize those words, "forthcoming fiscal year."
In the debate that took place at that time- I am repeating this because there are so many new members in the house-the former member for Winnipeg North Centre, shrewd as he was, did indicate that there might be a nigger in this proposition. He is quoted on January 28, 1958 at page 3935 as saying that an interim period might last for a long time.

I am afraid he was quite prophetic. At that time the Minister of Finance himself said that the immediate needs-I underline the word "immediate"-of the provinces had been met in the interim measure. He said that when the time was ripe and there was an opportunity-I emphasize the word "opportunity"-for a resumption of the dominion-provincial conference, of course one would be called. Hon. members of the government party who are friendly with the premier of Manitoba or with the premier of Ontario might indicate whether or not they think the immediate needs have been met in those provinces.
The hon. member for Essex East I think very shrewdly gave some ideas yesterday as to why this conference may be postponed. I would add that I am inclined to believe that in the case of the premier of Manitoba the conference may be delayed because that premier does not want to be shown up as less of a champion of his province than his predecessors when they came to dominion-provincial conferences. In the case of the premier of Ontario, I am inclined to think the difficulty may be that, unlike a year and a half ago, there may be no desire to have any display as to who today is the real sahib in connection with the Conservative party.
Last night the minister had something to say about "take it or leave it". In this respect I certainly think I can remind him of a publication which he himself quoted on several occasions in the past when we were debating matters of this kind. I refer to the interim report by the Canadian tax foundation in its comment upon the 1955-56 proposals. This refers particularly to this question of "take it or leave it". This is the comment of Mr. Perry in test 5 as to the desirability of a formula of this kind, and the "take it or leave it" question.
In this respect the author has achieved a delicate balance. There is almost nothing in it to sway a province toward one side or the other.
I ask the house, and the Minister of Finance particularly, what difference, except for one numeral, is there in the proposition he is sponsoring this session and last and the proposition of 1956 which received such bitter condemnation from him and his colleagues? There are two differences. There was the change with respect to one figure which increased a formula figure from 10 per cent to 13 per cent and, of course, there was another disadvantageous feature in so far as the provinces are concerned, in that the revised proposition omitted any reference to stabilization with respect to the new 3 per cent formula.
The Minister of Finance had some very bitter things to say about this formula in

1956. I want to give the house some indication of the kind of language he used then when he was screaming at the keyhole of events. On July 23, 1956 with respect to this formula, a formula which today he is prepared to put forward for the second time for the approval of the house, with the most minor changes and one of those in favour of the federal treasury he said, as reported at page 6287 of Hansard for July 23, 1956:
As to the details of the formula, suffice it to say at this point that it is an actuarial maze to most people. The formula itself would undoubtedly confuse most citizens. Talk of tax equalization payments, provincial revenue stabilization payments, tax rental agreements, gross national product, average personal income, and other expressions in which the formula abounds make it very difficult for the average citizen to appreciate the niceties of the formula.
Well, the niceties of the formula seem to have appealed to the Minister of Finance, because we have a resolution again advancing the formula with only the minor changes I have outlined. But I suggest to the house that the big point is this. The government is by no means consistent. They took the stand in 1956 that in the absence of evidence of agreement on the part of the provinces, this parliament should not be asked to accept the formula. I want to know whether anybody in the government will say that this formula, any more than the other, has received unanimous or majority support from the provincial premiers.
This was the attitude taken by Mr. Drew, the leader of the opposition at that time. He said at page 5999 of Hansard for July 16, 1956:
A government that fails to seek a solution of this problem and puts this matter into rigid statutory form before there has been approval is a government that is not fit to govern.
What evidence can the government give us that this is any more approved today? Yesterday the hon. member for Essex East very effectively gave the house comments from such premiers as the premier of Ontario and the premier of Manitoba. We have heard from the premier of Saskatchewan who sits perhaps in a neutral position in viewing the present government and the administration that went before. This is what the premier of Saskatchewan had to say in relating the present intention of this government to what took place in years gone by:
Former prime minister Louis St. Laurent and the late W. L. Mackenzie King had at least discussed dominion-provincial finances.
That, of course, is not what is done at the present time. The Minister of Finance endeavoured to twit the hon. member for Essex East last night when he was speaking on this proposition. His words were that clothes scarcely suit the hon. member for Essex 66968-9-55
Dominion-Provincial Conference East. Well, let me tell the Minister of Finance that there is always a very considerable increase in the amount of secondhand clothing when we have a Tory administration. I further want to remind the house that there has never been a dominion-provincial conference which has not resulted from some changes in a proposition advanced by a federal administration. That opportunity is not being provided when we are asked simply to renew the present formula.
I think we have to analyse why we are not having a dominion-provincial conference, despite the very firm commitments made by the Prime Minister in two election campaigns, despite the wording of the communique after the dominion-provincial conference of November, 1957, despite what the Minister of Finance said a year ago that this was an interim proposition for the current fiscal year. I think the hon. member for Essex East again had some shrewd observations on that point. He referred to the deficit; he referred to the obvious endeavour not to embarrass some Conservative provincial premiers who were soon to have provincial elections.
But I think there are reasons beyond those, and on this matter the Minister of Finance was singularly silent. He usually does not lack words, but in explaining why we were not having a conference he was, I say, singularly silent. I suggest that the primary reason we are not having a dominion-provincial conference is that the government, as in so many other matters, is lacking in capacity for constructive decision. They are merely carrying on the attitude they have shown on so many other urgent and important questions, a "wait and see" policy; and they are simply trying to sit the situation out.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) was pretty shrewd, as usual, in matters of this kind. On June 3, 1958, as found at page 804 of Hansard, he had this to say:
If the government does not act to change the statute in this session and if normal events follow we are going to be faced somewhere about next February or March with another urgent situation and we are going to have hon. gentlemen opposite saying another crisis has arisen because-and they will use words to this effect-"you talked so much we did not have time to have a federal-provincial conference", and we are going to be faced with another unilateral decree. That just is not good enough.
That again was most prophetic. Oh, the government gave some reasons. They were exceedingly puny reasons. One was that parliament was sitting. We have had many dominion-provincial conferences when parliament was sitting. It was said that the legislatures were sitting. We have had federal-provincial conferences when the legislatures
866	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Conference were sitting, and I have no doubt whatever that if the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance extended invitations right now to the provincial premiers they would see to it that their legislatures permitted their absence for time enough to attend a conference of this importance. I suggest that this should be done.
I think another real reason for the failure to hold a conference during all this period of time, despite the very Arm and ringing declarations about it, is that the present government lacks a policy to put before such a conference if it were held. They do not know what their policy is, and in this connection I think we find support for this view because when many prominent members of the present ministry were on the opposition side of the house they indicated that they were not at all happy with the type of formula we had for tax sharing between the federal government and the provinces. I can quote innumerable statements by members of the present cabinet that would lead anyone to the conclusion that they wanted something new in the way of policy. They talked about reallocating taxing powers and reallocating constitutional powers. I think we can very properly ask the ministry, are they abandoning and discarding the views they so often expressed in the house in the past?
I have here a statement of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). As found at page 6015 of Hansard for July 16, 1956 he said:
We in this party believe and have said time and time again that there should be a reallocation of responsibilities, that there should be a reallocation of taxation powers-
The Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) took this view. In that same year the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) - I will also quote what he said earlier-had this to say as found at page 6064 of Hansard for July 17:
But the root of the matter has not been attacked, and that is the division of responsibility between the dominion government and the provincial jurisdictions.
Then we have the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), as found at page 6335 of Hansard for July 23, 1956. He talked about the exchange of constitutional responsibilities. Is this what is in the mind of the government? If so, one can imagine that the provincial premiers would like to know it at the earliest opportunity. This indeed, was the view of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on May 10, 1955. As found at page 3647 of Hansard he said:
Dominion-provincial conferences may continue to be a necessity for Canada. If so, they should be
[Mr. Benidickson.l

restricted to the core of the problem, the division of administrative responsibility between the dominion and the provinces, and the division of fields of taxation.
We have heard that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is credited with being the architect of the victories of the Conservative party in recent election campaigns.

speechtext:
He credits himself, as somebody says; but in any event is this an indication that he is going to be the architect of policy with respect to dominion-provincial relations? I ask the house, Mr. Speaker, what is the chance of anything worth while being achieved by study groups consisting of officials of the provincial and federal governments if they are all wanting to know the views of the many new provincial administrations and the views of the new federal administration? They all know that the members of the federal cabinet have expressed so many views in the past that a very substantial change might be made in the set-up now that they have come to power.
I say that we are putting the cart before the horse when we suggest that officials acting in the dark, without instructions from political leadership, meet without knowing what are the policies of their political chiefs. There is doubt about equalization. How can officials of governments meet with any confidence when there is doubt even as to the type of thing that would meet with the approval of their political chiefs?
The Minister of Finance is very evasive with respect to his stand on equalization. Oh, he talks about equalization, but when an effort is made to find out just what kind of equalization we find that the minister is quite silent. On June 2, 1958, as found at page 742 of Hansard, an effort was made to try to find out what was the minister's view in this respect. The hon. member for Essex East asked the minister this question about equalization:
Does that mean that the hon. minister now accepts the principle of equalization on the basis of the position of the two highest provinces?
The Minister of Finance replied:
That is not what I said at ail.
Indeed, he was most vague with respect to the type of equalization he might provide. What are some of the other reasons for the lack of policy? I think the leader of the C.C.F. group made a pretty solid observation yesterday when he talked about suitcase government and said there were simply not enough ministers around who would have direct responsibility for matters of this kind during the recess. That is not a view held exclusively

by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). Quite a number of other people have expressed that view. I quote from the Winnipeg Tribune, which is not unfriendly to the present administration. That paper made this comment during the recess:
Led by the ever-mobile Prime Minister, the Conservative cabinet is emerging as the most footloose band of have briefcase-will travel administrators in Canada's history.
I think everybody who has been in the house for any length of time knows there is no one in the press gallery who is normally more friendly to a Conservative administration than our good friend Mr. Norman MacLeod. On January 14 last he made this comment:
-any log of the movements of the cabinet ministers since they assumed office would show a figure of absenteeism that no private enterprise could afford to admit. Literally, no international occasion has been too unimportant for some representative of the Canadian cabinet to attend.
The other day, after the reading of the speech from the throne, the Financial Times made this comment:
The moment of truth is now at hand. _______Let
Ghana for one moment rest on its laurels; let the world make statements about freedom unspecified and couched in no compelling terms. Let Asians mind, for only a brief moment, their own business while the government in Canada attends to its own.
These are comments by people outside this house. It was a fairly shrewd observation of the leader of the C.C.F. in that respect. I think perhaps another reason that we have not had the conference is that at a conference I have no doubt the present ministry, particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) would be asked about the money policy of this government. Certainly they did not hesitate to refer to that matter at the last convening on November 25, 1957. As reported on page 11 of the proceedings, the Prime Minister said this:
Here in Canada, quietly and gradually over the last three months, the tight money situation has been eased. Those whose business it is to follow the bond market will have noticed it-
Even in the election campaign the same kind of thing was said at a later date. As late as March 14, 1958, the Prime Minister in Calgary, is quoted in the Winnipeg Tribune, as follows:
The Prime Minister claimed that interest rates had fallen sharply as a result of government action since last June-
I must also quote the Minister of Finance; he would not want to be left out. When we had a similar debate a year ago, on January 27, 1958, as reported at page 3852 of Hansard of that date, he had this to say:
That tight money policy has now been eased- 66968-9-55J
Dominion-Provincial Conference
He referred to the municipalities.
-in line with the policies of this government.
The question that I raise-and I am sure the provincial premiers would raise it-is this. If when interest rates are going down the situation is due to the policy of the government, what is the policy of the government that has resulted in the most expensive interest rates we have had for 25 years or 30 years? Of course we know what the stock answer is. The stock answer is that on an upturn of interest rates the wicked Americans are responsible. But when interest rates were going down, both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance said the situation was due to the good management of the government. I want to know whether or not the administration feel that they picked up some votes by claiming that they were responsible for effecting the interest rates described in the quotations that I have given. We know what rates we have had in recent times.
