I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that this would be one of the questions that certainly would be raised by the provincial premiers because the cost of their money is so important to them. But, Mr. Speaker, I simply close on that subject by saying that even in the current issue of the Financial Post it is indicated that these interest rates are still likely to rise.
In debates of this kind in the past the Minister of Finance was always talking about making room for the provinces in connection with expenditures. He denounced centralization and said that the previous administration was not making room. He used a very striking phrase at one time. In 1956, as reported at page 6295 of Hansard, he said this:
The camel got its head into the tent, and instead of being content to share the tent with the former occupant has been busy trying to push the camel driver out.
When they look at the estimates that were brought down the other day, I wonder what will be the reaction of the provincial premiers, particularly when they know how difficult it is to raise the sums that will be required by them.
We heard a great deal about the municipalities. The minister for development in the province of Ontario this summer made a statement that any additional money that Ontario received from Ottawa would be passed on to the municipalities. That, of course, is exceedingly interesting to the municipalities in my province. In addition to that, we had many indications that something

Dominion-Provincial Conference in the nature of a new deal could be expected by the municipalities if we had a new administration.
Of course, they had an informal conference with the new administration and the answers that the government had in the election campaigns were certainly not the answers that they had for the municipalities when the municipalities met members of this administration last September. May I just quote some of the impartial observers who heard the lecture given by the Prime Minister to the municipalities. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) gave yesterday the six or seven points or requests that were made by the municipalities. I will not repeat them because my time is running short. However, Mr. Harvey Hickey had this to say:
it-
He refers to the conference with the mayors.
-was informal if the word is interpreted to mean that no one was giving anything away.
Then in addition in the same article Mr. Hickey said that after the Prime Minister spoke to the representatives of the municipalities, one newspaperman jokingly remarked to one of the cabinet ministers on the similarity between what the Prime Minister said and what Mr. St. Laurent used to say to the mayors and reeves, and the answer of the cabinet minister, as quoted in this article, was:
Maybe the same people wrote the speech-
There has not been much change of policy in this respect. I should like rapidly just to indicate some comments that were made at this time. I have one headline from the Winnipeg Tribune: "P.M. throws cold water on hopes for more aid". Another one indicates "Defense, welfare cost curbs cash to cities, P.M. warns mayors". This is not the way in which the former mayor of Oshawa used to talk and who is now in a key position in the present cabinet. I refer to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). He used fairly strong language in this respect as to the needs of the municipalities. He said, as reported in an article in January 1957:
A complete realignment of long-term taxing powers is needed.
Reference is made to shortsighted, pessimistic and unrealistic policies which result in expensive costs of money to the municipalities.
I have referred to some of these things. I think the administration should indicate what their attitude is to these matters which are of vital concern to the provinces and to the municipalities. Beyond what was mentioned yesterday in the excellent address by the hon. member for Essex East, I think
[Mr. Benidickson.l
that the provinces at a conference would want to know why there is any necessity for postponing until 1960 a conference on conservation. I think that many of them- particularly the western provinces and indeed the consuming provinces in eastern Canada -would want to urge the government to move quickly and to indicate what its policy is with respect to the rules for oil and gas industry. The Financial Post this week indicates that delay in matters of this kind may cost many people hundreds of jobs in 1959. The feature editorial states the urgency in this language:
The oil, gas and allied industries must promptly be released from their present purgatory of fear, apprehension and uncertainty so that important projects can get ahead in this coming construction season.
These are all matters that vitally affect unemployment. I am sure that the administration would benefit immensely by taking the premiers into their confidence because so many efforts along that line must be joint efforts. The fact that they are left in a vacuum, that they do not know the policies of the administration on such matters as I have indicated, and others, is contributing in a large fashion to the unemployment we have at the present time.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words must be words of congratulation to the administration for what I consider to be the policy which is the most forward-looking and the most sympathetic to the provinces in regard to provincial-federal relations in a quarter of a century. Since the last war, as all hon. members know, great inequities had developed between the provinces and the federal government as regards the sharing of the tax dollar. These inequities across those ten years became at times so acute that in some ways they seemed to threaten our federation, as the provinces and municipalities sought always a larger share of the national revenue to meet ever-increasing demands for public and social service. As the revenues of the federal government were increasing year by year the share of the tax dollar that was available to municipalities and to provinces was actually decreasing, while at the same time the demands upon those two levels of government kept increasing. Finally, in the face of continual demands, the former administration sought to try to quiet the outcry of the nation by calling the federal-provincial conference of 1956. From that conference, all hon. members know, emerged the formula, very grudgingly given which provided 10 per cent of income taxes, 9 per cent of corporation taxes and 50 per cent of the succession duty revenue to the provinces.

It was very interesting, Mr. Speaker, to hear the words of the member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), and to hear of the new consciousness in the Liberal party of the problem of federal-provincial relations. In a fiery, ringing speech he challenged the government on its record of keeping its promises to the provinces, and challenged it on the basis of meeting the needs of the provinces at this time. From the way he spoke he announced a policy which was new to all people who had heard the Liberals speak before on dominion-provincial relations. He suggested that if the Liberals were in office they would immediately call a conference with the provinces. They would open all the vaults of Ottawa, and every provincial treasurer could find here everything which he needed to meet all problems which arose in his province.
I sat and listened to his speech carefully. It sounded good, but I am from the maritimes, and down in the maritimes our experience has been to beware of the Grits bearing gifts. Our experience with the actions of the Liberal party has been that they are a long way from the policy we hear so clearly ringing out from Liberal members of the house today. We find often, when we examine Liberal policy on this matter of federal-provincial relations, that like so many other things, the policy turns out to be like the Cheshire cat in "Alice in Wonderland": As you examine it, "it fades away till there is nothing left but the grin."
I would like to take you back, Mr. Speaker, a few years, to 1955 and 1956. They were days when everywhere across this land could be heard the complaints of the municipalities and of the provinces, that they were being squeezed, that they had to skimp to keep from running into deficits. In my own province a deficit was always very near. In the budget and the accounts of 1956 Nova Scotia was very close to the wire. In the following year it faced a deficit, and all during this time, all during those so-called good years when municipalities in my own province were facing these tremendous problems the government at Ottawa was wallowing in tremendous surplus.
It had lots of other money for many other projects in Canada but none at all to meet the needs of the municipalities in their constant striving to provide for the need for social and public services. There was no money at all to meet the growing demands of the provinces. The continual requests and prayers of the municipalities and the provinces fell upon deaf ears here in Ottawa. Take any single factor of provincial life in Nova Scotia in 1955 or 1956 and you see the same thing. You see us with an educational
Dominion-Provincial Conference system in jeopardy, with many more students than we had schools to accommodate them. You see staggered student attendance; not nearly sufficient classrooms to provide for a decent education. Children were out of school more than in because seats could not be provided for them. We had a highway program that had shrunk, across the previous ten years, to the point where it was no longer meeting the needs of the province; it was totally inadequate. The program of new highways had slowed to a snail's pace, and there was barely sufficient money in the treasury of the province of Nova Scotia to maintain the already substandard highway system.
With regard to social welfare, we had nothing in the provincial treasury to help meet the increasing demands of our people and, as hon. members know, this is a particular problem in the maritime provinces, because the record of the Liberal administration in these provinces has been such that young people had to leave their homes year after year to find a living elsewhere. We have a much larger percentage than other provinces of people who are in need of social assistance. We have people of 65 and over who need pensions in order to carry on. We have people who are blind and disabled. We have more of them in the maritimes than anywhere else in Canada. Our provincial treasury could not meet the demands of these people for help and for services. At the same time, while municipalities suffered and skimped, while we in Nova Scotia and in the other maritime provinces went without, surpluses piled up here in Ottawa. No attention was paid at all to our needs.
Mr. Speaker, that was in 1956. By good fortune, by good luck for Canada, the arrogant government that centralized all money in Ottawa but could find nothing for the people of the provinces was defeated and a new government came into office. Immediately, in response to his promise to call a provincial-federal conference to discuss this most urgent question, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) arranged a conference of the provincial premiers to consider the immediate problems of federal-provincial relations. The result of that conference is known to all. It meant a 30 per cent increase for the provinces in the provincial share of income tax. It meant, of most importance to Nova Scotia and to the provinces toy the sea, the $100 million Atlantic adjustment grant, a grant which came just in time to save our provinces by the sea from bankruptcy. This extra $25 million a year poured into the Atlantic

Dominion-Provincial Conference provinces has meant a new lease of life for my province, as well as for our sister provinces. It meant tangible things.
For example, education, that had declined to the point where it might almost be called a disgrace, blossomed with the help of that money into a new program that has meant a terrific boost for Nova Scotia and a new life for our people. Mr. Speaker, over the last two years, with the help of this new aid from Ottawa, 162 new schools have been built in Nova Scotia, the biggest schoolbuilding program in our history. In 1956 we faced the position that because our treasury could not afford to pay decent salaries to our teachers, we were losing our teaching staffs. We were approaching the point where our educational staff would no longer be with us. The extra aid for the province and, in turn, the aid from the province to the municipalities in terms of assistance with teachers' salaries and so on meant that at least this problem of educational salaries had been met for the present.
I do not say that all problems of education have been met in Nova Scotia. It would be impossible in a year and a half, even with the help we have had, to turn back the clock and make up for 20 years of retrogression in Nova Scotia.
We come now to highways. In 1958, with the aid of the money made available to our provincial treasurer, the province of Nova Scotia paved 368 miles of highway, the biggest paving program in our history. Over the last two years the Nova Scotia department of highways has installed 236 new bridges, the biggest bridge building program in the history of the province. In addition, the federal government is making available under the roads to resources program the sum of $7,500,000 in the course of the next five years. This will mean an extra million and a half dollars a year for highways which we could not otherwise afford to spend. In my constituency alone the extra highway money will represent an increase of approximately $3 million in highway construction over a five-year period.
At the same time the municipalities are receiving much needed help through grants which could be made to them by the province from money which came from the government at Ottawa. In Nova Scotia in 1958 the province was able to pay 50 per cent of the cost of hospitalization to municipalities, and this great burden was lifted from the backs of the town and city councils and county councils in the province. Aid to the provinces has meant aid to the municipalities in terms of grants for the building of schools, and in terms of increased salaries for teachers. It

has also meant-and I emphasize this as being, perhaps, most important of all-that in many cases where municipal taxes have been rising year after year they now have a much greater tendency to remain constant.
I have read in some instances of county tax rates in Nova Scotia decreasing for the first time in many years. What it all amounts to is this: that the new policy of this government in the short one and a half years during which it has been in office has been a tremendous boon to Nova Scotia and, I am sure, to the other provinces of Canada as well.
In addition to the money provided as a result of the conference held in 1957 and under the adjustment grant, I should also like to draw the attention of hon. members to the tremendous volume of new assistance which has been made available across this nation under the conditional grants and the cost sharing programs. I should like to illustrate this point once more by referring to my own province of Nova Scotia. In addition to the adjustment money we have seen a great increase in money benefits under the Old Age Assistance Act, in blind persons pensions and in pensions paid to disabled persons. We have seen an increase in grants for hospital construction, in grants for the construction of the trans-Canada highway, in university grants and grants for building picnic and camping sites alongside the trans-Canada highway and elsewhere. I shall not take up the time of the house by putting on record all the figures showing the assistance we have received from these different programs during the relatively short period that this government has been in office, but let me say that in 1956-57, the last year of the former administration, Nova Scotia received by way of cost sharing programs and conditional grants the sum of $5,593,000. In 1957-58, the first year of the present administration, that amount rose to $8,990,000; an increase of 61 per cent in one year of Conservative administration. In 1958-59 the amount rose to $16,210,000, an amount which represents an increase of 190 per cent as compared with the amount paid during the last year the Liberal party was in power.
It is my hope that the generous policy of the present government toward the provinces and toward the maritimes provinces in particular will be continued. Nova Scotia needs help. It went down so far during the last 20 years and became so impoverished through lack of industry and lack of means to earn a stable living that it needs great help. Our maritime provinces need assistance more than any other province, and I must say we all appreciate the sympathy and assistance which the other provinces of

Canada showed at the conference in 1957 when they so readily agreed to the adjustment grant to the Atlantic provinces. If we continue as we are doing, if we continue to rebuild our education program and to go ahead with increased public services, and if we continue to industrialize the maritimes, I believe the day is not too far distant when we shall be able to support ourselves. We shall not have to come before the other provinces of Canada and before the government of Canada seeking help in order to maintain our essential services. Certainly there is a new approach evident today in dominion-provincial affairs. The provinces receive a sympathetic hearing in Ottawa; their problems are more quickly met. A continuing committee to deal with the fiscal problems of all the provinces is something we have needed for a long time.
We have only begun, of course, to repair the damage which has been done to provincial relations in the course of the last 20 years. We have only made a start. In the years that are to come we have a great job to do in building up federal-provincial relations and in seeing to it that each section of this great country has its fair share of opportunity. We must all keep in mind that each province and each region in this nation has its rights and that these rights must be safeguarded. When men from all parts of this land regard the problems of their neighbours with sympathy, and try to see their points of view, only then will we be able to make this nation the strong nation that it can become. We have made tremendous progress in provincial relations in the last year and a half. Even greater opportunities for progress lie ahead. I must say I was very pleased to hear this attitude expressed in speeches both today and yesterday by hon. members who belong to the Liberal party. In particular, the words of the hon. member for Essex East when he insisted that provincial rights should be respected and when he mentioned unity as being the key problem in Canada, were certainly good words to hear. Undoubtedly they represented a change in the policy of the party to which he belongs and which for 20 years would rather rely on the principle of divide and conquer, setting one province against another -Ontario against Quebec, the maritimes against Ontario and Quebec, and so on-than to foster Canadian unities.
Mr. Speaker, I hope the Liberal party is sincere in its new policy with regard to national unity. I hope, in particular, that their policy with regard to dominion-provincial relations has been renewed and refreshed. Hon. members will recall how interested the nation was in the question of
Dominion-Provincial Conference dominion-provincial relations in 1957. As an example of the outlook of the Liberal party on provincial relations at that time they allowed candidates to go from platform to platform in my province and to appear on the radio and television with this slogan: "Save Nova Scotia from the Diefenbaker-Frost alliance".
This, Mr. Speaker, is the very thing that weakens this nation. It strikes at the ankles of Canada. It was the attitude, the theme of the late Liberal government in the matter of dominion-provincial relations. I will say also, that the recent speeches of these Liberal members are a far cry from their former attitude. They are a far cry from the time when Liberal policy and philosophy in connection with dominion-provincial relations could be expressed in the very simple, straightforward phrase, which I recall particularly when I hear them speak of Manitoba and Ontario, the phrase, "not a flve-cent piece for a Tory province".

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
was very pleased indeed to hear about the wonderful progress that is being made in the province of Nova Scotia. I was very heartily in accord with the proposal of the government a year ago to make $7.5 million more available to Nova Scotia. If a relatively small sum like $7.5 million is able to work such wonders for one of the Atlantic provinces, I like to think how much more the proposed $150 million to be spent on the igloo to igloo highway program would do if it were used in the Atlantic provinces. I am sure the report would be even more glorious.
However, Mr. Speaker, the cruel fact remains that when compared to a year ago there is more hardship in Canada because of unemployment and there is much more economic uncertainty on the Canadian national scene. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) calls upon the government to call a federal-provincial conference at once to deal with serious problems of common concern such as unemployment and fiscal relations. Most of the speeches today have dealt with the matter of fiscal relations. I wish to underline the reference to unemployment. It is for that purpose now, Mr. Speaker, that I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding thereafter the following words:
"and should present for consideration of such conference federal proposals:
(a)	to assume complete responsibility for the welfare of the employable unemployed.
(b)	to ensure employment opportunities to all Canadians willing and able to work; and

Dominion-Provincial Conference
(c)	to reduce the burden of interest rates on new provincial and municipal borrowings".
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, when on Wednesday last I attempted to move the adjournment of the house in order to call specific attention to this matter of unemployment you reminded me, as is recorded on page 677 of Hansard, that there would be an opportunity for a general debate on Monday on a subject of the choice of the opposition. I am very pleased to note that the spokesman of the official opposition on this occasion has brought up the seriousness of unemployment and is calling for a dominion-provincial conference to discuss possible remedies for that problem.
I should like to recall to your memory, Mr. Speaker, the statements on that occasion of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) when he spoke on a point of order. He said that on the subject of unemployment the C.C.F., and these are his words, "had practically no suggestions to make." The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) went a little beyond that. He is usually not so conservative in his estimate of things as is the Minister of Public Works for whom we have very high regard in the province of British Columbia and who, as you know, did not say the C.C.F. had not offered any ideas. He said we had offered practically no ideas. However, the Prime Minister said, and these are his words as recorded on page 677 of Hansard:
-though hon. gentlemen opposite, having the opportunity to make suggestions, made none.
I think that was a very wild statement coming from the Prime Minister of Canada, because I am sure that if he will read even the speeches of some of his own members, he will find many proposals to deal with the situation known as unemployment in Canada. Certainly, in the speeches of opposition members there were many more.
It is because the Minister of Public Works and the Prime Minister are asking the opposition to present their program on unemployment that I mean to do so this afternoon, in exactly the same comprehensive manner as the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) on January 29 last presented our program on the subject of inflation. We consider these to be the two major problems, and they should receive the serious attention of thinking people not only in this house but throughout the whole of Canada.
The unemployment situation is very serious indeed. I believe it was the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) who pointed out that these people who are unemployed are actually in need, and that they are not to be regarded as merely so many numbers in

a recitation of cold statistics. We have once before in Canadian history gone through heavy unemployment, and we have seen the suffering and the misery that the people have had to endure. We have no intention of again going through a period such as that. In presenting our program I hope to present it as a program that might be presented by this federal government to a federal-provincial conference because we realize that the assistance of the provincial governments is necessary.
It will be seen that our program is evolutionary rather than revolutionary. We usually take account of past events when we make recommendations as to what should be done in the years ahead. I fully realize that the cost of our program may appear to some hon. members to be simply fantastic. However, we contend that it is not beyond the capabilities of our nation to meet this cost and we are quite prepared to tell the government how they can find the money necessary.
We would like to advise the government to cease this looking for scapegoats. It is hardly satisfactory to tell the wage earner that the farmer cannot buy the automobile he makes because the farmer has received more than he should. It is hardly satisfactory to tell the man engaged in agriculture that the industrial worker cannot buy the bacon and eggs because of these high wages. It is hardly satisfactory to blame communists for our own economic ills. It is hardly satisfactory to blame foreign competition, and I am very surprised when I see so many leading Canadians blaming the element of competition for our ills. It is hardly satisfactory to blame the type of flag we use or the type of anthem we sing for our unemployed. It will not do very much longer even to be blaming the former Liberal government for the state of unemployment in Canada. The people of Canada are not going to be misled by any kind of diversion, and they are not taking their eyes or their thoughts away from the problems that are facing us. The vision that is there, in fact, really exists in the imagination of the political propagandist whose responsibility it was to prepare the election program.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I now wish to raise a point of order and submit to you that this amendment is clearly out of order. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment which has been under debate since yesterday afternoon is one calling for the holding of a dominion-provincial conference to discuss matters of common concern to the dominion and the provinces, and unemployment and fiscal relations were mentioned by way of illustration of what are matters of common concern.
The amendment which has just been introduced by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam proposes to amend that amendment by adding these words:
And should-
This is a direction to the government. I continue:
And should present for consideration of such conference federal proposals:
(a)	to assume complete responsibility for the welfare of the employable unemployed;
(b)	to ensure employment opportunities to all Canadians willing and able to work; and
(c)	to reduce the burden of interest rates on new provincial and municipal borrowings.
Every one of those measures would involve the expenditure presumably of millions of dollars; every one of them. Here are three of them which my hon. friend in introducing his amendment has chosen to call the program of his party.
This is not put forward as something which the government might be invited to consider;

Dominion-Provincial Conference this is put forward on the basis of a direction from the house to the government to submit to a dominion-provincial conference proposals which would call for the expenditure of millions of dollars. Such an amendment at any time would be most manifestly out of order. The only way in which such a measure, whether it be a resolution, a bill or an amendment, could originate in this house is on a recommendation of His Excellency the Governor General and placed before the house by one of His Excellency's ministers. On that ground this resolution is completely out of order. Nothing could be more manifestly out of order than this kind of resolution which constitutes a direction by the house to the government to bring forward proposals which call for the expenditure of millions of dollars.
This is not the only ground on which this resolution is out of order, Mr. Speaker. This resolution has nothing in common with the amendment which it purports or proposes to amend. This is something entirely new: this is something not germane to the amendment now under debate in the house. I can think of other reasons why this amendment is clearly out of order, but I think the point is so plain and clear that I do not need to detain you or the house on the point. But I will refer to the ruling of Mr. Speaker Black on May 24, 1932. You will find it recorded in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, at page 710. The gist of the ruling is as follows:
A private member cannot move, on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair for committee of supply, an amendment to the effect that the government should proceed without delay with a certain undertaking involving an expenditure of public money.
This ruling was made on the occasion of a government motion to resolve the house into committee of supply. A private member moved an amendment but I will not attempt to read the full text of the amendment which was a very lengthy one. In effect, it sought an expression of the opinion of the house that the government ought to proceed without delay with certain steps which would have involved the expenditure of money. I quote:
Mr. Cahan raised the point of order: That the proposed resolution involved a very large and unparalleled expenditure of money by way of nationalizing the Beauharnois power project and developing and extending it, and such a resolution could be introduced only by the government, with the approval of His Excellency the Governor General, who should recommend it to the house.
Mr. Speaker Black said:
In my opinion the objection raised by the secretary of state is well taken.

I will pass over the next few sentences.
-it is not in order for a private member to move the resolution, nor would it be in order for a member of the government to move it without following well-defined procedure relating to the presentation and discussion of such resolutions, as defined by standing order 60 of this house, which further safeguards the principle by prohibiting the consideration and debate of a motion which involves any public aid or charge upon the people, even when made by a member of the government, upon the day it is made-
He then proceeds to quote section 54 of the British North America Act, quoted in Bourinot at page 406, and then gives this further quotation from Bourinot:
No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian commons receiving the authority of the crown through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer.
Mr. Speaker Black went on to say:
In my opinion this resolution if passed would be a direct order from the house to the government to do certain things which would involve an expenditure of public money. Therefore I say such resolution is not in order when moved by a private member.
That was the ruling of Mr. Speaker Black on May 24, 1932. You have before you, Mr. Speaker, a resolution of precisely the same nature that comes within precisely the same ban. This resolution now before you, in the language of Mr. Speaker Black, "if passed would be a direct order from the house to the government to do certain things which would involve an expenditure of public money." For this as well as the other reasons I have put forward I submit that this amendment is clearly out of order.

speechtext:
If I may say a word on the point of order that has been raised I should like to deal first with the contention that the subamendment is not relevant to the amendment. The amendment moved yesterday by the hon. member for Essex East reads as follows:
This house is of the opinion the government should call a federal-provincial conference at once to deal with serious problems of common concern such as unemployment and fiscal relations.
Our subamendment reads in part as follows:
-and should present for consideration of such conference federal proposals:
(a)	to assume complete responsibility for the welfare of the employable unemployed.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that is a very relevant amendment to the section of the

main amendment having to do with unemployment. Subparagraph (b) of our amendment reads as follows:
(b)	to ensure employment opportunities to all Canadians willing and able to work.
Certainly that has to do with the whole question of solving unemployment. The main amendment calls for a federal-provincial conference to deal with serious problems of common concern such as unemployment and fiscal relations. I would suggest that within the realm of fiscal relations certainly comes the whole question of the interest policy of the government and the interest rates that must be borne by provinces and municipalities in connection with their borrowings. The fiscal policies of the government and its fiscal relations with the provinces have a very definite bearing on the question of interest rates.
I take it that the main contention of the Minister of Finance as to the validy of the subamendment is that its terminology would force the government to spend many millions of dollars. I submit that the wording of the subamendment is in the traditional form. First of all it says that "this house is of the opinion", merely expressing an abstract opinion of the house. I do not have the reference here but I can remember that a few years ago the house expressed its opinion to the government in power at the time that the subsidy on milk should be continued. This opinion was expressed unanimously by the house. The government did not comply with the expression of opinion but nonetheless the opinion was expressed.
If an amendment containing an expression of opinion is passed it does not force the government to bring in measures involving a cost of millions of dollars. If that were the case it would be farcical to debate private members' motions because almost every single private member's motion on the order paper, if it were considered by the government to be a direction to the government, would be a direction for the expenditure of money. The phraseology of such motions is in the traditional form, namely that in the opinion of the house the government should consider the advisability of doing so and so. The phrase "in the opinion of the house" is in the main amendment moved by the hon. member for Essex East and in the subamendment we ask the government to present certain proposals to the conference for consideration.
In the past we have had a government present green book proposals to such a conference for consideration and one could argue that as a result of these proposals having been submitted there had been no cost to the federal treasury. I submit that having regard to the terms in which the amendment 66968-9-56i
Dominion-Provincial Conference and the subamendment together are drafted the subamendment merely asks the house to express an opinion. It asks the government to give consideration. It asks the government to present certain proposals to the conference for consideration.
I submit that in the traditional sense this in no way constitutes an expenditure of money by the house. After having given the subamendment the most careful consideration, I submit to Your Honour that it is definitely in order.

What is submitted to you here, Mr. Speaker, is not that in the opinion of the house the government should consider something but that in the opinion of the house the government should present for consideration to the dominion-provincial conference, which is an entirely different matter. This is not submitted for the consideration of the government. This is a direction to the government.
I invite the attention of the Chair to the fact that similar words were used in the amendment of May 24, 1932, which Mr. Speaker Black ruled out of order. The amendment which he ruled out of order ran thus:
Inasmuch as parliament . . . declared the Beau-harnois canal and the works appurtenant thereto to be a work for the general advantage of Canada-
Note these words, Mr. Speaker.
-it is the opinion of this house that the government should proceed without delay to determine the legality of the claim of the province of Quebec-

-and should it be determined that the ownership of such power is properly vested in the dominion then this government should submit, at the earliest possible date, the necessary legislation enabling the government to exercise the said rights of ownership to nationalize the whole project-
And so on.
And further in the opinion of this house that the government should without delay take all necessary and proper steps to determine whether or not the act passed by the legislature of Quebec . . . and the amendments thereto are ultra vires- And further in the opinion of this house a royal commission should be appointed to investigate the reasons-

Dominion-Provincial Conference
And so on.
Mr. Speaker, the amendment introduced today must have been drawn with some eye on the language used in the amendment of 1932 because it could scarcely be more completely on all fours with it or more completely governed by the decision made by Mr. Speaker Black on that occasion when he ruled that amendment out of order as one which would be a direct order from the house to do certain things which would involve the expenditure of public money.

I believe the hon. member has the rest of the amendment. We believe that on this matter of unemployment which is being proposed as one for discussion at the proposed meeting of the dominion government with the provincial governments there are a number of immediate actions that must be taken at this time. We have therefore divided our proposals into two definite and distinct sets
[Mr, Fleming (Eglinton) .1

of recommendations. We have listed proposals of immediate urgency. The first one is that the government, in view of the length of time that many people must be unemployed, should immediately make to the provinces an offer to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act in such a way as to increase the weekly benefits payable thereunder. We believe that the government should immediately offer to utilize the offices of the unemployment insurance commission across Canada in order to deal with all employable unemployed, thereby removing these people from the jurisdiction of provincial and municipal departments of social welfare. We believe that an employable unemployed person ought not to be treated in or dealt with by a social welfare department. Rather, we believe that he properly belongs in the offices of the unemployment insurance commission. The third immediate recommendation is that the unemployment insurance benefits be payable until work is again found, the cost of such expansion of benefits to be borne entirely out of federal consolidated revenue and not out of the revenues of the provinces as is the case at the present time.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may continue with my advice to the government with regard to what offers it ought to make to the provinces on the subject of unemployment,
Dominion-Provincial Conference I propose that this government should also immediately offer to extend coverage under the Unemployment Insurance Act so as to include more, or if at all possible all, Canadian workers. This alone would relieve the provincial governments of considerable responsibility in looking after unemployed who have not the protection of the Unemployment Insurance Act at the present time.
I believe that the federal government should offer to the provinces to enlarge the scope of the Unemployment Insurance Act so as to give some protection to whole communities against the closing of any major industry. At the present time, the closing of Kitimat becomes, to a great extent, the responsibility of the government of British Columbia. The disaster in Nova Scotia becomes the major responsibility of the government of Nova Scotia. We have on numerous occasions, by means of resolutions, suggestions-and the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) has one on the order paper now, No. 14-called for the establishment of some type of machinery to be incorporated in the Unemployment Insurance Act whereby the provincial governments and municipalities will not have to bear the brunt whenever a major industry ceases to exist.
We recommend that the federal government should offer to extend their winter work program to May 1, and the federal government should offer to pay a larger share of the costs than they are at the present time. We recommend that the federal government should offer to re-activate the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act so as to make available low interest funds to municipalities who will participate in the winter work program.
Then-and this is, I think, maybe not of specific urgency, but certainly of immediate urgency-the federal government should offer to the provincial governments to undertake to share the cost of a major adult education and training program. Canada still urgently needs trained doctors, dentists, nurses, librarians, social workers, teachers, physical education teachers, civil servant officers, veterinarians, technicians and so on, to be trained in a program similar to that available for veterans after world war II, and to include a living allowance for these adult students while they are being trained to fill a national need. Mr. Speaker, many of these people, because of age or because of technological advances or automation, will, unless given training in some new occupation, never again be able to find useful employment. The federal government should relieve the provincial governments by recognizing the problem and undertaking to take the lead in this

Dominion-Provincial Conference regard. We believe that at this proposed conference the federal government should once again do as the federal government did in its 1945 green book proposals, that is once and for all to assume the complete cost of looking after Canada's employable unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, we have also long term solutions which we feel Ottawa should offer in its discussions with the provinces. However, we realize that that might not be possible at just one conference. Many, many conferences might be needed. Mention was made by the previous speaker of the aid that Ottawa has given in the field of highway building in his province of Nova Scotia. We feel that the federal government must offer to aid provinces and municipalities to meet their social investment capital needs. Under those capital needs of the provinces and municipalities such offers could be made as the sharing of the cost of a national highways program, rather than the present policy of sharing the cost of only one trans-Canada highway. We feel that the federal government should offer to share in the capital cost of education. This would leave the matter of curriculum to the autonomy of the provinces, and yet would go a long, long way toward relieving the burden on municipal and provincial taxpayers. We believe that Ottawa should offer to increase the present $2,000 per bed grant for building of hospitals to at least $5,000 per bed. We believe that Ottawa should offer to undertake a program to supply Canada with modern penal institutions. Some penitentiary buildings in Canada are a disgrace, and most of them leave much to be desired. We believe that the federal government should offer more aid to the provinces and municipalities for the building of houses at low interest rates, including housing for senior citizens. We believe that much greater financial assistance should be given to provincial governments to encourage the development of community provincial and federal parks and recreational facilities. We believe that Ottawa should offer to reactivate the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act so that municipal governments could get low cost long term capital for the building of sewers and waterworks.
The main solution to unemployment will, of course, be recognized by leaders on both levels of government. The main solution is to find adequate markets for Canadian production. Since the end of the war the situation in regard to markets, both overseas and at home, has been rapidly deteriorating. We believe that Ottawa could offer much to restore the purchasing power of the Canadian public. They could enlist the aid of the

provinces toward the establishment throughout Canada of a minimum wage of not less than $1.25 per hour. I am very pleased that this recommendation now has the support of one of the Conservative M.P.P.'s in the Ontario house. I understand that yesterday he recommended that the minimum wage for the province of Ontario should be $50 a week. We believe that much could be done to supply employment if there were throughout Canada, both by provincial and federal legislation, a maximum 40-hour work week for everybody. We believe that the federal government itself could, by its own actions, do much to restore markets and purchasing power by paying adequate wages to some categories of its own civil servants. In this regard, I have mail carriers particularly in mind. We believe that with the co-operation of the provinces there could be established a national pension plan so that not only those who are able to work but all Canadians could enjoy an adequate minimum purchasing power. We believe that family allowances could be raised by this government to restore their original purchasing power. We believe that this government should enlist immediately the help of provincial governments so as to establish marketing legislation at both levels of government, and take other measures so that farmers will have parity prices and will also be able to act as consumers in Canada's economic life.
The federal government should offer to the provincial governments that if they will reduce the cost of living by removing some of the direct sales taxes which are being levied the federal government in its part will do its share and remove the 10 per cent sales tax on essential commodities. Employers would expand production in Canada if they could be assured that markets were available for their products.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to move, seconded toy the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma and by adding the following words:
And should consider the advisability of presenting for consideration at such a conference the following proposals:
(a)	To assume complete responsibility for the welfare of the employable unemployed.
(b)	To ensure employment opportunities for all Canadians willing and able to work, and
(c)	To reduce the burden of interest rates on new provincial and municipal borrowings.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
In my submission this amendment, like the previous one is out of order. It is a little difficult to follow without having a copy in one's possession, but I will do my best to follow it in the light of the comparison you have indicated with the previous resolution.
Here, the hon. member is seeking to circumvent, if I may use that word without offence, the ruling which the Deputy Speaker made a few moments ago when he was in the chair in ruling out of order an amendment similar in form which proposed to add to the amendment of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) certain words which began: "and to present for the consideration of such conference federal proposals" and so on to (a), (b) and (c)-(a), (b) and (c), all being matters involving the expenditure of public money and, indeed, of very large sums. That amendment was ruled out of order on the ground that it would have constituted a direction to the government to proceed with a matter which would involve expenditure, something which can only be initiated in the house by a minister with the recommendation of His Excellency, the Governor General. That was not the only ground of objection taken to the earlier amendment introduced by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, but it was the ground upon which the Deputy Speaker ruled that amendment out of order. He did not comment on the other grounds upon which I argued that the amendment could not be accepted.
Now the hon. gentleman has simply added four words to those he is asking to have added to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Essex East. The amendment asks now that the government should consider the advisability of these proposals, all of which relate to the expenditure of large sums of money.
I turn now to one of the other grounds upon which I submitted that the first amendment was out of order. Even if it be contended that the present amendment does no more than ask the government to consider a certain course, I submit that it is clearly out of order on several grounds. The first is the ground of relevancy. We have had under debate for the past 24 hours an amendment relating to the calling of a federal-provincial conference. The amendment is proposed in a form which simply seeks an expression of the opinion of the house that the government should call a federal-provincial conference at once to deal with serious problems of
Dominion-Provincial Conference common concern such as unemployment and fiscal relations. The whole substance of that amendment concerns the calling of a dominion-provincial conference. What have we added here, Mr. Speaker? We have added here a whole group of proposals, far-reaching in their scope, which the hon. member says the federal government should submit to the provinces. These cover such a wide field as assumption by the federal government of complete responsibility for the welfare of the employable unemployed, ensurance of employment opportunities for all Canadians willing and able to work, and-an entirely different subject-the reduction of the burden of interest rates on new provincial and municipal borrowings. I submit that this amendment is clearly out of order on the ground of irrelevancy. This amendment is not relevant to the amendment which has been under debate for the past 24 hours.
In the second place-and this ground is not unrelated to the first ground-this amendment purports to enlarge very widely the scope of the amendment. That is not open to an hon. member of this house in relation to an amendment at any time, let alone an amendment to resolve the house into committee of supply. The rule is plainly stated in Beauchesne, fourth edition at page 171, as follows:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed. The law on the relevancy of amendments is that if they are on the same subject-matter with the original motion, they are admissible, but not when foreign thereto. The exceptions to this rule are amendments on the question of going into supply or ways and means.
On the matter of the enlargement of the scope of the motion may I refer to page 169 of Beauchesne, fourth edition, paragraph 202, sub-paragraph (3):
Since the purpose of a sub-amendment is to alter the amendment, it should not enlarge upon the scope of the amendment but it should deal with matters that are not covered by the amendment; if it is intended to bring up matters foreign to the amendment, the member should wait until the amendment is disposed of and move a new amendment.
The amendment now submitted so widens the scope of the main amendment as to make it quite unrecognizable. On this ground, and on others I could mention, I submit that the amendment is completely out of order.

If I might, I should like to say a word on this point. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) sat down he said that, for this and other reasons which he did not care to go into for the moment, the subamendment was out of order. Perhaps if this amendment needs to have one or two words deleted from it the minister could advance these other undisclosed arguments which he has and which he would not allow the house to hear.
It is just about an hour since the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) rose to speak. I think if the house had dealt with the first amendment he presented, in the terms in which he presented it the business of the house would have been expedited. The question is, however, whether or not the proposed subamendment is in order. The deputy speaker in advising us that the phraseology of the first subamendment was out of order said that it would mean an expenditure of money by the federal government. This was the main reason, I think the only reason, why the Deputy Speaker felt that the subamendment, as it was originally drafted, was not in order. However, that particular omission in the subamendment has since been corrected.
In so far as relevancy is concerned, I could scarcely understand the Minister of Finance attempting to make a case that the subamendment was not relevant because it is related to the terms of the amendment presented by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). It has to do with the calling of a federal-provincial conference to deal with unemployment and fiscal relations. Certainly, any consideration of the advisability of the proposal to assume complete responsibility for the welfare of the employable unemployed is very pertinent to the whole question of unemployment. The same thing could be said of subparagraph (b), which asks for the consideration of the advisability of presenting for consideration of such conference federal proposals to ensure employment opportunities to all Canadians willing and able to work. Surely, that is very much a part of the discussion of the unemployment situation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Order. I am disposed to agree with the hon. member that the amendment is relevant. It would save the time of the house if he allowed me to enquire whether or not there is any member who would like to advance different or other grounds for considering the proposed subamendment to be irregular? If not, I feel that the initial objection which was taken to the subamendment in its first form has been cured by the addition of the words which no longer make it mandatory for the government to proceed if the house adopts the amendment. All the present subamendment calls for the government to do is to consider the advisability of presenting these proposals, and if this subamendment were adopted it would leave the government free, after consideration of the advisability of presenting these proposals to a dominion-provincial conference, to come to the conclusion it should not submit these matters. There is not, therefore, necessarily an expenditure of public money involved in the amendment.
On the question of relevancy, I am relying on the reference which the minister gave me to Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 202, which deals generally with these matters. It seems to me that the scope, and "scope" is the word Beauchesne uses, of the initial amendment proposed by the hon. member for Essex East covers anything that would come properly within the purview of a dominion-provincial conference. The things which were mentioned in the original amendment as being desirable for consideration by such a conference were unemployment and fiscal relations. The subamendment repeats unemployment in item (b) in these words:
(b) to ensure employment opportunities to all Canadians willing and able to work;
It does not, therefore, really add anything to the initial amendment. The subamendment also proposes that two further items, (a) and (c) be considered for submission for such a conference. One of these deals with the employable unemployed which, as I understand it, has been a subject of discussion between the provinces and the dominion over the years. The final one is to reduce the burden of interest rates on new provincial and municipal borrowings. Perhaps this is less purely a matter for a dominion-provincial conference although it has certainly been involved in discussions of the relations of these two sets of governments.
In my view, the amendment is sufficiently relevant to allow it to go to a vote. Is the house ready for the question?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
It is a little difficult to hear down in this corner, Mr. Speaker. Sometimes we cannot hear everything that is going on up there and this causes us some hesitation.
This amendment moved by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) is one which would always give rise to a very good debate in the house. Anything that has to do with federal-provincial relations is of very great interest to all members of parliament. It is also of interest to all members of provincial legislatures and municipal councils and to anyone who has anything to do with government.
When the hon. member for Essex East commenced his address he mentioned that under our constitution we are a federation of states. Our form of government, of necessity, does call for a certain amount of discussion between the various levels of government. I think we would all agree with him on that but I would also like to mention that I think the type of government we have in this country is a form of partnership. When it was first considered we had four provinces in what was called Upper and Lower Canada and we had the maritime provinces. I should like to say to hon. members that it was not those who were governing the maritime provinces who came up here seeking to join with the provinces of Upper Canada. As the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) said this afternoon, it was those in Upper Canada who
Dominion-Provincial Conference came down seeking union, or the consideration of union, with us. I believe it was a great move on their part and I am glad that union took place, but in that union we created a partnership under which one part of Canada undertook to help other parts of Canada. Not only did we undertake that in that partnership but we undertook the duty to protect the freedoms, the rights and the traditions of each of the two great nations of this country.
In discussing this question of federal-provincial relations we must keep that before us at all times. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) said last night, it has been the policy of the Conservative party and also the policy of the original Liberal party that went into confederation that at no time would the constitution-if you wish to call it that-or the partnership be changed unless there was thorough discussion arid agreement among the provinces involved.
The question that the amendment brings before us, if I may paraphrase it, is that we in the house are to decide that there be a federal-provincial conference called at this time. I think that is the question put to us.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Right.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR RECONVENING OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I listened attentively to and I enjoyed the speech made by the hon. member for Essex East. From his point of view I think he presented very strong arguments. As I read it over I came to realize that he put forth the position that we should have a federal-provincial conference called at once, not next week, but at once. He went on to cite quotations from members who formed the opposition a few years ago, some of whom are in the government today and some of whom are not, to indicate that at that time the government of that day could call a conference at once. They were pressed to call a conference at once and therefore the government today could call a conference at once.
I then looked for the reasons why this conference should be called at once and I found that, as far as I could see them spelled out in the very interesting outline, there were three outstanding reasons he gave. The first one was a constitutional amendment. I am not going to take issue with him on that; I am not going to take issue with him on the principle of constitutional amendments. If constitutional amendments are necessary, then I believe a conference should be called before any amendments are undertaken. Is there any great rush to call a conference to amend the constitution? I do not think any have been cited. I do not know of any great rush. I see no reason to stop the
882	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Conference business of this house or of any provincial legislature for that purpose. There are no constitutional issues before us and I see no reason to call a conference between the provincial and federal administrators for that purpose.
The second point the hon. member raised quite clearly was that of human rights. I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) answered that point quite well today in answering questions on the orders of the day. I think he very well answered the argument there. I wondered what the hon. member for Essex East expected to attain by asking for the calling of a conference of the federal and provincial governments on the question of human rights. I cannot see anything to be gained. Would it be possible that there might be a political motive behind such an item as this? I would hope not. Nevertheless, as J have said, I have read the hon. member's speech. I cannot find the particular quotation I would like to use but if I am wrong in what I say I know the hon. member will correct me. In effect he said that a few years ago the government of which he was then a minister undertook to call a conference to consider amendments to the constitution or did call one for that purpose, and it was not successful. Of course, he tried to flatter the Prime Minister and this government by saying that we were much more friendly with the provinces that objected at that time, and that may be true. But I do not believe that we have travelled far enough along the road yet to change the opinions of the gentlemen concerned. I do not blame them. I believe that we must guard-we do believe it down east and they believe it in the province of Quebec-the constitution very carefully, and it must be considered very carefully before we undertake to bring in amendments. But suppose all that the hon. member says were true. What is the great rush?
With respect to human rights, I can see no great rush for calling a federal-provincial conference in order to enlighten us on a question we are going to have to vote on if the bill of rights comes before the house. There may be differences of opinion but I am satisfied that hon. members will have the right to vote and as they see fit on the bill of rights according to their consciences. I think it is something that should not be considered until the bill is placed before us and we can see whether there have been any amendments. I do not see any reason for it there.
The third one is unemployment. I think that is quite a legitimate reason because according to the figures unemployment is a very serious problem in the country today.


We have heard about it ever since parliament opened and we are in no position to do anything but admit that it is bad. In fact, unemployment is bad if there are two men in the country out of work who want work.
I was listening to the radio the other morning and heard a report of something that unfortunately is not isolated. I do not know whether the report was true but it came from Smiths Falls, Ontario. I do not know whether it is a small town or a large one but that town or city had arranged for some work under the winter program. They went to the unemployment insurance office to get men to do the work and the report that came over the radio was-if it is wrong I should like to have it denied-that they could not obtain anyone to carry on that work. No one listed as wanting work with the unemployment insurance office would go to work. The officials of the town had to go out into the country and hire people there. It may be that they got men in the country who where out of work. It may be that they got men from the country who were glad to work. As a matter of fact, the constituency in which I live is rural and you can always get a man if you want a job done. As a rule he is willing to work but he is not looking for work in the wintertime, and that is just about the situation.
I know that that might be an excuse for calling a conference but I listened to the Minister of Finance last night and I believe the hon. member for Essex East requested an answer. There have been conferences between the provinces and the federal government concerning unemployment. Apparently the provinces, the municipalities and the federal government have been getting together. They have devised a program, are carrying it out and everything is being done that could be done if we had a conference. So, Mr. Speaker, I think any weight in that request has been taken away.
I think the hon. member for Essex East brought this matter forward quite legitimately. It was a good thing to bring forward. It was a good thing that the government had a chance to explain what has been done. I do not suppose he knew what was going on. You cannot blame him for that and I do not because I think he presented his case in a wonderful way. At the same time, I think that the Minister of Finance answered his arguments in a better way.
May I also say that I have a lot of confidence in the provincial premiers and the members of the legislatures. It seems to me that we spend a lot of time in the house arguing, debating and saying what we should

do for the provinces. I wonder whether we are not wasting a great deal of time. Under our constitution the provincial legislatures have full control of the subject matters allotted to them under the British North America Act. The people elect their representatives to those legislatures. In doing so they must have confidence in them and if they have confidence in these men I am sure I have. Frankly, I am prepared to leave it to the men charged with the responsibility of dealing with provincial affairs to look after their own business. I think they are quite capable of doing so and in my opinion we have plenty to do in the federal field if we attend to our own business.
In my view we waste a terrible amount of time. I know that some hon. members may say that when I was sitting in the opposition I did so too but I have learned something in the few years I have been here. I really think we waste considerable time so I am prepared to leave the problems of the provinces and the problems of the municipalities, which come under the authority of the provincial governments, to the men in charge of the provinces until such time as the provinces come to us and say that they cannot cope with their problems.
I think that this debate has wandered far afield. An amendment was presented before I began to speak, and although I did not hear the ruling I believe it was ruled in order and we will have to vote on it. Regardless of how it was worded it did seem to indicate what some members belonging to the C.C.F. party are thinking. I do not know whether or not they all agree on this point but it looked to me like they were taking advantage of the opportunity to place their social program on the record through the back door. If the federal government said to the provincial governments, if the provincial governments said to the municipalities or if the municipalities said to their school boards, "we will assume all responsibility, we will hire your teachers, we will raise their salaries, we will build the schools, we will buy the buses, we will transport the children to school, we will build gymnasiums for them to play in and it will not cost you anything", human nature being what it is can you imagine anybody on a county or town council turning down such an offer? I do not think so. I have had a lot of experience on county councils. Neither would the provinces turn down such an offer. As the Minister of Finance said, if we invite them here and offer them all these things we may as well make up our minds right now that they are going to take them. Why should they not do so? We will be responsible for raising the money and raising money, as every member knows, means taking it from
Dominion-Provincial Conference the people. I do not believe in turning out money by machine. There is only one way by which to get the money to do the things mentioned in the subamendment and that is by raising taxes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned at 6 o'clock I was discussing generally the necessity for the calling of a federal-provincial conference. I had tried to look for the reasons for it and I was trying to make the point that I had grave doubts that good reasons for it had been advanced in the argument supporting the amendment. As I said, I trust that provincial members will look after their own affairs fairly well. As far as I know, that is so. I can only speak more or less for the east or at least for my own province; I should confine it to that.
Not knowing that I was going to be discussing this issue and not knowing that this issue was going to be up for consideration, a few days ago I had the privilege of meeting and having a long chat with one of the cabinet ministers in my own province. They seem to be quite happy down there in view of the fact that for a number of years, ever since the war the premiers of the maritime provinces have been pressing for certain rights or what they felt were rights. They were asking for special grants at each one of those conferences. In 1952 the tax rental agreement was renewed and improved. They appreciated that action. In 1955, when the matter came up again for discussion, they pressed their case again. It is interesting to note that politics was not a part of that program as far as the maritime premiers were concerned. At that time there were Premier Hicks of Nova Scotia, Premier Matheson of Prince Edward Island, both good strong supporters of the federal government at that time, and Premier Flemming. I do not need to take much of the time of the house but I think it is worth while to refer shortly to what each of them had to say. I am referring to the proceedings of the federal-provincial conference of 1955, dated October 3, 1955. I am going to quote Premier Hicks first. These remarks will be found at page 43. The premiers were pressing their claim. They had been pressing it previously. Here is what he said:
It is now evident that the relative capacity of the different provinces to provide even a minimum
884	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Conference
standard of services cannot be determined byreference to population figures alone. If, therefore, population does not provide a satisfactory yardstick to measure the extent to which a province should share in the general tax revenues of Canada, what yardstick can be applied? I suggest that any formula which might be devised should take into consideration not only the population of the province but also its tax potential.
He then goes on to support that proposition by a strong argument. As I said this afternoon, the maritimes came into this union or into this partnership and it was recognized at that time that they must have something to compensate them in view of the revenues that they were giving up, the location they were giving up, because at that time their trading area was not east and west-it was not west as far as we were concerned

their trading area was north and south. That was recognized by confederation.
I should also like to mention what Premier Flemming said because, again, they were asking for the same thing. He said this:
However, experience has indicated that the tax rental agreements do not go far enough to meet the needs of low-income provinces in that they are largely based upon a per capita plan of compensation. We are firmly convinced that these provinces should receive a national adjustment grant to compensate them for their lack of taxable capacity in respect of those sources of revenue remaining to them.
As hon. members know, at the time of confederation there was taken away from these provinces the right of indirect taxation, so to speak. If they wanted to raise taxes they were obliged to do it directly. As all hon. members know, that is the type of tax that seems to hurt the worst, is the hardest to collect and therefore is the most unpopular. After quoting some parts of the Rowell-Sirois report, something which I am not going to do, he ends up by saying this:
The government of New Brunswick urges with all the force at its command that, in addition to the tax rental agreements, there should be adjustment grants to the low-income provinces, and we submit herewith a formula, based on relative per capita personal income which would, we consider, accomplish this purpose in a simple and equitable manner. The formula is as follows:
1. Determine the average amount in dollars by which the per capita personal income of each province falls short of 85 per cent of the capita personal income of Canada for the latest three years for which this information is available.
And so on. I am not going to go into that matter now because I have not the necessary time. I think hon. members are familiar with the formula. Premier Matheson backed him up. I just want to read a word or two of what he said. It is all in the report and there is no need of my taking up the time of the house unduly. Premier Matheson said this:
In 1946 we accepted the tax-rental agreement offer, not because it represented some recognition 

of fiscal need but with a hope that during the lifetime of that agreement a more satisfactory formula would be devised. In 1952 the federal government proposed a new guaranteed minimum payment based on the one allotted to a province under the 1947 agreement with an increase proportionate to change in provincial population and per capita gross national product between 1942 and 1948.
No recognition of a province's fiscal need problem or its tax-raising ability was taken into consideration in the re-allocation or distribution of the tax moneys-
I think that is generally conceded. At the end of the conference the maritime premiers went home feeling that they had not been given the consideration which they should have had.
I can speak for my own province. In 1957, after that conference of 1956, and after the legislation was brought down in this house permitting the payments which the federal government said they could make and apparently could not go any further, here is what the provincial secretary treasurer of the province of New Brunswick said in presenting his budget in 1957. First of all he quoted the New Year's message from the premier of New Brunswick:
The goal of your government since 1952 has been to do everything possible to narrow the economic gap which has existed for so long between this province and some of the wealthier provinces.
One of the avenues by which this "narrowing of the gap" could be done, we believed, was through the medium of a national adjustment grant to supplement the new tax rental agreement. Our proposal was that this adjustment grant go to provinces whose per capita income was below 85 per cent of the national average.
And he goes on:
Failure by the federal authorities to recognize this principle of a national adjustment grant is, we believe, a shocking disregard of the problems faced by the poorer provinces.
That was the feeling after the 1956 conference, and after the legislation went through. That was the feeling which existed in the maritime provinces. So are you very much surprised that the election which followed showed Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia coming back here practically unanimously for this government?
Then a conference was called. There is no need to go into the argument whether or not it should have been called or as to when it should have been called, or whether it was called as quickly as the Liberals think it should have been called. The fact is that a conference was called after the election in June at the earliest date which the government could arrange, and the matter of a month or two does not make much difference in the affairs of a nation. Those premiers came back, although Premier Hicks had been discarded by Nova Scotia and in his place came a new premier. Nevertheless, the new
