maintopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL PLAN
subtopic: REFERENCE TO INADE- QUACY OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a very few minutes of the time of the house to present a grievance which I think deserves the attention of the government in the immediate future. I, therefore, take advantage of the first opportunity to present it as a grievance. The subject I wish to speak about has to do with the development of the national capital plan and the national capital commission.
Hon. members will recall that since 1899 the federal parliament has seen fit to legislate on this subject and has provided, in one form or another, for a commission to deal with the development and beautification of the capital of the country. The history of that development is rather interesting, but I promise the house I will not take the time to develop it here tonight. The first act setting up the Ottawa improvement commission was brought forward in 1899 by the government headed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Succeeding

governments from that day to this have tried to carry on the plan to meet the needs of the times and have, I think it is fair to say, done so in a way that has met with the general approval of all parties in the house. There may at times have been minor differences, but I think that has been the approach to the problem.
It will be recalled that the work was continued under the government of Sir Robert Borden which followed. Then in 1927, as changing circumstances required, the Ottawa improvement commission was changed to the federal district commission. The legislation was amended and developed. In 1946 further changes were made enlarging the commission. Then at the last session of parliament the name of the commission charged with the responsibility of developing the national capital was changed to the national capital commission. That legislation had been proposed by the former government and was adopted and brought forward by the present government and enacted at the last session.
By the very nature of the work of developing the national capital and particularly by reason of the fact that jurisdiction over real estate resides in the provinces and through them to a limited extent in their statutory creations, the municipalities, it is necessary that the work be done in full co-operation between the federal, provincial and municipal governments. With all the difficulties inherent in the problem a high degree of cooperation has been developed over the years and fair success achieved in the field of co-operation.
One of the big contributing factors to that co-operation was the knowledge the municipal bodies particularly affected gained through the membership their representatives had on the commission, and in particular is that true of the city of Ottawa and the city of Hull. It is a matter of history that the mayors of Ottawa and Hull were on the commission by virtue of a clause permitting the corporations to make those appointments. When the new commission was appointed some few days ago the representatives of these two corporations and of the two large townships on the Ontario side were omitted. None of them was appointed.
Not only were they omitted but the appointments were made and announced in a way that can only lead to a loss of co-operation between the bodies concerned with the national capital development. Instead of the announcement being made in the House of Commons with the appropriate explanation as to the reason, if any, for not appointing the mayors of the two cities and any other ap-
National Capital Plan
propriate municipal officials, it was made through the newspapers without any explanation whatever. The launching of the national capital commission in this way only means that the new commission, which I am sure everyone in the house wishes well, is being handicapped. I am sure it is the hope of everyone in the house that their work will be successful over the years ahead.
I would ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Dief-enbaker) to consider this matter carefully, to do what he can to rectify the situation and take advantage of the first available opportunity to correct the damage done. The situation of the mayor of the national capital itself having to read in the newspapers that his services are dispensed with is not a happy one when it is necessary that the federal government and the mayor of the national capital must co-operate with respect to so many of the plans of the commission.
The same thing is true of the situation concerning the mayor of the adjacent city of Hull. Indeed, it is also true, as I think the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) will agree, with respect to the reeves of the townships of Nepean and Gloucester. I do not want to belabour the subject unduly but I feel that I would almost be justified in using the word "clumsiness" to describe the manner in which the matter was handled. I ask the Prime Minister to rectify the situation at the earliest possible opportunity, to explain at least why the extraordinary action he took was taken and to take any other appropriate measures to bring about the degree of co-operation required so that the national capital can be developed in the way that I am sure members of all parties represented in parliament wish it to be developed.

speechtext:
The same matter. (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, following the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Mcllraith), I feel it is my duty to tell the house something of the views of the people who live on the Quebec side of the national capital. We all know that, originally, the idea behind the setting up of a national capital was, above all, to set up something patterned after the district of Columbia. I know that Sir Wilfrid Laurier often referred to "the Washington of the North" and that Mr. Mackenzie King, for some time, was of the opinion that we should make of our capital a district similar to that of Columbia.

National Capital Plan
We also know that Mr. Greber proved to him, beyond all doubts, that the district of Columbia, U.S.A., had been a complete failure.
When a district is being set up on the pattern of the district of Columbia, the commission responsible for its administration has to make decisions that can involve considerable expenditures. The commission then pays half the cost, but the other half falls upon the shoulders of the people, with the result that taxes go up considerably.
That is one of the reasons which impel us to ask the national capital commission to include among its members representatives of the municipal councils of Hull and Ottawa, those obviously most directly concerned.
At present, mayors from outside localities are sitting on the commission. It also includes an alderman from the city of Aylmer. I agree that they were not appointed as such, but they none the less represent their municipalities while the mayors of Hull and Ottawa were completely ignored. The commission has serious decisions to make, and those decisions might often be such as to hamper certain municipal projects. I shall give but one example. In the past, one of the main purposes of the federal district commission was the removal of the Eddy plants from the city of Hull. It was claimed at the time that it was a disgrace to see paper plants surrounded by woodpiles just across the river from parliament hill. There were even offers made to this firm, and they were objected to by the representatives of the municipalities in the federal district commission. We are all for beautification, esthetics, as I have said before and as I repeat now, but we are first and foremost for letting people keep their livelihood. Many such problems can arise, and I know of no one who is more interested in preventing such situations from developing than the representatives of the municipalities on the commission.
We all know also that the commission meets in camera and that its decisions are made known by means of press releases issued by the chairman. A press conference enables the chairman to say what he sees fit; he does not have to report everything that is discussed. Therefore, the municipalities have no way of knowing what goes on and so anything can happen within the commission without the municipalities being aware of them.
It is therefore necessary that municipalities be represented on the commission. They were in fact represented under the previous act, and they were not represented by the mayors of Ottawa or Hull but by people appointed

by the municipal councils concerned. In each case the municipal councils appointed their mayor to represent them on the federal district commission. The mayors were thus able to look after the interests of their respective municipalities. Far from enjoying the same privilege under the new act, the municipalities of Hull and Ottawa lost their representation on the commission.
The former act provided for the appointment of representatives for the city of Hull; there was also a representative for the district of Hull, the last of whom was Mrs. Fontaine, and before that, Mr. J. Wilfrid Ste. Marie, barrister.
This means that we then had two representatives on the commission. Besides, there were on the national capital planning committee an alderman from the city of Hull and an alderman or a controller from the city of Ottawa. Under the old act, we had three representatives. Now, the city of Hull, which is enormously interested, has only one representative, Mr. Aime Guertin. I have confidence in Mr. Guertin and I would say nothing to disparage him. He has proved in the past that he was of sufficiently independent mind to stand up to all those who would try to contradict his views. I do not say that I have always agreed with Mr. Guertin on federal district matters, but I do say that he will be a worthy representative of the city of Hull. However, Mr. Guertin is not on the municipal council; he will represent the city of Hull in general, but he cannot represent the interests of the municipality, as could be done by the mayor or a member of the municipal council.
And again, why were not the mayors appointed to the commission? Many reasons have been given, including the matter of efficiency.
According to Le Droit of January 26 last, the mayors of Hull and Ottawa made strong protests against this change in the provisions. Here is what Mr. Nelms said:
I still wonder what could be the reason for the federal government's decision stated Mr. Nelms. The mayor of Hull, like the mayor of Ottawa, has always played a leading role on the F.D.C. There are so many problems that require solution at federal and at municipal levels.
When I know mayor Moncion's views and when I get additional information, I shall make a statement to the press, probably at the meeting of the board of control tomorrow afternoon.
For the time being, I wish, as mayor of the capital city of Canada, to express my painful surprise. If any two men are in a position to help the federal agency are they not the mayors of Hull and Ottawa?

This morning, the office of the Prime Minister stated that the omission of mayors of Ottawa and Hull from membership in the new National Capital Commission was due to a practical reason.
Well, Mr. Speaker, what is that practical reason? Did the representatives of those cities do anything in the past that could hinder the progress of the national capital plan? I do not believe so.
When I was mayor of the city of Hull, 1 had the opportunity to sit on the commission and I realized, while we were there, that the federal district commission has enjoyed the fullest co-operation from the municipal authorities on both sides of the river. Nevertheless, the mayors of Hull and Ottawa are now being removed from this agency without any explanation. Could it be that a few backward persons still entertain the idea of developing a national capital along the lines of the district of Columbia? If so, they can be assured that this will never happen, and we, on both sides of the river will fight it tooth and nail, as we intend to retain our autonomy and independence, and we have no intention of knuckling down to a small group who are seeking to create jobs for themselves in the national capital.

baker) is in favour of such a project, no. But the Prime Minister is not eternal. There have been other prime ministers in the past who favoured such a project; so I claim that we must put all the weight of our opinion against such a project, and the best way to protect ourselves against those who share that view is to have representatives for Hull and for Ottawa.
Besides, the Prime Minister could remedy the situation; first of all, there are other appointments to be made. He could also simply amend the act, in such a way to provide that each year both the Ottawa and Hull municipal councils could appoint one of their representatives to the national capital commission, in order that the municipal interests of both cities be well protected.
The problems to be faced will be numerous. There is the matter of water pollution, which could be very costly, not to mention the problems of sewers from upper Aylmer to beyond the Gatineau.
So then, if the commission is given a free rein, we might very well be forced to shoulder the burden of heavier taxes. And yet, heaven knows that the people of our municipalities are sufficiently burdened with taxes. According to the Citizen, it has been stated by some one that the reason why the mayors of Hull and Ottawa were ignored was the fact that there had been some discontent in regard to Miss Whitton's attitude, when she was mayoress of Ottawa, and that it was claimed she had caused the commission to waste its time.
Well, even if it were true, so-and I admit she caused the commission to waste a few hours-she was nonetheless the representative of the city of Ottawa, delegated by the city council, and therefore represented the views of the people of Ottawa, and, as such, was entitled to some respect. In any event, the way things look now, it is unlikely that she will return as mayoress of Ottawa, and therefore there is no danger on that score.
Mayor Nelms and mayor Moncion, were competent representatives who gave their best to the national capital and at the same time to the people of the municipalities they represented. That is why I feel the Prime Minister made a mistake in failing to appoint the representatives of Hull and Ottawa. As was stated by the member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith), I hope he will reconsider and correct the monumental mistake he committed in ignoring the municipalities of Hull and Ottawa.

speechtext:
I do not claim to be privy to all that concerns the make-up of the national capital commission. However, after hearing the speeches of the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) and of my colleague, the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron), I must rise to make a few remarks on this controversy about the appointment of the mayors of Hull and Ottawa on this commission.
It has been said there might be practical objections, and indeed I can quite clearly see the nature of those objections. I have no wish at all to deny the qualifications of the mayor of Ottawa, Mr. Nelms, or of the mayor of Hull, Mr. Moncion, to sit on this commission. Both are well known, and, in this regard, I join with my colleague, the member for Hull, in praising their high abilities. Yet there is a well-known judicial principle under which a person having some interest in a particular problem should not be a member of a commission responsible for making decisions on the problem. In other words, a judge who might be interested in a dispute must disclaim competence, just as a company director who personally stands to profit from a decision of the board of directors must refrain from voting.
As the member for Hull has just said, there will be many cases where there might be a conflict of interests between the national capital commission and the cities of Hull or Ottawa. As things stand, the mayor of Ottawa or the mayor of Hull can certainly be more outspoken in expressing the views and interests of their electors and municipalities, because they will not have, as we say, to sit on the fence, since neither is a member of the commission.
For that particular reason, I believe it was very wise not to appoint the mayors of these two cities on the commission. On the other hand, another point was raised which should be considered and it is this: as the country expands, the people of Canada consider Ottawa, the capital, as something that belongs to the country as a whole. An effort is being made to get rid of the idea that Ottawa and Hull together are the capital. Nothing prevents the mayors of those cities from making representations to the commission, as was done in the past by the mayors of other municipalities. Therefore when these people have to deal with the cities of Ottawa

and Hull they will be able to do so freely while the representatives of those two cities will be in a much better position to express their opinion.
All in all, I think that the decision is a wise one.
Reference was made to the representative of the Quebec side of the national capital, Mr. Guertin. I am happy to associate with my colleague the hon. member for Hull in praising the high efficiency of this member. Yet I must say that there is also on that commission another member representing the western part of the province, Mr. Nelson Morin, of Aylmer, whose ability is also well known and who will no doubt be able to speak on behalf of the important section of western Quebec, part of which is situated in the constituency of Pontiac, which is part of the national capital.
It could be that some day certain industries like the E. B. Eddy Company might have to move out of Hull. That will certainly happen only in a more or less distant future. Nevertheless I would like to take this opportunity, in case a relocation of that industry was ever decided, to invite the directors to come and set up their plant in my constituency of Pontiac which is not that far away and which provides a great part of the natural resources used by that company.
All in all, I believe that the members of that commission have been quite wisely chosen. This was not meant to reflect at all on the qualities of the prominent citizens who have been elected to run the affairs of Hull and Ottawa. I believe though that the taxpayers of these two cities have chosen these people to look after their interests but not in the hope that they would be appointed on the national capital commission. If they restrict their energy to the welfare of the citizens of these two important cities, they will certainly be in a position to realize the dreams which the member for Hull (Mr. Caron) might entertain for the future. In fact I believe that if it was ever considered to replace the present administration of the cities of Hull and Ottawa by a federal district like that of Washington in the United States, for example, then the mayors of those two cities would no doubt be in a better position to fight such a plan since they would be uncommitted to the commission, having only to look after the interests of those under their authority.

Mr. Speaker, at the very outset of my remarks, I must say I disagree with the views expressed by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau). Rather do I agree with the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) and the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron). Like them, I find it strange that the government, in appointing the new members of the national capital commission, should have by-passed the mayors of Hull and Ottawa. The development of the national capital includes the city of Ottawa and the city of Hull, as well as an area around those two cities, of which the constituency of Gatineau, which I have the honour to represent, forms a large part. In view of the fact that the cities of Ottawa and Hull have no official delegates on this commission, the latter is deprived of the services and advice which those men would be in a position to provide.
As regards the appointment of Mr. Morin, of Aylmer, to represent the municipalities adjacent to Hull, in the province of Quebec, I feel the choice is sound. Mr. Morin is fully qualified to properly represent that part of the province of Quebec comprised in the national capital development plan. However, it is strange that the recommendations made by the municipal councils, and more especially by the union of the chambers of commerce of western Quebec, to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), concerning the appointment of Dr. Matte, to represent that part of the province of Quebec on the commission, should have been ignored.
If I have expressed regret that the government has not appointed the mayors of Ottawa and Hull, nor Dr. Matte, I cannot but approve, on the other hand, the attitude taken by the government in regard to the establishment of a green belt around the national capital. I know that the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) does not share my views on this matter. I also know that the new representative of Hull, Mr. Guertin, has never shared my views on the proposed green belt. However, I share the opinion of the government that a limit should be set once and for all to the area covered by the city of Ottawa, or by the national capital. And I commend the government for its policy of expropriating the land required to develop a green belt around the city of Ottawa. This is of benefit not only to the city of Ottawa, but to all of Canada, since the responsibility of the govern-
National Capital Plan
ment in this field will thus be limited. Without this limitation, the Canadian government would have to spend tremendous amounts for developing and beautifying the capital city, whereas with a green belt its expenses will be limited to that part of the capital city that is included in the green belt.
I am pleased to note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has increased the grants for improving the national capital.
May I add that the government and the national capital commission should take steps to complete the development of Gatineau park in the near future. It can be said, Mr. Speaker, that Gatineau park will be the only national park in the province of Quebec. For my constituency and for the constituency of my hon. friend from Pontiac-Temiscamingue, as well as for the constituencies of the western part of the province of Quebec, Gatineau park will be a great tourist attraction.
Mr. Speaker, once this park is completely developed, the Canadian government travel bureau can invite American as well as Canadian tourists to visit it, and they will find everything they can hope for: hunting, fishing, scenery and natural beauty.
Those who want to indulge in their favourite sports of hunting or fishing, will find in the park employees who can give them information, and say to them for example: Hunting is not allowed in the park, and fishing is restricted. Move on to Gatineau, to Pontiac or the Lievre, and there you will find everything you want to suit your interests.

In the light of past experience I think there is little fear of undue influence being asserted by any one member of the commission, even if that member should be the mayor of the capital city.

maintopic: KETTLE VALLEY RAILWAY
KETTLE VALLEY RAILWAY
KETTLE VALLEY RAILWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I am as successful in ringing as a big bell with my grievance as the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) was when he was speaking. I might explain that some hon. members may consider me to be somewhat repetitious in stating this grievance and they may have a dim recollection that I have mentioned the matter in the past. I am presenting this grievance because it is based on sound grounds and the protests of my constituents and because I have been asked to raise the matter in this house on every appropriate occasion.
My grievance concerns the completely inadequate passenger train service on the Kettle Valley railway and the lack of adequate facilities. As I said before I have mentioned this on other occasions but it is a serious matter to those persons who live along the Kettle Valley railway which runs from Hope in British Columbia to Lethbridge in Alberta. This grievance was the result of the action of the Canadian Pacific Railway in October 1957 which prior to that time ran a passenger train with sleeping and dining cars and adequate day coaches. When the company changed this service it substituted a Budd car and the service now provides no sleeper or cafe car. The action on the part of the company was seriously resented by the people who live along that railway. Later there were further reasons for complaint because of a reduction in the

schedules on which this Budd car ran owing, as the C.P.R. explained, to some temporary unfortunate local circumstances in my and adjoining constituencies. These did prove to be temporary because the difficulties have not been experienced for some months now.
I do hope I get the sympathy of the house in this connection. Here is a district in which live about 100,000 people who are affected by this change in service, an area which has an annual production of over $200 million in the forest industry, in manufacturing, in smelters and in agriculture. This populous and highly productive area is now forced to depend on the uncertain and unpleasant service of a Budd car which runs every other day or so and which provides no sleeping accommodation or cafe car.
Protests with regard to this matter have been well organized. All the municipalities have protested this present service by resolutions, by briefs and by their representatives meeting with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) when he was in the Kootenay district during the last election trying his level best to make certain that I would not return to this house. All the unions and the chambers of commerce have protested the present .arrangement and in speaking on this question I represent the views of all political parties in my constituency and I am sure all those in the adjoining constituencies.
The people in this area are not asking for expensive service. It is important to remember that the Kettle Valley railway is one of the most profitable sections of the C.P.R. because it hauls the ore of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company from Kimberley to Trail-thousands of tons daily- and it hauls thousands of tons of the products of consolidated mining to coastal points, or south to points in the United States, or to prairie and eastern Canadian points. As a result of this large tonnage the C.P.R. is able to operate this section of the railway at a profit but it has reduced the passenger service. It is interesting to remember that the service has been reduced in the area which produces the majority of the profits that the C.P.R. enjoys at the present time because the C.P.R. owns 51 per cent of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.
As I said before, the people in this area seek only to be provided with a Budd car, sleeping accommodation and a cafe car so that the aged will have some reasonable comfort, the sick may be attended to and the people travelling with children may do so in decency and with a measure of comfort.
At the present time freight trains are running regularly along the line hauling

Requested Program for Lobster Fisherman
thousands of tons of ore, manufactured goods, fertilizers, chemicals and things of that sort. We in the area appreciate that the cost of patrols are heavy. There are patrols on the railway and lights on bridges in order to protect the raildoad against possible bombings and other forms of aggression.
I should now like to outline why the provision of this service is of particular importance to our district. The railway service is important the year round but it is particularly vital during the winter months. Owing to the nature of that part of the country planes often fail to land at some of the inland airports such as Castlegar. They are not allowed to land if the clouds lie below the tops of the mountains and therefore this winter, day after day, Canadian Pacific Air Lines planes have been unable to land at Castlegar. There has been no transportation into that district, no airmail, no opportunity to get the sick to the coast in a hurry or to fly out accident victims and others in need of medical care. This passenger service is essential at all times but particularly during the winter months.
The C.P.R. will say that the traffic has greatly decreased in recent years and so it has particularly since the Budd car has been put on the line. There is no reason why anyone would choose to travel in discomfort if they could arrange to travel in any other way. Those who travel from Vancouver to Fernie are faced with the prospect of sitting up in a day coach for 36 or 40 hours existing on dry sandwiches and lukewarm coffee. That is not proper in this present age. Because of the existing service the former somewhat limited traffic has been reduced. I am informed by representatives of municipalities, chambers of commerce and other organizations that if this train service were improved and operated daily with a Budd car plus a sleeping car and a cafe car there would be a great increase in the patronage of this train.
I am speaking only briefly at this time because I know many other hon. members have grievances to bring to the attention of the house. As I said, I have raised this grievance before and I promised my constituents that I would continue to mention it until this disgraceful state of affairs has been remedied. I urge the minister to do all he can as a step in the right direction toward calling a meeting between the officials of the company, representatives of the employees and representatives of people in the district to find out exactly what they wish so that the company will realize that the requests of the people in the area are reasonable and modest. They are not asking for something
that is going to cost the company a great deal of extra expense. As a result of this get-together on the part of the various groups concerned they should be able to devise and arrange for a satisfactory service. Because of the extra costs of patrolling the tracks and the provision of lights there may be some consideration given in those discussions to assisting the company to cover the cost which would be relatively small compared to the operation of the railroad in toto between the points I have mentioned.
I bring this to the attention of the house at this time and seek the support of hon. members from all parties who may come from British Columbia to get this most unfortunate and unnecessary imposition on the people of the southern interior remedied as soon as possible.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR EDUCATIONAL PROGRAM FOR LOBSTER FISHERMEN
REQUEST FOR EDUCATIONAL PROGRAM FOR LOBSTER FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the house the subject of which is altogether different from the subjects of the grievances which have been discussed this evening. On many occasions since becoming a member of this house I have brought to the attention of the Department of Fisheries the unfortunate situation that exists with respect to illegal lobster fishing in the Atlantic provinces.
While speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I touched on this subject. On that occasion I mentioned that I was taking no exception to a certain statement made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) to the effect that he and his department would prosecute-to use the minister's own words- "as vigorously as the law requires anyone catching or canning lobsters illegally." On that occasion I also mentioned that it would be advisable for the department to spend more time on and to pay more attention to the education of the fishermen and more particularly of the lobster fishermen.
I realize that on the last occasion when I brought this subject before the house my remarks were misunderstood. I am not taking the part of the poachers. I am not one of those members who has been after the minister or his department every time that a poacher in my constituency was caught or arrested for breaking the lobster fishery regulations. But I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the Department of Fisheries should give some consideration to the education of the lobster fishermen. I have placed this request before the department at every session since 1953. If the department would realize that by establishing a system of education for the
894	HOUSE OF
Requested Program, for Lobster Fisherman fishermen, by showing them that when they destroy small lobsters or berried lobsters they are working against their own interests, I am convinced that the activities of the protection branch of the department in so far as preventing illegal lobster fishing is concerned would be much more effective.
A program should be instituted through public meetings, through the showing of films, through the public schools in the area where lobster fishing operations take place. When I brought this point to the attention of the house during the course of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I mentioned that there was a danger for the department and for the officers of the department in using the methods which they are using at this time. In saying this, Mr. Speaker, I am not casting any reflection whatsoever on the inspector of fisheries or on the different protection officers who have to enforce the lobster fishing regulations. These men receive instructions from the department and they carry out those instructions to the best of their ability. I know it is a difficult job for the fisheries inspector, for the captain and the crew of a patrol boat to be exposed at all hours of the day-some of them are working at times even 24 hours a day-and carry out the instructions which they have received from the department or from their superior officers.
If the department would realize once and for all that what is needed is a good, well-prepared educational program I am positive that the work of the officers and the department would be much easier and they would get much better results than they are getting now.
Again, I want to emphasize that I have great respect and admiration for those officers of the Department of Fisheries, and particularly for those who are engaged in the enforcement of the fishery regulations. I know that just recently certain officials of the department in the maritime provinces gave certain information to the newspapers which was directly in reply to the remarks which I had made in this house during the course of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They said that the Department of Fisheries had done everything possible to try to educate the lobster fishermen. They mentioned that meetings had been held; that pamphlets had been circulated; that films had been prepared; that even the help of the clergy had been requested in certain areas. Mr. Speaker, I want to state that the activities of the Department of Fisheries in this field have been limited and too limited to produce any satisfactory results.
[Mr. Robichaud.l

I remember that in 1954 or 1955 the officials of the department did hold a few public meetings in the province of New Brunswick in the counties of Kent and Northumberland and in my own constituency of Gloucester. But why did the department not carry on with this program? Why did they not keep on with those meetings? Why did they stop this educational program which they had started, because when they were carrying on this program they were on the right track? Just a few meetings had been held and I realize that the results may not have been within expectations.
I suggest that if the Department of Fisheries feels that it does not have the personnel -and I fully realize the fisheries officers, whether of the inspection or protection branch, may not be the right type of men to institute and to put into practice this educational program-the officials of the Department of Fisheries know and the minister knows that we have in the Atlantic provinces at St. Francis Xavier University what we call the adult education branch and we have a similar plan operating from Sacred Heart University in my own constituency. I have good reason to believe that the extension department of St. Francis Xavier University and the adult education branch of Sacred Heart University would be prepared to accept the challenge of the Department of Fisheries. They would be prepared to take this matter in hand and carry on with this program for the education of the lobster fishermen. They would be prepared to hold meetings in the different centres where lobster fishing is carried on; they would be prepared to meet with the fishermen; they would be prepared to convince them through education that when they are committing offences against the lobster fishery regulations they are working against their own good.
After all, those regulations have been enacted after a careful study by scientists and others of the life of the lobster. We know that in the Atlantic provinces we have different lobster seasons; we have different size limits and those regulations, those size limits and those lobster seasons are there to protect the lobster population. If the department is sincere, and I know it is, I know it wants to do away with this illegal practice, I feel that it would be in the best interests of all concerned to give serious consideration to the establishment of an educational program which would take care of the situation.
Just a few days ago a question of mine on the order paper concerning the lobster fisheries of the maritime provinces was answered. I asked what was the total number of convictions for infractions of the lobster fishery

regulations in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island for the years ended March 31, 1954, 1955, 1956, 1957, and 1958. The reply I received indicates that in 1954, for example, there were 69 convictions in New Brunswick, 150 in Nova Scotia and 215 in Prince Edward Island, and this, Mr. Speaker, in spite of rumours which are circulating that New Brunswick fishermen are the worst offenders. The figures for the years 1955 to 1958 are almost in the same relative proportions.
In order to secure these convictions the fisheries officers have to be on the job, and again I sympathize with them. I sympathize with a man who has to brave storms and rough seas in order to patrol the shoreline and try to carry out his duties. But now that the Minister of Fisheries is in his seat I want to make it clear again that I take no exception to the statement he made last fall and has repeated since that it is the intention of the minister and the department to prosecute as vigorously as the law requires anyone catching or canning lobster illegally. I sympathize with the minister and his officers because I know what these men are up against and I want to make it clear that it is the duty of the department to see that the law is enforced to the limit.
But I would appreciate it, and I know that those interested in the lobster fishing industry would also appreciate it, if the minister would give consideration to an educational program, and when I say "consideration" I mean serious consideration. I feel that if the department could be convinced that it should establish such a program the whole problem would be much easier for the department. Such a program would produce results.
The figures to which I have referred show that since 1954 the situation is getting worse and worse every year. I understand that in the last two seasons the fishing was poor and the fishermen were up against it and had to find a way of getting additional money to provide for their families, but just the same that is no excuse for fishermen to break the law. The law is there for a reason; for the protection of the industry.
Before resuming my seat I ask the minister once again to give this request very serious consideration, and once again I want to make it clear that at no time have I approached the minister or his officials to ask them to protect those who were breaking the law.

SUGGESTED CHANGE IN METHOD OF VOTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to rise at this time
House of Commons
because I realize that the house is anxious to get on with the vote. However, after watching us spend approximately three-quarters of an hour on standing votes accompanied by the very excellent feat of memory of the second clerk assistant I feel impelled to suggest that in the age of electronics the house should perhaps give consideration to the introduction of an electronic voting system such as is used in the United States at present whereby each member could record his vote by pressing a button and the result would be available in approximately 30 seconds.
I make this suggestion, because in one of the assemblies in the United States having approximately 254 members they are able to make an estimated saving of some 100 hours. In my opinion the time of hon. members is relatively valuable and when we spend almost one hour out of two of an evening sitting in standing up and having our names called I believe I am justified in taking a couple of minutes to suggest that such an electronic machine might merit the consideration of the house.

Mr. Speaker, may I call the attention of the house on a new grievance arising from a fairly recent incident, since it occurred last Sunday. We all know that we have trouble trying to settle the C.B.C. French network producers strike. Before the strike went on, we all regretted that the government had done nothing to seek an agreement or to conduct negotiations in order to prevent it.
Last Sunday, 2,000 letter carriers and postal employees, many of whom came from major centres of the country, met in Montreal. Newspapers have also announced that another large meeting called for the same purposes had been held in Winnipeg. I understand that the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) has said this afternoon that he had been invited to the meeting, but due to a previous appointment, was unable to attend. I do not know where he went, but there is no doubt that the invitation he had accepted was more important and was more directly related to his department than the one he received from the mail carriers. Anyway, we know that the Postmaster General, despite the invitation he had received, was

Business of the House not able to attend that meeting which seemed important, since more than 2,000 mail carriers attended it in Montreal.
